Trump denies US weapons shortage and says information 'leakers' being 'hunted down'

BBC News Thu, 06 Aug 2026 18:53:51 GMT

President Donald Trump has denied reports that the US is suffering a munitions shortage and vowed in a social media post to seek "long term jail sentences" for those suspected of leaking information.

"The U. S. has massive amounts of 'munitions,' especially of certain types," Trump posted on Thursday morning. "Additionally, large amounts are being manufactured and shipped to the US as needed."

Trump and the Pentagon face mounting questions about the state of the military's arsenal, with the war now in its sixth month and a peace deal remaining elusive.

Iran responded to reports of shrinking US supplies by saying its locally produced weapons gave it the ability to respond to "any threat".

"Each day, the signs of the enemy's diminishing capabilities become more apparent," Defence Minister Majid Ibn-e-Reza posted on X. "But our Armed Forces - backed by the nation's defence industry - are fully equipped to respond to any threat."

He added that "those who are now seeking to buy security and military superiority through imported systems will soon realise that Iran's indigenous technology is superior to any system in the region".

After the US spent vast quantities of difficult-to-manufacture weapons during the combat operation known as Operation Epic Fury and the tit-for-tat strikes since, the Trump administration has sought to assure Americans that the country's missile stockpiles remain robust.

CBS News, the BBC's US partner, reported the US has gone through much of its global stockpile of long-range precision missiles during the war, citing two unnamed sources with direct knowledge of the subject.

Meanwhile, the Washington Post reported on Wednesday evening that Trump had confronted Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth last week over a possible weapons shortfall, also citing unnamed sources. The BBC has not confirmed the report.

"The 'leakers' of these treasonous statements are being hunted down," Trump said in the post on Truth Social. "Long term jail sentences will be sought!"

He directly addressed the Washington Post's story in a later post, saying: "I really believe their fake 'reporting' is treasonous!"

"I am extremely happy with the job that Pete Hegseth is doing," he also posted.

Precise information on US missile stocks remains classified. Since becoming secretary, Hegseth has sought to put in place strict controls limiting the information that reporters can gather from the Pentagon, as well.

Using publicly available data, the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a national security think tank, estimated that by the end of July, the US had between 759 and 827 Patriot missiles left - about a third of the 2,330 available before the conflict began.

It also estimates the US has now used around 60% of terminal high altitude area defense (THAAD) missiles, which are deployed to intercept strikes, Mark Cancian, a retired Marine Corps colonel and senior adviser at CSIS, said on Wednesday.

The US is facing demand for its weapons beyond the conflict with Iran, which could also put a strain on supplies.

It has given Ukraine significant numbers of Patriot missiles since Russia invaded in 2022, but as US stocks shrink Cancian expects the Pentagon will hold onto them. At a cabinet meeting on Friday, Trump told reporters that granting Ukraine's recent request for additional Patriot missiles would be a "big step", but the two countries were "still talking about" it.

Many modern weapons have long funding, order, production, and delivery timelines, making it hard to swiftly replace munitions once they are used.

The administration has consistently stated the US has enough in its stockpile.

Trump told the Wall Street Journal last month: "We have far more munitions than anyone in the world, and far more than we need."

Hegseth, meanwhile, called reports of a stockpile shortage a "manufactured story" on a 14 June appearance on CBS' Face the Nation.

But the administration has also indicated it is ramping up production, with Hegseth saying the US was working quickly to manufacture more weapons.

Last month, he asked the US Senate for emergency funds totalling $87bn (£68bn) to pay service members and "rapidly replenish equipment and munitions."

Israel charges settler over killing of Palestinian involved in Oscar-winning West Bank film

BBC News Thu, 06 Aug 2026 18:37:12 GMT

Israeli prosecutors have charged a settler over the killing of a Palestinian activist in the occupied West Bank who helped film Oscar-winning documentary No Other Land.

Yinon Levy was charged with reckless manslaughter over the July 2025 shooting of Odeh Hathaleen, according to Israel's Southern District Prosecutor's Office.

Israeli rights group B'Tselem said it was the first time an Israeli had been indicted for killing a Palestinian in the West Bank for nearly three years.

A lawyer for Hathaleen's family said they hoped the charges marked a "turning point" in the consequences settlers face for violence against Palestinians.

In a letter seen by The Associated Press, Levy said he would fight for his innocence in court.

He wrote that prosecutors should not penalise acts of self-defence and accused them of providing "de facto support for terrorism", the news agency reported.

A lawyer for Levy, Avichai Hajbi, told the AP the prosecution had made a "mistaken decision".

The charges against Levy also include ​armed trespassing and malicious property damage during the incident in which settlers operated an excavator in the Palestinian village of Umm al-Khair, leading to a confrontation with residents.

According to the indictment, at some point during the confrontation Levy cocked his gun and fired in the direction of residents, hitting Hathaleen. He then fired another shot into the air, prosecutors said.

Footage of the incident was shared widely online. Levy has previously denied firing the shot that killed Hathaleen.

The indictment is the first since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attack on southern Israel which triggered the Gaza war and led to a rise in settler violence in the West Bank, B'Tselem said.

At least 1,110 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli soldiers and settlers in the West Bank since then, according to the UN. At least 41 Israelis have been killed either by a Palestinian armed group or civilian in the West Bank during the same period, the UN said.

B'Tselem described the decision to indict Levy as the "exception that proves the rule".

"The impunity Israel grants to soldiers and settlers who harm Palestinians is not a failure of the system - it is a central component of a policy designed to allow the violence to continue and escalate," it said.

Mattan Berner-Kadish, an Israeli-American activist who was at the scene, told the BBC: "I think the general reaction is happiness that anything is happening while also feeling that it should be a murder charge and a longer maximum sentence.

"Mixed feelings but also certainly pleasantly surprised and happy there might be consequences," he added.

Hathaleen, a teacher and father-of-three, was a prominent voice against settler violence in the occupied West Bank.

He featured in the 2025 Oscar-winning film No Other Land, that follows the legal fight between the Israeli government and Palestinians over Masafer Yatta, a West Bank community of about 20 villages.

Israel's Supreme Court ruled to allow the demolition of homes and expulsion of more than 1,000 villagers in 2022.

Levy, a leader of an outpost farm, was sanctioned by the UK in 2024 because he "used physical aggression, threatened families at gunpoint, and destroyed property as part of a targeted and calculated effort to displace Palestinian communities", the UK government said at the time.

He denied the allegations to the BBC in 2024.

He was also sanctioned by the US under the Biden administration but those sanctions were subsequently lifted under President Donald Trump.

Additional reporting by Mallory Moench

Wigan thrash Saints in opening Super Four game

BBC News Thu, 06 Aug 2026 18:27:53 GMT

Anna Davies is the joint leading try scorer in the 2026 Women's Super League

Betfred Women's Super League

St Helens (6) 6

Tries: McColm Goals: Gaskin

Wigan (22) 44

Tries: Derbyshire 2, Hunter 2, Davies, M Jones, Wilton, Foubister, Coleman Goals: Rowe 4

Wigan Warriors maintained their 100% record in 2026 as they comfortably saw off rivals St Helens in the first match of the new Super Four format.

It was a fifth successive win for them over Saints in the past 12 months, including a 54-6 demolition in the Challenge Cup final at Wembley, as they underlined why they are the team to beat in the Women's Super League.

The defending champions scored nine tries with two apiece for Ellise Derbyshire and Eva Hunter with further scores from Anna Davies, Molly Jones, Remi Wilton, Jenna Foubister and Mary Coleman at the BrewDog Stadium.

St Helens were outclassed on home turf and had only a Luci McColm try on the stroke of half-time on a difficult evening.

Whatever the format, though, there is no doubt that Wigan are the standard-bearers for the rest to catch.

They scored from their first set as a high kick into the sun on the last tackle was spilled by young Saints full-back Liv Leach and bounced invitingly for Derbyshire to score.

That was soon backed up by a fabulous individual try from Woman of Steel Hunter as she received the ball inside her own half and showed an irresistible combination of power, pace and sidestepping to score.

To make matters worse for Saints, Leach had to be carried off the field and by the 15th minute the contest was nearly over as Davies went over in the corner after a gorgeous kick over the top from Izzy Rowe.

Derbyshire and Hunter crossed for their second tries and only a poor conversion rate from Rowe prevented Wigan from being out of sight.

With this, Saints finally gained some possession and repeat sets and McColm went over just before the interval.

However, hopes of any kind of comeback never materialised as Jones' try on her first appearance of the season after a knee injury got Wigan moving again.

And the champions simply were too hot to handle in the final quarter as Wilton, Foubister and Coleman went over as Denis Betts' side picked up from where they had left off in their last match nearly four weeks ago.

This was the opening match in the new Super Four format introduced for the 2026 season.

After seven rounds of games, with all sides playing each other once, the league has been split into a top four and a bottom four although all points have been carried forward.

There are now six rounds of games over the next six weekends with home-and-away fixtures against the other three teams in their section in an attempt to have the best teams playing each other more often to increase competition and intensity.

So Wigan play Saints, Leeds Rhinos and York Valkyrie twice, with the side who finishes top at the end of that securing a direct place into the Grand Final, second and third having a play-off to decide who else reaches that game and fourth missing out completely.

Meanwhile in the Shield, for the sides from fifth to eighth after seven matches, the side finishing bottom at the end of the season will play the winners of the National Championship for the final remaining Super League spot in 2027.

Artificial Intelligence used to design brand new viruses

BBC News Thu, 06 Aug 2026 18:01:52 GMT

Artificial Intelligence has been used to design brand new viruses that are fully functional and can replicate in the laboratory, say US researchers.

It is the first time whole genomes have been successfully designed by AI.

The resulting 16 novel viruses were created to infect bacteria and pose no threat to people.

The breakthrough has been labelled a "very significant turning point" in science that could unlock a new era for treating disease. But experts have also warned AI-designed viruses raise "urgent" safety and security concerns.

AI tools are rapidly advancing and have already been used to design new antibiotics.

But that is relatively simple compared with designing a new viable virus from scratch.

"This is a next step in the complexity that's designable by generative AI, this is the first time generative AI has been used to design a complete genome, it's something that can replicate and have other functions inside cells… this was new territory for us," Brian Hie, assistant professor at Stanford University, told the BBC.

The technology works similarly to large language models, like ChatGPT, which predict sequences of text.

In this instance the AI models, known as Evo1 and Evo2, predict the language of life rather than words.

The AI models were trained on genetic codes from viruses, bacteria, plants and people.

They were then refined to produce a type of virus, known as a bacteriophage, which infect only specific species of bacteria.

The Stanford researchers picked the most promising 302 AI designs and synthesised them in the lab. Of these, 16 proved effective at killing E. coli bacteria.

Samuel King, a PhD student in the lab, said they realised the phage were working in the early hours of the morning.

The phage were placed on petri dishes growing a layer of bacteria on them and the scientists waited for signs their new viruses were enjoying the feast.

"We were starting to see these clear spots and it was just extremely exciting," says King. When the results were shared with the wider team "the room spontaneously burst into applause", Hie recalls.

Developing new phage could lead to new ways of treating infections that have become resistant to antibiotics.

But the breakthrough also points to the ability of AI to design new biology that goes beyond the natural world – what is known as synthetic biology.

Hie argues this has the potential to "massively improve human health" by developing new drugs and therapies.

But concerns have already been raised that the same technology could be used maliciously to create new diseases.

In a commentary accompanying the publication in the journal Science, Dr Thomas Inglesby and Dr Moritz Hanke from the Center for Health Security at Johns Hopkins University wrote that the findings raise "urgent biosafety and biosecurity questions".

They said it was no longer a question of "whether generative viral genome design will exist" but whether it can be used without "enabling serious harm".

For example, they said new viruses with the potential to cause disease "should not be pursued".

The researchers themselves took steps to maximise safety. They excluded viruses that could infect complex organisms from the training database, performed the research on phage rather than viruses that infect people and it all took place in a secure laboratory.

Hie argues even existing safeguards go a long way towards "ensuring that the technology is used for good".

Viruses are not alive and it would take another significant leap for AI to generate living organisms.

The genetic code of the phage is around 5,400 base pairs (letters) long. The smallest genome of a living cell is around 500,000 base pairs. The human genome is three billion base pairs.

Hie says "it would probably be a lot of work, but not impossible" to attempt some simple organisms and they were "definitely interested in working towards" that.

Prof Marc Güell, from the synthetic biology lab at Pompeu Fabra University in Spain, said the study was a "very significant turning point" because for the "first time in history, we are beginning to design biology on a computer".

He said it "allows us to dream of exciting possibilities for tackling humanity's greatest challenges" such as developing phages to tackle disease, enzymes to treat genetic disorders and antibodies that could be used in immunotherapy.

Prof Patrick Cai, chair of synthetic genomics at the Manchester Institute of Biotechnology, said the study was an "important milestone".

"The significance extends far beyond phages – it suggests that genome language models are beginning to learn the design principles encoded by evolution, opening the door to AI-assisted genome writing."

Le Court of AG Insurance-Soudal, who also crashed early on in the stage, was forced her to change bike just 15 km from the end.

Le Court, 30, had just enough performance left to launch a sprint with 300m to go, holding off French rider Cedrine Kerbaol on the line to seal victory, with Puck Pieterse of the Netherlands taking third place.

Movistar's Reusser retains the yellow jersey after the 153.4km ride from Montbrison to Tournon-sur-Rhone, holding a 12-second lead over Dutch rider Demi Vollering.

Friday's stage seven - the queen stage - on the nine-stage event is 146.8km from La Voulte-sur-Rhone to the summit finish at the famous Mont Ventoux in the French Alps.

This was Le Court's second stage victory in the Tour de France Femmes following her win in stage five last year from Chasseneuil-du-Poitou to Gueret.

Le Court said her team was "amazing" during her bike change, adding: "They brought me back slowly but surely to the bunch, and I got back on top of the [second-to] last climb, which was a really big effort.

"Then I just tried to stay patient and recover from this big effort.

"I had to close the gap myself and I was really, really dead, I was on the limit. I can't believe I still had the legs to sprint."

Calls for inquiry into Army teen college after reports of rape and abuse

BBC News Thu, 06 Aug 2026 17:42:27 GMT

Warning: This article contains sexual language and details of sexual assault

Calls are growing for an independent inquiry into an Army training college for teenagers following allegations of rape and sexual abuse against female recruits.

Four young women told the BBC they were sexually assaulted and harassed while attending the Army Foundation College (AFC) at Harrogate in North Yorkshire.

They described a culture of misogyny and sexual violence at the college, which they all attended when they were 17.

Sarah Atherton, former MP for Wrexham, told the BBC that public confidence in the college could "only be restored through an independent inquiry".

Emma Lewell MP said: "If this was any other school or residential environment for children, it would have been closed down."

Meanwhile, two Lib Dem MPs have written to Defence Secretary Wes Streeting calling for an independent inquiry into the "culture, leadership and safeguarding practices" at the college.

Atherton, who previously served in the Army's Intelligence Corps, led a 2021 government review into the experiences of women in the armed forces.

The review, which took evidence from over 4,200 women, reported cases of rape, sexual exploitation of under 18s, and women being drugged before being assaulted.

It concluded that women were being "denied justice" by a "woefully inadequate" military complaints process.

Speaking to the BBC on Thursday, Atherton said: "Concerns at AFC Harrogate were raised years ago, and subsequent data and complaints suggest the problems continued without adequate action".

An independent inquiry, she said, was "the best way to establish the facts, restore public confidence and ensure the Army can recruit and retain the talented young people it needs".

"Parents, staff and recruits deserve clear answers, accountability where necessary, and confidence that every possible lesson has been learned," she added.

Lewell, who sits on the Defence Committee, said: "I think as a matter of urgency there should be an independent inquiry into the college led by someone with significant safeguarding experience, and they need to be able to speak to the children there.

"There's been an ongoing complaints for a long time now around sexual assault, bullying, sexual abuse and physical abuse so it's a matter of urgency."

The letter to the defence secretary from the Lib Dems MPs was written by Tom Gordon, who represents Harrogate and Knaresborough, and James MacCleary, the party's defence spokesman.

They said "it is essential that the full facts are established openly and that meaningful action is taken to restore confidence".

"Such an inquiry should examine not only the specific allegations that have emerged, but also whether there are systemic barriers preventing victims from coming forward, whether existing reporting mechanisms are fit for purpose, and whether appropriate safeguarding arrangements are consistently being implemented," they add.

The Child Rights International Network, a human rights organisation, said it had been involved in documenting allegations at the college, adding the case for an independent inquiry was "urgent and essential".

The Army said "unacceptable and criminal behaviour has absolutely no place in our Armed Forces" as it called for victims and witnesses of criminal behaviour at the college to come forward.

It said several reforms had been introduced to support victims, including the Defence Serious Crime Command providing specialist support through the justice process - outside of the Army chain of command.

AFC is the largest military training establishment for under-19s in the UK and it receives all the Army's 16-year-old recruits.

North Yorkshire Police told the BBC in a response to a Freedom of Information Act request it had received 16 reports of sexual offences linked to the college in the year to June, including allegations of exposure, voyeurism and sexual assault.

No information was included on whether the reports had led to prosecutions.

A total of 176 complaints of inappropriate sexual behaviour at the college were made between January 2018 and June 2025, according to Ministry of Defence (MoD) data.

The women, whose names have been changed to protect their identities, all attended AFC over the last five years.

One woman, Tilly, told the BBC she was 17 when she was raped at AFC by several fellow soldiers who invited her into their room.

"They started taking my clothes off and then this led to them doing stuff I didn't consent to.

"And then I was raped… by multiple junior soldiers, same age as me. It went on for hours. I felt like a piece of meat."

Another woman's story was shared with the BBC by her mother, who said her daughter Amy was sexually assaulted and subjected to almost daily sexual harassment during her training.

Because the lock to Amy's room was not working, her mother said "she found herself sleeping across the door to stop male soldiers coming in".

Another woman, who said she was sexually assaulted and harassed at AFC, described how misogynistic attitudes and behaviour of AFC staff rubbed off on some of the male teenagers.

She recalled one of the instructors saying: "It's all about the pussy and how much of it you can get."

The MoD told the BBC that the college "welcomes external scrutiny and challenge".

It said that AFC had in the last year "hosted the safeguarding bodies, parliamentarians, the Children's Commissioner's office and the Armed Forces Commissioner, as well as receiving an outstanding report from Ofsted".

Ashleigh Percival-Borley, a veteran who served for 13 years in the British Army as a sergeant and multi-disciplinary instructor, said "incidents like this have "really taken my confidence out of the institution and that makes me really sad".

She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme there was a "level of frustration" from women who wanted to serve in the army.

She said hearing the allegations "sickened" her as a female veteran as well as a former instructor who knew "the embodiment of the army's values and standards" needed for the role.

The Children's Commissioner for England Dame Rachel de Souza said she would ensure the "appalling attacks" were investigated and "those responsible, including for failing to safeguard these girls, are held to account".

She said all children living away from home had a right to contact her team for support, and that she would make sure all girls at AFC could do so.

An MoD report last year found that 67% of women in the armed forces had experienced at least one sexualised behaviour in the previous 12 months, compared to 34% of men.

Last year, an ex-army sergeant major was jailed for six months for sexually assaulting a 19-year-old soldier, who later took her own life.

Warrant Officer Michael Webber, 43, pinned down Royal Artillery Gunner Jaysley Beck and tried to kiss her in July 2021. She was found dead five months later in her barracks at Larkhill, Wiltshire.

The inquest into her death ruled the sexual assault and the Army's failure to take appropriate action "more than minimally" contributed to her taking her life.

Jaysley's mother, Leighann McCready, told BBC Breakfast Jaysley was 19 when she reported what happened to her chain of command, but she was "disbelieved" and branded "a female trouble maker".

"This is the problem that soldiers are facing - what they are going to be branded afterwards," her mother said.

"If a junior solider can follow their policies and procedures then those above should do exactly the same. Had they had done, I believe our daughter would have still been alive", she added.

AFC remains committed to creating a professional, supportive, and safe environment for all recruits, the Army said.

It added: "Any suggestion otherwise contradicts the values of respect and inclusivity that we stand for."

South Korea space agency shares Moon images after SpaceX rocket debris crash

BBC News Thu, 06 Aug 2026 17:38:51 GMT

South Korea's space agency has released images that show the Moon after part of a SpaceX rocket crashed into its surface on Wednesday.

The Korean AeroSpace Administration (KASA) said lunar orbiter Danubri captured images after the impact, which it shared alongside photos of what the Moon's surface looked like before the crash.

Rocket debris struck the Moon at around 06:35 GMT on Wednesday, according to the South Korean space agency.

SpaceX has said the impact was not intentional.

Re-usable Falcon 9 rockets were designed to allow part of the rocket to return to Earth (the upper stage) and other sections to be shed in space. SpaceX has used this type of rocket on several missions.

The empty upper stage of this Falcon 9 rocket, which scientists predicted would hit the Moon at a speed of about 5,400mph (8,700km/h), is about the size of a five-storey building and weighs approximately 4,000kg (630st) on Earth.

The short, dramatic flash created when the rocket part hit the Moon would have been hard to catch by amateur astronomers even with high-end telescopes, but larger observatories - including Seoul's space agency - are analysing the information.

While the impact did not pose any danger to Earth, Matt Bothwell, astronomer at the University of Cambridge, raised concerns about space debris.

"Space is getting more and more crowded," he said, as each year "we launch more stuff into space".

"It could feasibly be within a few decades that it's actually quite hard to get past Earth's orbit because space is so crowded," Bothwell warned.

This Falcon 9 was in orbit since January last year, when it blasted off from Florida.

The same booster section from the January 2025 mission is due to set off on its 18th flight on 10 August. SpaceX says the mission hopes to launch 29 Starlink satellites to low-Earth orbit.

The rocket that blasted from Florida last January was carrying two lunar landers into space.

Its job was to fire the upper stage hard enough to send both of the landers out of Earth's orbit and onto a path towards the Moon.

The spent stage was left drifting in a long, looping orbit that swung out towards the Moon and back again.

Over the next 18 months, the gentle gravitational tug of the Earth, Moon and Sun, along with light from the Sun, gave it a faint push.

Astronomers tracking the rocket part eventually worked out that those small nudges had put it on a course towards the Moon, and it was picking up speed every day.

The impact on Wednesday happened in broad daylight for many parts of the world, but the tiny flash it produced would have been far too faint to see, even through a telescope.

Thousands of migrants still in Ceuta after border crisis, local leader says

BBC News Thu, 06 Aug 2026 17:36:07 GMT

Between 3,000 and 5,000 migrants remain in the Spanish territory of Ceuta following the arrival of many times that number of people last week, the north African exclave's leader has said.

Juan Jesús Vivas told the European Parliament of his "profound sorrow" over the "irreparable tragedy" of 100 deaths that had occurred after roughly 78,000 migrants from neighbouring Morocco arrived by sea in a matter of hours.

His comments come as new calls for mass crossings circulate on social media, according to Moroccan media.

The crisis has created tensions among EU nations who share open borders and has sparked criticism of the Spanish government.

However the EU Commission has commended Spain's "swift response" to the crisis, which has included deploying armed forces to Ceuta and its other territory on the north African coast, Melilla.

Vivas, a conservative, was critical of the national government's response while addressing the European Parliament on Thursday, saying that he had personally told Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez that it had been late and insufficient.

"The fact that we don't have numbers on how many are still in Ceuta shows how few resources we have to deal with this situation," Ceuta's mayor-president said. Previous warnings by local officials of an increase in migrant crossings by sea had been ignored, he said.

Vivas said that while the return of nearly 75,000 migrants to Morocco had "considerably alleviated" the situation, Ceuta had not yet returned to normal.

There was still a humanitarian emergency and disturbances to public order in the territory, he said, while it was "basically impossible" to return the minors who had crossed because this required their consent.

Spain's interior minister has said the government had allocated €25m (£21.4m; $28.8m) to assist minors in Ceuta.

However, Spanish newspaper El Mundo reports that 4,860 migrant children have been registered by volunteer groups in Ceuta - double official estimates.

"Neighbours are taking them into their homes, but the situation is unsustainable," a volunteer told the paper.

So far no migrant children have been moved to mainland Spain, with right-wing local authorities reluctant to take them in, according to El País.

While some on the right have pointed to an agreement with Morocco stipulating co-operation on returning migrant children to their families, Melilla's conservative leader has called for a "gesture of solidarity" from his mainland colleagues.

It is unclear exactly why tens of thousands of migrants attempted to cross into Ceuta on Thursday and Friday last week.

The EU's Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner has suggested criminal networks spreading disinformation were to blame - an assertion Sánchez has agreed with.

The crossings came after Spain's Supreme Court ruled that migrants stopped at sea while trying to reach Ceuta or Melilla cannot be summarily returned to Morocco.

The two exclaves have long been a bone of diplomatic contention between Spain and Morocco, which does not recognise Spanish sovereignty over them.

The number of people swimming to Ceuta at once has raised questions about why Morocco's border guards did not attempt to stop them. Vivas characterised the incident as an "unequivocal attack".

"Our people feel sad, helpless, anxious, fearful and worried - and they have good reason to, because it is inevitable to wonder whether this will happen again," he commented.

Spain's interior minister has said he was working "firmly" with Morocco to avoid further "violations", and that any migrants still in Ceuta would be returned there as soon as possible.

Brunner said the EU should use all the leverage at its disposal, including visa policy and trade, to secure co-operation from Morocco on migration.

Morocco, for its part, has laid blame for the crisis on Spain's Supreme Court, with an unnamed government source briefing local outlets that "the deterrent element of the system collapsed and the dam gave way, not under the weight of the criminals, but of a judge's decision".

Meanwhile, Moroccan media is reporting fresh online calls to co-ordinate another mass border-crossing attempt, similar to what was seen before the influx last week.

News site Hespress reports that posts and messages were circulating on social media to join closed WhatsApp groups, along with hashtags linked to migration to Spain and work opportunities there - despite warnings from Moroccan authorities that people promoting irregular migration could face prosecution.

The Ceuta crossings have also caused a diplomatic rift among EU nations that share open borders as part of the Schengen area.

Italy suspended its Schengen arrangement with Spain, backed by Finland and Denmark, while the Czech Republic called for Spain's membership to be temporarily suspended - despite Sánchez noting Ceuta was not part of the Schengen area.

Brunner said the EU was "ready to do more" in Ceuta but had not received a further request for EU border guards from the Spanish government.

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor said he came face-to-face with an alleged stalker wearing a balaclava who chased after him in a confrontation close to his Sandringham home in Norfolk, a court heard.

Alex Jenkinson, 39, from Stowmarket, Suffolk, is accused of causing the former duke to "fear unlawful violence" during an encounter as he walked his dogs on 6 May. Suffolk Police is applying for a civil Stalking Protection Order against Jenkinson.

The trial is expected to begin on 21 December.

Deputy Chief Magistrate Tan Ikram read out parts of the statement in which Mountbatten-Windsor said he spotted a car which he assumed belonged to press photographers, and then he and his security detail "drove past the car".

He said a man "turned and faced me – he was wearing a balaclava face covering".

He provided a description of the "out-of-place" man, and added in his statement: "I then saw a loose dog running towards him.

"Then he realised who I was and began to sprint after my vehicle."

The court hearing took place in Jenkinson's absence as he was blocked from the building after arriving with his dog.

The defendant's lawyer, Claire Howell, told Judge Ikram the dog was her client's support animal, as he has ADHD, was homeless and needed his dog with him.

She conceded that she has no documents to prove Jenkinson's medical condition, or his need for a support animal.

Jenkinson denies the public order offence against Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor and has also pleaded not guilty to a further charge of using threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour with intent to cause fear or provoke unlawful violence against another man, Stephen Terry, in King's Lynn, on 5 May.

Boxer charged with killing aid worker in Athens after his wife gave police 'key' details

BBC News Thu, 06 Aug 2026 17:26:56 GMT

An Afghan boxer was accused of killing a Scottish aid worker in Greece after his wife gave "key" details to police, the BBC has been told.

Sharif Ahmadzai, 26, has been charged with homicide with intent – equivalent to a murder charge in Scots law - alongside robbery and weapons offences.

The body of Elisabeth Ross, who was 38, was discovered in a suitcase by a homeless man in a derelict building in the Kypseli area of Athens on 18 July.

Ahmadzai's wife, Alaina Hall, is said to have given information to police, including location data which placed her husband and Ross at the same apartment on 15 July – the day Ross is thought to have been killed.

Appearing in court earlier, Ahmadzai asked for an English translator but did not respond to the charges.

His lawyer, Christos Erdas, said his client had exercised his right to remain silent, and that his rights had been "violated" through leaks of evidence and documents from the case file - including his right to the presumption of innocence.

The lawyer said that when Ross was found, she had no injuries and any apparent cause of death was "entirely absent".

He said his client wanted the forensic medical report and the "toxicological and histological examinations of the deceased" to be included in the case file.

Erdas added: "His [Ahmadzai's] stance towards the prosecuting and investigating authorities did not constitute a stance of denial but, on the contrary, one of reservation, so that he may present his defence in full once the case file has been completed with the above essential documents – which were not sought by the preliminary investigating authorities – with the sole aim of establishing the substantive truth for both sides."

Ahmadzai was remanded in custody until his trial, which could take up to 18 months.

Ahmadzai was initially detained on illegal weapons possession charges and is facing a charge of homicide with intent, as well as allegations that he stole more than €10,000 (£8,500) from the victim's bank accounts using her bank cards.

The police union in Greece said that initially, the coroner's report cited an undetermined cause of death, as the body showed no signs of external trauma.

It said following a more detailed investigation, autopsy and post-mortem examination, "asphyxiation was listed as the probable cause of death".

The union has now told the BBC that officers arrested the accused after his wife provided them with "key" and "decisive" details.

Officers involved with the case said these details included sharing a location-tracking app, which placed both Ahmadzai and Ross at the same apartment.

Hall, who has a child with Ahmadzai, told police that she and her husband met Elisabeth – known as Lisa - while volunteering for a refugee charity in Athens in February 2026.

She described the victim as a "very pleasant and sweet person, kind-hearted, with a good soul".

Hall claimed that after the three had gone on a walk, her husband remained in touch with Ross for several days. The aid worker is believed to have asked Ahmadzai to help deliver bibles.

Court documents claim that on 15 July, Hall said she saw a text message sent from Ross to Ahmadzai which read: "Thank you for your intention to come with me."

Hall claimed in a statement that she awoke later that night to find that her husband had left their home without warning.

She is quoted as saying: "I checked his location on my cell phone. I saw that he was inside the apartment on Rethymno Street.

"I was surprised because there was no particular reason for him to be there at that time."

She claimed her husband told her that he was watching football at a café and headed to the apartment to use the toilet – which she initially believed but no longer did.

Hall said that in the days that followed, her husband appeared to be particularly upset, blaming the death of a relative in India. She said he suggested they leave the city unexpectedly.

She said after this, her husband appeared to be happy once again, bought her a new iPhone 17 Pro and later gave her €2,550 (£2,180). Hall said he could not "convincingly" explain where this money came from.

When news broke that a woman had been found dead inside a suitcase close to where the couple lived, Hall said she woke up in the middle of the night on 29 July and thought it could be Ross.

She told investigators that after messaging the aid worker, the replies "were not in Lisa's style both in terms of her level of English and the use of emojis that she never used". She said this prompted her to become concerned that Ross could be the woman in the suitcase.

She told police: "All of the above made me feel strange. Especially combining the dates, the messages and my husband's behaviour.

"I have various thoughts that make me feel uncomfortable."

After the body was identified, Hall said she received threatening messages with photos of herself and her baby. She told police she became so afraid that she and Ahmadzai left their home and spent the night in different places.

The BBC has been told Ahmadzai denies homicide with intent but admits moving the body, claiming that he did so because he feared he would be blamed for her death.

A statement from the police's organised crime directorate said Ahmadzai was brought to a police station on 30 July.

"In particular, it emerged that the 26-year-old placed the body in a suitcase and transported it to the abandoned site," the statement said.

Ahmadzai is accused of killing Ross, then sending a series of messages from her phone to her friends and family before switching off the device.

Greek newspapers Proto Thema and Ta Nea have reported that he bought a phone and texted Ross's friends in Athens, impersonating an unnamed jihadist saying he had killed the Scot because of her religion.

The newspapers reported his wife told the police she suspected her husband's involvement in the killing when she woke up to find he was not in their apartment and tracked his phone to where Ross was staying.

Police said Ross - who is from Edinburgh and is known to family and friends as Lisa - had been volunteering with a refugee support group based in Athens.

She arrived in Greece on 26 June and stayed in the Keratsini area of Piraeus until 10 July.

Ross is believed to have died a number of days before she was found.

Greek officials contacted Interpol and American authorities were able to identify her fingerprints.

The investigation was carried out by Greece's organised crime directorate.

Additional reporting by Daphne Toli in Athens and Georgina Hayes.

Judge grants Trump's request to delay handing financial records to BBC

BBC News Thu, 06 Aug 2026 16:49:51 GMT

A judge has granted Donald Trump's request to delay handing over financial records to the BBC as part of his $10bn (£7.4bn) lawsuit against the broadcaster.

The US president is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the 2021 Capitol riots.

The BBC has asked for some of Trump's financial records in relation to his argument that the documentary damaged the president's business interests.

A judge granted that request in July and the first documents were due to be filed on Thursday, but another judge has now agreed to an emergency motion filed by Trump's lawyers earlier this week to pause the disclosure.

The president's legal team said disclosure of the financial records would cause him "irreparable harm".

They argued that no such revelations should be made until the court rules on an objection to the order requiring the disclosure.

Trump has also recently asked to amend his main case, which his lawyers said would make the document release unnecessary.

The president has asked for his central complaint against the BBC to be amended so it no longer claims the documentary damaged his brands and businesses. His lawyers have asked that the case is amended to claim for damages for "the reputational injury to the President, full stop".

In a ruling on Thursday, the judge said the order for financial information disclosure would be paused until the amendment question is resolved.

The BBC had said Trump's request for a delay to disclosure was "a transparent effort to evade this court's clear and direct order and to continue to avoid the discovery obligations that the plaintiff took on when he chose to file this lawsuit".

"In fact, this is just the latest in [Trump's] months-long refusal to provide documents, sworn answers to interrogatories, deposition dates, any meaningful information to support his pursuit of $10bn from the BBC for a documentary the BBC never aired in the United States."

Trump's lawsuit - filed in Florida - accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously, and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave outside the Capitol on 6 January 2021.

The BBC has apologised for an editing error that gave "the mistaken impression that President Trump had made a direct call for violent action".

However, the BBC has asked the court to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that the programme doesn't meet the legal criteria for defamation and wasn't made available on its US platforms.

Last month, Trump's lawyers admitted they had no evidence that the documentary was available in the US on the BBC's BritBox subscription service, as they had originally claimed, or on BBC. com, BBC Select or through US broadcasters.

Trump also recently agreed to drop the BBC's commercial arm BBC Studios from his lawsuit, after the BBC argued the company had "no role in creating or producing the documentary".

BBC News Thu, 06 Aug 2026 16:38:03 GMT

Reality TV contestant Stephen Bear is back in prison after admitting breaching a restraining order that banned him from posting online about ex-partner Georgia Harrison.

The order was imposed when Bear was jailed in 2023 after he filmed and shared a video of the pair having sex on OnlyFans and WhatsApp without Harrison's knowledge.

The 36-year-old was told not to post or incite comments on social media about that case or Harrison but did so multiple times in 2025 while she was pregnant.

In a statement read to Chelmsford Crown Court, the Love Island star and campaigner said Bear's online presence left her "feeling petrified" and she feared for her safety. He was jailed for 16 months.

Bear, of Walthamstow, east London, admitted the charge of harassment – breaching of a restraining order, at a previous hearing in June.

Judge Christopher Morgan, who presided over the original trial in 2023, said Bear's posts and videos in 2025 were "to ensure the maximum harm [was] caused to Georgia Harrison".

"You knew all of that was untrue, and yet you posted it," he said.

"You left Miss Harrison, I'm afraid, at the mercy of any individual who had aligned themselves with your lies."

In addition to the prison sentence, the judge extended the restraining order to stop Bear from contacting Harrison's mother and her friend, which remains in place until a new order is imposed.

After serving half his original sentence, Bear was released from prison, but between 1 March 2025 and 21 July 2025 began posting on Instagram, TikTok, X, YouTube and Facebook about the case and Harrison.

The court heard these were "consistently posted messages of the most abhorrent and harmful type".

Addressing Bear, the judge said: "What you did in that three to four-month period is simply victim-blaming."

Harrison did not attend court, but the prosecution read out a statement in which she described feeling isolated, exposed and unsafe, and asked for the restraining order to be extended.

She said the significant stress had made her worry about her unborn child and caused her to "spiral" on some occasions.

"I shut him out of my mind for a long time and it's not fair that he's managed to crawl his way back in," she said.

Bear arrived for Thursday's sentencing with his wife, who is eight months pregnant.

As he walked in to court, he refused to answer questions but gave a thumbs-up and said: "Wish me luck guys. See you soon, hopefully."

As his barrister spoke about why there should be a reduced sentence, Bear appeared to briefly cry.

He shook his head as he was taken away to begin another prison term.

Senior crown prosecutor Andrew Young said Bear "used his platforms to amplify abuse and encourage others to target" Harrison.

The Crown Prosecution Service said Bear had looked to cast doubt on his convictions, including by alleging Harrison and her mother had conspired to pervert the course of justice.

He also created an online petition seeking support for a retrial.

Young added: "No woman should be made to live in fear because someone refuses to accept the restrictions placed on them by a court."

In a separate statement released through Essex Police following sentencing, Harrison said she was grateful to the force because it "took me seriously when so many women in my position are overlooked".

"They treated this as the serious crime it is – not a celebrity story. It is a real offence against a real person," she said.

"They built the case properly, they stayed with it, and when the order was breached, they acted instead of shrugging. From the messages I get every day, I know how rare that still is.

"If every force treated this the way Essex Police did, thousands of women would feel safer today."

No-frills airline EasyJet has agreed to be taken over in a £5.7bn deal by US firm Apollo after a rival bidder dropped out.

The takeover was agreed after US investment firm Castlelake, which had made a series of offers for the carrier, said it was withdrawing from the bid battle.

Apollo said it wants to help the airline grow and that it does not intend to cut any jobs in the first 12 months after the takeover has been completed, implying that passengers can expect largely the same service.

EasyJet is one of Europe's largest airlines. It employs more than 19,000 people, and flies around 1,200 routes across 35 European countries.

It was founded by Sir Stelios Haji-Ioannou in 1995 to offer cheap air fares to Europe from the UK. Its first flights took off in November 1995 flying from Luton to Glasgow and Edinburgh, with its first international flights the following year.

Sir Stelios and his family still own around 15% of the business, and he said he supported Apollo's plans for the airline "to create more growth".

"My family and I intend to remain invested as long-term major shareholders of EasyJet for the next chapter in the company's journey," he said in a statement.

The future ownership of EasyJet has been uncertain since it emerged in late May that Castlelake was considering a bid for the airline.

Castlelake made a number of approaches for EasyJet, which were rebuffed initially after the carrier accused the US firm of trying to buy it "on the cheap".

In early July, EasyJet and Castlelake said they had agreed a deal in principle, but then Apollo - which owns Wagamama parent The Restaurant Group - swooped in with a higher bid.

Under the offer from Apollo, EasyJet shareholders will receive £7.15 per share.

AJ Bell's head of financial analysis, Danni Hewson said while the offer was significantly above where the company's shares were trading before the Iran war, the figure was "still woefully short of the company's pre-pandemic highs".

Apollo said it was "highly supportive" of the airline's existing strategy, adding there was "a significant opportunity to accelerate the operational and commercial ambitions" for the EasyJet Group.

"EasyJet is a leader in European aviation, having built a differentiated market position through its compelling customer proposition, expansive network and strong brand," said Alex van Hoek, partner and European private equity lead at Apollo.

EasyJet chief executive Kenton Jarvis said "We welcome Apollo's commitment to our business and our people, and believe that its experience in the aviation sector makes it a strong partner for EasyJet."

The deal will still need to win approval from regulators, including in the EU where rules mean EasyJet's owners will have to be majority EU-based.

Apollo anticipates this can be achieved by making the Haji-Ioannou family, and other EU-based shareholders, owners of around half of the business.

Apollo said though it does not intend to cut any staff for at least 12 months after the deal goes through, if the deal completes and EasyJet delists from the stock exchange to become a private company, some jobs related to maintaining its public-listed operations could go.

The firm said that would be a "limited number of roles in specific areas."

AJ Bell's Hewson said the potential loss of another well-known name from London markets will be seen as a blow.

"Air travel might not be as sexy as space travel, but retail investors understand it and names like EasyJet can't easily be replaced," she said.

Uefa says boycott may still go ahead as FA withdraws Infantino support

BBC News Thu, 06 Aug 2026 16:11:30 GMT

Gianni Infantino apologised following a Fifa executive meeting in Morocco on Wednesday

European teams could still boycott competitions including the World Cup as Uefa says Fifa's defence of its president Gianni Infantino "changes nothing".

The English FA has sent a letter withdrawing its support for Infantino in reaction to the plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

European governing body Uefa said in a statement its conditions had not been met, despite Infantino's plan being aborted.

"First, the proposals to sell off the major competitions had to be withdrawn and secondly," Uefa's statement said. "Assurances have to be made that such attempts to disfigure the game in this way will never be made again.

"These conditions have not been met."

Uefa has already said it has lost confidence in Infantino, calling the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal a "shabby, back room, opaque deal".

Infantino sorry for errors but stays Fifa president

If Infantino goes, who might replace him as Fifa president?

Infantino had offered all associations $40m (£30m) if they backed a proposal for private investment in its tournaments, including the men's and women's World Cups, through the FFE subsidiary.

World governing body Fifa said during Wednesday's meeting "mistakes" regarding FFE were "acknowledged", saying it was "not the intention" for the Fifa Council and members association to "feel excluded from the process and that the process should have been handled differently".

Uefa's statement in response added: "Uefa made it abundantly clear in its statement on Saturday that it has lost confidence in Gianni Infantino's presidency. That position holds.

"Yesterday's announcement that some people employed by the Fifa president (and whose careers depend on his favour) agree with him changes nothing."

Fifa has been approached for comment.

Infantino arrived at Fifa's offices in Rabat, Morocco on Wednesday in now-familiar fashion, chauffeured to the building in a motorcade, sitting in the back of a Mercedes with blacked out windows.

Some questioned whether he would still be the Fifa president when he left.

Yet if anything, on the surface at least, Infantino appears emboldened.

This was not the 56-year-old being ordered to a hearing to explain his actions.

It was Infantino who summoned members of the Fifa management board to sit around the table with him, to talk through the events of the last week.

Secretary general Mattias Grafstrom, Infantino's right-hand man, had been critical in an internal memo to staff, calling the FFE proposals "a sad and reproachable series of events".

After the meeting finished it appeared to be water under the bridge, with Infantino and Grafstrom pictured sat next to each other and smiling at a Women's Africa Cup of Nations match between Malawi and Zambia.

If there were clear-the-air talks, they appear to have worked.

Other members of the Fifa management board to attend the meeting included finance chief Thomas Peyer, legal chief Emilio Garcia Silvero, chief of staff Daniel O'Toole, chief of member associations Elkhan Mammadov and media relations director Bryan Swanson.

BBC Sport has been told that Fifa's chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, was not invited.

Lamour strongly criticised Infantino's FFE plan, saying it was "the project of one person", and "the time has now come for football's political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions".

He added: "I lose my job, then so be it. At least I'll sleep well tonight."

Lamour has declined to comment to the BBC. Fifa has been approached for comment.

What concerns Uefa is that this meeting was a gathering of employees who are themselves part of the regime.

It is unknown if Infantino was forced to answer difficult questions about his plan. Questions such as: who was involved? Whether there was a competitive tender process? And if he stood to benefit personally?

While Fifa said "mistakes made were acknowledged" and an "apology was made", there was no direct accountability for the controversy.

Uefa still wants answers to those key questions and will not be content until it gets them - or Infantino leaves.

This video can not be played

Why Uefa could still boycott the World Cup

Uefa is in something of a pickle as it tries to get rid of Infantino.

The easiest route to success was the slow turning of the vice throughout this week, hoping to exert enough pressure to force him to quit.

Yet the Swiss appears to have no intention of walking away.

European football looks like an outlier, struggling to gain enough support to topple him.

On Thursday, Lamin Kaba Bajo, the president of the Gambia Football Federation, praised Infantino's "courage" and for the U-turn, and said he was "willing to give him my support more than ever".

Only Jordan, one of the few countries which did not back Infantino before last week, has publicly stated it will not vote for his re-election in March.

Concacaf, which oversees football in North and Central America and the Caribbean, also issued a public statement after the proposal was aborted but, unlike Uefa, it did not go as far as to say it had lost confidence in the Fifa president.

Conmebol, the South American confederation, said on Thursday it would not support "any action or procedure that disregards" Fifa's mechanisms before the presidential election.

The Confederation of African Football (Caf) said its executive committee "unanimously reconfirmed" its support for Infantino and thanked him for his support for African football over the years.

Ideally, Uefa would force an emergency meeting of the Fifa Council, to provide what it would consider to be a true chance to hold Infantino to account.

But getting the necessary 19 of 36 confederation and football association heads to support it has proven to be exceptionally difficult.

Uefa has also kept on the table the option of a vote of no confidence, which it can trigger via an extraordinary congress any time it wishes.

However, it would need a majority of Fifa's 211 member associations - 106 votes - to pass the motion. It would be a de facto presidential election without a second candidate.

If Uefa does not think it can get to 106, which looks a stretch, then there is little point in triggering the vote.

The other option is to try to find a unity candidate to stand against Infantino in the election next March. The favourite would be Concacaf president Victor Montagliani.

Any option which takes time gives Infantino space to build bridges, and with Fifa due to announce new funding to member associations by the end of the year he could dangle another carrot for his re-election.

Unless Uefa sticks by the nuclear option - and goes through with its threat of a boycott.

This has issues, and it is not a lever you can pull very often, otherwise it gives the impression of riding roughshod over the rest of the world.

It is one thing to use it to jettison the FFE proposal, another entirely to effectively dethrone the president with it.

Uefa's stance will soon be tested, with the Fifa Women's U20s World Cup kicking off in Poland on 5 September. Six European countries are due to take part, including England.

Some at the European confederation claim Wednesday's statement shows exactly why the beleaguered president must step down.

The feeling within Uefa is that the statement was far from representative of the entire world governing body, and that there has been a lack of consultation with the council or membership.

There is also a view that Infantino is trying to swerve personal responsibility by sharing out the blame for the aborted proposals, and that he alone should have apologised - rather than issue his expression of regret alongside his deputy Grafstrom.

In stark contrast, within Fifa, the view from one Infantino loyalist is that the outcry, especially in Europe, is bordering on "hysteria", and fails to acknowledge the legitimacy he has globally.

By clinging to power, Infantino has mounted the start of an attempted fightback. But it could yet fuel the revolt against him, both from outside and within Fifa. And it looks increasingly likely his opponents will have to identity the rival candidate that could challenge him at next year's presidential election.

First OpenAI, now Meta - why do AI hacks keep happening?

BBC News Thu, 06 Aug 2026 15:59:34 GMT

Over the last fortnight, reports of AI models going beyond their expected bounds - be that technically or morally - have been seemingly unavoidable.

What started with a trickle - ChatGPT-maker OpenAI admitting their AI had hacked the site Hugging Face - has turned into a flood of groups revealing they had discovered instances of AI going out of control.

Claude-maker Anthropic, Meta and the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) have now each reported incidents which seem to paint a worrying picture of a world in which tech going rogue is the norm.

In reality, each case offers a window into the risks posed by increasingly capable AI agents - and the importance of testing their limits before they are released to the world.

The OpenAI incident has, as Hugging Face's co-founder Thomas Wolf described it, come as a "wake-up call" for the tech industry since it happened at the end of July.

It was a big moment which caused big companies to reflect on their own systems - and, in some cases, check they hadn't missed something similarly shocking.

Anthropic was the first to act. On Friday, the company found three instances out of thousands where its model Claude had managed to gain access to the internet.

Then on Tuesday, the AISI, the UK government agency which evaluates cutting-edge models, then said it had detected a "security incident" during a routine evaluation.

It had been testing models by both OpenAI and Anthropic, and found they too tried to carry out cyber-attacks - calling for "scrutiny, transparency, and action".

Finally followed Meta, which revealed one of its AI models had inadvertently been allowed to access the internet due to a "misconfiguration" during a third-party test.

In disclosing the incident, it is following in the footsteps of those before it.

Before AI models are released to the public, they are put to the test in a series of internal and external evaluations.

The aim is to figure out their potential to do good or bad, as well has how they perform in benchmarks measuring their skills.

These typically take place in what are known as "sandboxes". These are protected spaces designed to mirror real systems - but with strict guardrails in place.

In the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident, the AI attacked the sandbox itself, finding a vulnerability which let it access the internet and "go rogue".

Meanwhile the AISI said its own incident, which saw two powerful AI tools create fake human profiles to try and trick people in attempted cyber-attacks, was not down to an issue with the sandbox.

Instead, it was due to how it went about its tests.

The models it tested were granted access to the internet, and the AISI also disabled in-built filters that would usually block dangerous cyber-attacks.

"To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour," it said, while noting its unexpected "signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours".

Prof Alan Woodward, professor of cyber-security at the University of Surrey, said these cases - while distinct in what happened and why - tell an important story.

"For 30 years, one rule of software testing held firm: whatever happens in the test environment stays in the test environment," he said.

"In the past month, that rule has been broken three times."

"One model broke out. One walked through a door left open by mistake. One was deliberately given the keys so testers could measure what it would do."

He said these were different causes, but they had the same lesson - "the testing lab is now where the risk lives".

He told the BBC that as models become more capable, more must be done to secure the environments where they are tested.

"Testing an AI agent is less like checking code and more like handling a hazardous material: sealed rooms, constant monitoring of what leaves the building, a rehearsed containment plan," he said.

"AISI contained its incident within an hour. The next organisation may not."

For those developing AI tools which are designed to take actions on a person's behalf, there is a careful balance to be struck between harnessing their benefits and exposing their risks.

The benefit is significant. In theory, we could be able to liberate ourselves of dull, menial tasks, such as replying to emails, going to meetings or managing calendars and diaries, by delegating these to capable bots.

The downside is that with great power comes great responsibility, and risk.

It's something particularly realised when handing power to tools which are not, like us, able to bring a range of values, context and understanding to decisions we made.

"Recent incidents of frontier AI models carrying out unsanctioned actions and, in some cases, human-like deceptive behaviour on the open internet are a serious reminder of the risks AI capabilities pose," said Ollie Whitehouse, the National Cyber Security Centre's chief technology officer on Tuesday.

Some believe the sheer volume of tasks that will be handled by these tools will mean human oversight might not be enough to contain the problem of models going rogue.

But in the meantime, many feel strengthening oversight overall is vital if development continues at its same, frenzied pace.

It is unlikely Meta will be the last to emerge with findings of models showing they have, as Prof Woodward puts it, "gone to school" - and learnt our own ways of finding and exploiting gaps in systems.

For some, these episodes point to clear security failures on the part of AI companies leading the charge on this game-changing, era-defining tech.

For others, they are merely another vehicle for tech firms to hype up their powerful models and compete with rivals.

For me, both theories hold some grain of truth.

But in rearing their head one after another, these events have nonetheless spurred fears about AI's capabilities and where these are headed as developers forge ahead.

And the question inevitably moves to what regulators can and should do next.

Michael Birtwistle, associate director at the Ada Lovelace Institute, makes the point that the UK lacks legal incentives for AI firms to prevent systems from developing capabilities which could pose dangers, and that there are no repercussions if testing protocols fail.

More broadly, Dr Imogen Stead, AI policy manager at the Centre for Long-Term Resilience, told the BBC that with opportunities to test frontier AI systems narrowing for many, governments should follow the UK in setting up dedicated institutes for testing.

Improving third-party evaluations with initiatives such as a "trusted tester scheme" for the most risky types of challenges could also be used to limit adverse impacts, she said.

Rather than fear an AI-cyber apocalypse in the meantime, Prof Woodward says, "it's a case of 'keep calm and fix stuff'".

Additional reporting by Philippa Wain and Imran Rahman-Jones

Serious questions for Cambridge after professor at centre of plagiarism row resigns

BBC News Thu, 06 Aug 2026 15:08:05 GMT

The University of Cambridge is facing serious questions about its academic standards and push for diversity after its youngest black professor resigned amid allegations of copying other academics' research.

Jason Arday's appointment in 2023 was hailed at the time as a progressive moment. Now, Cambridge says it has launched an investigation after "new information" emerged about his academic qualifications and honorary appointments.

There are two fundamental questions for the university.

Did it fail to adequately check Arday's credentials when appointing him, and did it defend that decision because of an institutional push to position itself as more diverse?

For one of the world's leading universities known for academic excellence and globally significant research, this is about its institutional culture and decision-making at the highest level.

The biggest reputational risk surrounds the accusations of academic plagiarism now under investigation - and denied by Arday - because they get to the heart of what a university is about.

The University of Cambridge uses the common definition of plagiarism as "passing off someone else's work as if it were your own without appropriate acknowledgement".

There is no allegation more serious that can be levelled at an academic.

One of the fundamental purposes of a research-led university is the creation of knowledge through original thinking, insights and inquiry.

The quality of this is the foundation of Cambridge's reputation, and a source of significant funding.

Arday did not start his university journey at an elite institution.

He has a degree from the University of Surrey in education studies and physical education, a master's from St Mary's University in London, and a PhD in education awarded by Liverpool John Moores University.

The reason the PhD has attracted so much attention is because it is the first major piece of original research anyone wanting a career as an academic must complete.

Arday's critics claim that his work relied on copying other academics without properly crediting their work from the outset, which he denies.

He went on to become an associate professor at Durham University and professor of sociology of education at the University of Glasgow.

In other words, there is a line of institutions behind Cambridge now facing similar questions about their appointment processes.

The entire higher education system relies on accepting the qualifications awarded by another institution in good faith. Regulation and standards are meant to create a common currency.

That has now unravelled with what began as a blog a couple of years ago escalating in recent weeks, with more journalists unpicking aspects of Arday's life story and asking questions.

It is at this point Cambridge faces questions about whether it was defending its own reputation as much as an individual academic.

Just a couple of weeks ago, the university was briefing journalists that this was a campaign against a black academic, its appointment system was rigorous, and it would be robustly defended.

So why might Cambridge have had a blind spot that delayed an investigation which could settle the matter?

The university has spent the last decade working to redress the perception that the institution is a bastion of affluent white privilege.

Roger Mosey, the former master of the university's Selwyn College, said Arday's academic background was "unconventional" for a Cambridge professor, but that his life story as an autistic man who said he could not read until he was 18 was what had seemingly "made him a compelling candidate".

Equality, diversity and inclusion are reasonable goals for a leading university, Mosey wrote in the Times, but risk becoming contentious "when they are baked into inflexible policies and questionable appointment processes".

Part of the answer may also lie in how black academics feel in general as part of a tiny minority in the wider university community.

In the last academic year, only 75 of Cambridge's 6,180 academics at all levels were identified as black, according to the Higher Education Statistics Authority (HESA).

If you look at professors across the UK, 270 are identified as black out of a total of more than 26,000, according to HESA definitions - around 1%.

The University and College Union has previously highlighted an ethnicity pay gap and called for it to be redressed. It declined to comment on this case.

Both Cambridge and Oxford have faced sustained scrutiny over their whiteness as institutions, with vocal critics over the last 15 years including the MP David Lammy.

He extracted data from the universities showing how few offers were made to black students despite the number being awarded top A-Level grades which would potentially qualify them for a place.

In 2018, Cambridge said it needed help to attract more talented black students, and unexpectedly the rapper Stormzy answered the call by setting up a scholarship to encourage students to apply.

Although the support was for a handful of students, it was a reputational coup for the university - allowing it to position itself as a more open and inclusive institution.

Now it will have to balance the potential reputational fall out of the Jason Arday row for its academic credibility, with how that might be perceived by future talented black students and academics.

Burnham orders review of grooming gang early releases

BBC News Thu, 06 Aug 2026 13:56:53 GMT

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has ordered an "urgent" review to identify any grooming gang members who may be eligible to be freed from jail under the government's early release scheme.

The announcement comes after Tory leader Kemi Badenoch raised concerns that child sex offenders could leave jail well before the end of their sentences.

She pointed out that indecent assault was not included in the list of offences that the government said would be excluded from the early release scheme.

Five men convicted of indecent assault as part of a historical grooming-gang case in Bradford are among the prisoners whose offences were not included in the list of exclusions.

The prime minister's spokesperson said Burnham had asked the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) to "conduct an in-depth review of cases to ensure that grooming cases were identified".

"This work is happening urgently," Burnham's spokesperson said.

"This is extremely important to the PM and he has personally intervened to ensure everything possible is being done so that vile groomers are dealt with in the way their victims deserve."

It is understood that at this stage the review will only seek to identify offenders who might be released early.

The government has not confirmed whether the review will lead to the prevention of any early releases of offenders convicted of grooming-related crimes.

Badenoch described the intervention as "another U-turn secured" and "another review from Burnham following my letter".

The government is planning to release about 5,000 offenders in England and Wales early in an effort to make space in overcrowded jails.

Burnham launched a review of the scheme after he became prime minister and this week he announced that some prisoners convicted of rape, serious child sex and other grooming offences would barred from early release.

But in a letter, Badenoch said many more types of offenders - including those convicted of sexually assaulting children - could be freed early.

"On Tuesday, you told the country that those convicted of grooming offences would be excluded," she wrote. "Your own government has now put in writing that some of these men will be released early anyway."

Highlighting that indecent assault was not excluded from the early release scheme, Badenoch said "many cases of child sex abuse committed before 2004 were charged this way, including Rotherham and Rochdale".

Badenoch branded this a "betrayal of victims", and urged Burnham to publish the full list of offences that remain eligible for early release.

Under changes made by Burnham, people sentenced for rape, serious child sex and grooming offences will now not be eligible for early release from October.

But some prisoners who are not excluded could be freed after serving a third of their total custodial sentence rather than after 40% or 50% of their term.

Burnham said he had wanted to exclude more offenders, but prison overcrowding prevented this.

The prime minister said making more prisoners exempt was not possible without the prison system collapsing and putting the public "at much greater risk".

The prison population in England and Wales on 3 August was 86,495, which was 97% of useable capacity.

The number of places in jails in England and Wales has not kept pace with the significant rise in the prison population in recent decades under successive governments.

There are cases of offenders who were convicted of indecent assault under section 14 and 15 of the Sexual Offences Act 1956.

These sections of the 1956 Act were not included in the government's list of exclusions, suggesting prisoners convicted of these crimes could qualify for the early release scheme.

Five men who were jailed in October 2005, after being convicted of indecent assault for abusing a teenage girl in Bradford in the early 2000s, could be eligible for early release under the scheme.

In December 2024, Ajaz Karim was jailed for 21 months after he was convicted of indecent assault for sexually abusing a 13-year-old girl at the school where he was a sports coach.

In another case, Shahid Hussain was jailed for eight years in September 2024, after he was convicted of indecently assaulting a 14-year-old girl in Rotherham in 2003.

The government has not yet confirmed exactly which offenders will be released.

The mother of PC Andrew Harper also said she was "devastated" to learn two men jailed after her son was killed will still be eligible for early release.

PC Harper, 28, was killed in 2019 when he was dragged by a car down a country road as three teenagers fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Berkshire.

His family previously said they had received a letter from the Ministry of Justice confirming that two of the offenders could be included in the early release scheme.

Earlier this week, Justice Secretary Alex Norris apologised to families affected by the early release scheme, saying they were "carrying the can from previous failures".

The justice secretary said about 5,000 extra releases will take place in 10 batches from October - down from about 6,000 before the revision.

The changes are due to be phased in, beginning with prisoners serving sentences of fewer than 575 days, going up to inmates jailed for 12 years or more being eligible for early release in June 2027.

The number of individuals released each time will depend on the prison population, which the government says will evolve between now and implementation.
