The 85-million-year timeline of human evolution

New Scientist August 06, 2026

Reconstructing the origins of our species requires many kinds of evidence: fossil and archaeological evidence like bones and artefacts, but also molecular evidence such as ancient DNA, and data on past climates and environments.

The pace of discovery has accelerated over the past few decades: the story has been extended further back in time, and has become increasingly complex with the discovery of new sites that hosted our ancient ancestors and new species to add to the human family tree.

Because the archaeological record is incomplete, it’s difficult to determine when and where something first appeared, and how long it lasted. The oldest known example of something may be a poor guide to when that thing actually emerged. Hence this timeline often gives wide ranges, and particularly uncertain dates are marked with a question mark.

Advertisement

Primates – the group that includes monkeys, apes and humans – emerge. The first primates are small and spend a lot of time in trees; they resemble modern tree shrews or squirrels.

It’s uncertain exactly when primates first evolve. It may be before or after the extinction at the end of the Cretaceous Period, 66 million years ago, when an asteroid strikes Earth and wipes out many species, including all dinosaurs apart from birds.

Genetic studies comparing DNA from different primates suggest they evolve before the extinction. However, primates only show up in the fossil record afterwards – and it’s not always clear they are “true” primates. For instance, a little over 100,000 years after the mass extinction, animals called Purgatorius live in North America. They are plesiadapiforms, closely related to primates.

By 55 million years ago, there are unambiguous primates. They include Archicebus, found in eastern China, and several species of Teilhardina, which live in the Americas and Eurasia.

It may be significant that Earth experiences a global heatwave called the Palaeocene-Eocene thermal maximum around 55 million years ago. This enables tropical forests to spread widely, giving early primates a huge habitat.

The first apes evolve in Africa. Genetics suggests apes separated from monkeys as early as 30 million years ago, but again the fossil evidence comes along later.

Rukwapithecus is the earliest known ape or ape-like primate, living 25 million years ago in Tanzania. The 17-million-year-old Masripithecus, from Egypt, may be close to the last common ancestor of all extant apes.

Apes do well in Africa for several million years. Kenya is home to Nacholapithecus around 15 million years ago and Nyanzapithecus 13 million years ago. However, apes become increasingly rare on the continent – or at least, their fossils become sparse.

Grasses become common in East Africa and savannahs begin expanding in areas that were previously dense forests. This creates a new habitat – but it’s not clear how or when apes and hominins begin living in it.

Meanwhile, as early as 17 million years ago, some apes enter Eurasia. There they thrive. Eurasian apes develop more upright postures and curved, grasping fingers – traits we still see in great apes today.

Eurasian apes are a diverse bunch. Pierolapithecus lives in Spain around 12.5 million years ago: it has hands that are specialised for vertical climbing, so it probably can’t swing from tree branches. Its contemporary Dryopithecus has similarities to modern gorillas, while Hispanopithecus seems to have been ideally adapted for swinging. The 11.6-million-year-old Buronius may be the smallest ape, weighing just 10 kilograms.

Some Eurasian apes may start walking upright, or bipedally. This would mean that a key step in human evolution – the transition to bipedal walking – happened in Eurasia rather than Africa.

However, the evidence is disputed, largely because it relies on partial fossils. These include fossils from Danuvius, which lives in Germany 11.6 million years ago and has leg bones that show signs of upright walking. Likewise, the 10-million-year-old Rudapithecus from Hungary has a pelvis that may be adapted to allow a flexible lower back – a key ingredient for bipedal walking.

Even if some of these apes did walk bipedally, they are not necessarily our ancestors: bipedality may have independently evolved in multiple groups.

An incredible Denisovan skull is upending the story of human evolution

The last common ancestor (LCA) lives around this time. This unidentified animal is the most recent ancestor of both our closest living relatives – chimpanzees and bonobos – as well as humans and human-like hominins.

Some genetic evidence suggests the LCA lives at least 7 million years ago, but it may be earlier than that, 10 million years ago or more – or more recent, just 5.5 million years ago. The population split may be drawn-out rather than sudden.

It’s also not clear where the LCA lives. Because the earliest unambiguous hominins are known from Africa, many researchers have assumed an African LCA, but others argue for Eurasia. The fossil record is spotty in both places. Kenya’s 9.8-million-year-old Nakalipithecus may be quite close to the LCA – but unfortunately is only known from one jawbone and a handful of teeth.

Sahelanthropus tchadensis, the oldest known hominin, lives in what is now Chad.

Our information about it is limited because we have only a few bones, representing six to nine individuals, all from one small area. The remains include a skull known as Toumaï, fragments of lower jaw and some teeth, one thigh bone (femur) and two upper arm bones (ulnas).

Ever since Sahelanthropus was described in 2002, debate has raged about its nature. Some argue it walked bipedally, but others say the evidence doesn’t support that. In turn, some classify it as a hominin, while others contend it is more likely to be an ape.

Someone, or something, leaves a set of footprints on the tiny Mediterranean island of Trachilos. Some researchers argue the footprints are made by a bipedal hominin, in which case they are evidence that even early hominins venture beyond Africa. However, there is no consensus over who makes them or when.

Orrorin tugenensis lives in what is now Kenya. Their leg bones suggest they are bipedal hominins. Adults are 1.1 to 1.4 metres tall. They still have ape-like arms and curved fingers, ideal for climbing trees.

Hominins known as Ardipithecus live in East Africa. They walk fully upright, but also have grasping big toes like those of great apes, ideal for climbing trees. Their brains remain relatively small and their teeth suggest a varied diet.

Two species are known, from different time periods. The earlier species is Ardipithecus kadabba from 5.8 million years ago, which is known from only a handful of remains. It has large canine teeth like those of apes, but evolution causes these to shrink over the next few million years.

The second and better-known species is Ardipithecus ramidus, from 4.4 million years ago, represented by a female skeleton dubbed “Ardi”.

Ardi is the oldest near-complete hominin skeleton, offering some of our best evidence about the last common ancestor. Initial interpretations claim that Ardi is quite unlike chimpanzees, suggesting the LCA is also not like a chimp, but more recent analyses suggest Ardi’s hands are well adapted for swinging from branches like chimpanzees.

Hominins called Australopithecus live widely in Africa. They retain some ape-like traits, like relatively small brains and long, powerful arms suited for tree climbing. However, their skeletons strongly suggest that they habitually walk on two legs, and there is evidence that they make and use tools. Some Australopithecines may be the ancestors of our own genus, Homo.

Multiple species of Australopithecus coexist in Africa. The earliest known is Australopithecus anamensis, which lives in East Africa about 4 million years ago: it may be the ancestor of most or all of the later species.

Later, East Africa is home to Australopithecus afarensis. Many individuals of this species are known, the most famous being “Lucy” from the Afar region of Ethiopia. Lucy’s species rubs shoulders with another group called Australopithecus deyiremeda, who have more robust jaws – suggesting they eat tougher food.

Australopithecus are not confined to East Africa. In central Africa, in what is now Chad, lives Australopithecus bahrelghazali. Unlike the other Australopithecines, they seem to eat a fairly limited diet, mostly grass.

Further species live in southern Africa. One is Australopithecus africanus, exemplified by the Taung Child skull. A famous fossil called “Little Foot” may be the same species but has sometimes been placed into its own species – Australopithecus prometheus. The other South African species is Australopithecus sediba. They live as recently as 1.98 million years ago, meaning they share the continent with some of the earliest Homo – but they retain their Australopithecine traits like long arms for tree climbing.

Kenyanthropus, one of the least understood hominins, lives in Kenya. They are known from a handful of fossils from a site called Lomekwi, including a cranium that is badly squashed. Their cheek bones are fairly pronounced and their teeth small, both of which are more human-like traits.

Because there are so few remains, not everyone is convinced that Kenyanthropus is really a separate genus of hominins.

The oldest known stone tools are used in Lomekwi, Kenya. The Lomekwian tools are crude, produced by bashing one stone down onto another and knocking flakes off. There are tentative claims of older stone tool use, in the form of apparent cut marks on animal bones.

It’s not clear which hominins make and use the Lomekwian tools, or how hominins invent tools; one suggestion is that they first use naturally sharp stones, then find ways to make new ones.

Savannahs, which have been expanding for millions of years, finally reach all the way to southern Africa. Hominins now spend much of their time in mixed environments, with both trees and open grasslands.

Hominins called Paranthropus live in eastern and southern Africa. Given how late in the story they appear, they are remarkably ape-like, with smallish brains. They have dish-shaped faces due to huge chewing muscles and large teeth. Their teeth lead some to dub them “Nutcracker Man”, but the nickname is misleading as they probably don’t eat hard foods, but rather tough and chewy ones like grasses.

Three species are known. Paranthropus robustus lives in southern Africa, while Paranthropus aethiopicus and Paranthropus boisei live in the east. The relationships between the species are unclear. However, it does seem that Paranthropus is closely related to Homo.

Despite their ape-like bodies, there is growing evidence that Paranthropus make and use tools. Their hands are both strong and dexterous, and their remains have been found alongside Oldowan tools (see below).

The first members of the Homo genus appear in Africa. The earliest fossils are extremely limited: a lower jawbone and teeth from Ledi-Geraru in Ethiopia.

The earliest known Oldowan stone tools are used. Named for Olduvai/Oldupai Gorge in Tanzania, they are relatively simple, produced by chipping flakes off pebbles – but still require a degree of coordination, skill and forethought. Oldowan tools are widely and habitually used for over a million years.

Palaeoanthropologists have sometimes assumed that Oldowan tools were made only by members of Homo. However, the oldest known Oldowan tools are associated with Paranthropus fossils, suggesting Paranthropus may also use them.

Homo habilis lives in East Africa. While the species is one of the most famous, its fossil record is highly incomplete so it is not well understood. In particular, we have only partial skulls, and fossils have sometimes been assigned to H. habilis simply because they don’t fit anywhere else. What does seem clear is that H. habilis still has long arms, suggesting they spend a lot of time in trees.

H. habilis is often described as the first Homo species. It may have been around before 2 million years ago, but the purported older fossils are so partial that it’s hard to be sure. The Ledi-Geraru jawbone from 2.8 million years ago and an upper jawbone dubbed AL 666-1 from 2.3 million years ago seem to be Homo but don’t quite fit H. habilis.

Earliest evidence of Homo erectus. This species goes on to be one of the most widespread hominin groups and survives for nearly 2 million years. The earliest fossils are found in the Ethiopian highlands and at Drimolen in South Africa. Later, they are also found in North Africa, notably at Tighennif in Algeria around 700,000 years ago.

Compared with earlier hominins, H. erectus have significantly larger brains. They have shorter arms and longer legs, making them more like modern humans and less like apes. They also seem to have longer childhoods than earlier hominins, as evidenced by the famous fossil “Nariokotome Boy”.

Ancient teeth hint at links between Denisovans and Homo erectus

For the first time, some hominins move out of Africa into Eurasia.

The earliest widely accepted example is H. erectus, who live in what is now Georgia 1.8 million years ago. Some H. erectus head east, reaching China by 1.7 million or 1.6 million years ago, and going all the way to the island of Java in Indonesia. The Javan population lasts longest, remaining until as recently as 108,000 years ago. Curiously, there is little evidence of H. erectus in western or central Europe, apart from some partial face bones from Sima del Elefante in northern Spain that cannot be confidently identified.

There are disputed claims of earlier migrations into Eurasia. Other animals do make the trip, so it may not be all that difficult.

The out-of-Africa migration, in which ancient humans went on to inhabit every other continent except Antarctica, may not have been one moment in time, but a long and slow process. Columnist Michael Marshall examines how archaeologists are rethinking this critical part of our history

Earliest evidence of hominins using fire, from Wonderwerk cave in South Africa and various sites in Kenya. Similar traces appear at more recent sites in South Africa and the Levant. Some of these early fires may be created opportunistically from wildfires: the oldest hard evidence of hominins starting fires from scratch is from Britain around 400,000 years ago.

Hominins may use fires for cooking, which may help fuel the growth of their brains, as cooked food is more nutritious. There is also evidence of hominins using fire to modify stone tools as early as 300,000 years ago.

The earliest evidence of Acheulean stone tools, which include hand axes shaped like teardrops and are harder to make than the Oldowan tools. H. erectus may be the first to use them.

We can finally hear the long-hidden music of the Stone Age

Ancestor X – the last shared ancestor of our species (modern humans or Homo sapiens) and our other cousins, the Neanderthals (Homo neanderthalensis) and the Denisovans – lives at this time.

We do not know the identity of Ancestor X. Various species have been proposed, including Homo antecessor (see below) and Homo heidelbergensis (see below). But none quite fits the bill.

There is also uncertainty about the timing. Comparisons of the genomes of modern humans, Neanderthals and Denisovans suggest Ancestor X lives 500,000 to 700,000 years ago. However, some fossils point to an earlier date. Hominins from Morocco from 773,000 years ago may be close relatives of Ancestor X: they share traits with modern humans and Neanderthals, but also the much earlier H. erectus. More dramatically, a skull from China called Yunxian 2 is between 940,000 and 1.1 million years old. It may be a Denisovan, implying Ancestor X predates this time.

H. antecessor lives in northern Spain, making it the first hominin known to live in western Europe. The species is known from only one site, the cave of Gran Dolina. There is also a lower jawbone from the nearby Sima del Elefante, which is 1.1 million to 1.3 million years old, but it’s not clear if it’s H. antecessor or another Homo species.

H. antecessor has several features seen in later species, including our own, such as flat faces – perhaps hinting that they are our ancestors.

This is the Middle Pleistocene or Chibanian period, which is sometimes referred to as the “Muddle in the Middle” because the hominin fossil record is so confusing. Many fossil remains, from both Africa and Eurasia, are difficult to categorise.

This is exemplified by H. heidelbergensis, first identified from a 609,000-year-old lower jawbone from Mauer, Germany. Various fossils in Europe, Asia and Africa have been suggested to be H. heidelbergensis, but all these claims are disputed and it may be that H. heidelbergensis is solely European.

Earliest evidence of hominins using pigments, especially the red-orange minerals known as “ochre”. They may first use the pigments to paint their own bodies. Around this time, someone – perhaps a H. erectus – scratches a zigzag pattern into a clam shell on Java, creating the earliest known decoration.

Hominins may also be starting to make and wear simple clothes. Key evidence comes from hide scrapers: stone tools used to clean animal hides, a necessary step in making clothing from fur.

The oldest preserved wooden artefacts: a set of interlocking logs that may have formed part of a large structure such as a building, from Kalambo Falls in Zambia. The oldest known wooden tool, a shaped stick found in Greece, is about 430,000 years old.

It’s likely that hominins make and use wooden artefacts long before this, but these have not been preserved, because wood is perishable.

The Neanderthals (Homo neanderthalensis) live in Eurasia. They make an array of tools and artefacts, including jewellery. They may be the first hominins to make long-term homes. Neanderthals show many signs of human-level intelligence and ingenuity – even making a stone circle deep in Bruniquel cave, France, 175,000 years ago.

The oldest known Neanderthal remains are from Sima de los Huesos in northern Spain and are 430,000 years old.

Genetics indicates that Neanderthals sometimes interbreed with other hominins, including modern humans (H. sapiens) and the Denisovans of East Asia. While some of the hybrids may struggle with genetic mismatches, enough survive to leave traces in the genomes of all three groups. Many people today have some Neanderthal DNA.

The last reliably dated Neanderthal remains are about 40,000 years old, suggesting the species disappears around this time. Many factors may contribute to the extinction, including climate change, the Neanderthals’ small and isolated populations, and the arrival of H. sapiens in Europe. The last Neanderthals live in southern Europe.

Modern humans (Homo sapiens) emerge in Africa. The oldest known fossils are from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco and are between 250,000 and 350,000 years old. A skull from Florisbad in South Africa may also be early H. sapiens and is 259,000 years old. Later, there are 195,000-year-old remains from Omo Kibish and 160,000-year-old specimens from Herto, both in Ethiopia. Already, our species is widespread and diverse.

Homo naledi lives in what is now South Africa. They are known from only one site: the Rising Star cave.

For such a recent species, H. naledi have small brains. Nevertheless, there is evidence that they use fire to cook and make etchings on cave walls. Most controversially, they may bury their dead in the cave, indicating that even small-brained hominins feel the need to commemorate death through ritual.

If ancient humans with brains a third the size of our own buried their dead, as some archaeologists are claiming, then our species may be less special than we thought

Denisovans live in eastern Asia. They are a sister group to Neanderthals, named for Denisova cave in Siberia where the first fragmentary fossils were found. Denisovans are the first hominins to be identified primarily through ancient DNA.

They appear to be large-bodied, with big teeth and thick skulls. However, we still have only limited fossils and few stone tools and artefacts, so our understanding of their bodies and behaviour is limited. It’s also unclear how long they were around and what happened to them: we have only a partial reconstruction of their population history.

What is clear is that Denisovans are widespread and diverse. They interbreed with H. sapiens, so today many Asian populations carry some Denisovan DNA.

Homo floresiensis, diminutive hominins often known as hobbits, live on the island of Flores in Indonesia. Remains excavated from a cave called Liang Bua show that the hobbits stand barely 1 metre tall and have correspondingly small, but advanced, brains.

It’s unclear how and when H. floresiensis evolve. The earliest stone artefacts linked to them are 190,000 years old. The hobbits may be descendants of H. erectus who evolve smaller bodies as an adaptation to island life. A second site on Flores called Mata Menge also has small hominin remains, this time from 700,000 years ago. These may be the ancestors of hobbits.

The last traces of the hobbits are from 50,000 years ago, so the species may go extinct around that time. A drying climate and the arrival of H. sapiens may contribute.

Climate change may have killed ancient ‘hobbit’ hominins

Homo luzonensis lives on the island of Luzon in the Philippines. Only a few bones and teeth have been found, in Callao cave, so little is known. There is an ongoing debate over their age: as young as 50,000 years old on some measures, at least 134,000 years old on others.

Modern humans (Homo sapiens) migrate out of Africa and spread around the world. It’s unclear why they do so now; previous migrations may have been unsuccessful as they have left no genetic traces in modern populations. Arabia may be a key crossing point.

In Eurasia, modern humans replace the Neanderthals and Denisovans (after some interbreeding). Some get all the way to Australia by perhaps 65,000 years ago – a journey that requires multiple sea crossings.

Reaching the Americas takes longer, because it requires settling in the far north-east of Russia and crossing an ice bridge into Alaska. People do this between 33,000 and 14,000 years ago. From there they spread out, some going all the way into South America and the Amazon rainforest.

H. sapiens, and probably other hominins like Neanderthals and Denisovans, create rock art such as cave paintings. Rock art has been found on every inhabited continent.

At time of writing, the oldest known cave art is at least 68,000 years old: it is a hand stencil on a cave wall on Sulawesi, Indonesia. The oldest known narrative art, a painting of a pig surrounded by humans, is at least 51,200 years old and is also from a cave on Sulawesi. The oldest known drawing of any kind is a set of red lines daubed onto a loose stone using ochre. The stone was found in sediments in Blombos cave, South Africa, and seems to be 73,000 years old.

Around the world, many of the same symbols are repeatedly engraved or painted onto cave walls. The symbols may be a code, intended to convey important information. They are not writing, because they are too limited, but may be a precursor to it: “proto-writing”.

Some Eurasian wolves become domesticated, becoming dogs: the first domestic animals. Their bodies become smaller and their canine teeth shrink, among other changes. By about 14,000 years ago, these “incipient dogs” have become modern dogs and there is evidence that humans care for them.

Around the same time, some animals begin living alongside humans and getting benefits from doing so, such as food – but they remain wild. These synanthropic animals include foxes, pigeons and gulls.

Many other domestications follow, including wheat, chickens and cats (although cats are only sort of domesticated) – but millennia later, after people begin farming.

The Neolithic. Multiple societies begin relying heavily on farming for food, instead of hunting and gathering. This happens in the Fertile Crescent in western Asia, parts of Africa, the Americas, East Asia and Papua New Guinea, within a few thousand years. Some societies start living in dense villages and towns – some of which develop into powerful, hierarchical states. The first true writing systems emerge around 5300 years ago.

Discover some of the world’s oldest known cave paintings in this idyllic part of Northern Spain. Travel back 40,000 years to explore how our ancestors lived, played and worked. From ancient Paleolithic art to awe-inspiring geological formations, each cave tells a unique story that transcends time.

Wool: New season NZ market cools, but still booming for growers

New Zealand Herald August 06, 2026

Kells Wool owner Richard Kells. Photo / RNZ, Alexa Cook

By Monique Steele of RNZ

A long-awaited recovery in New Zealand wool prices is easing as buyers become reluctant to spend top dollar on the clip this new season.

However, a North Island auctioneer believes the mid-winter market might have hit its floor, after a strong lead-up.

Buoyant prices, including premium clips even cracking the $7-a-kilogram mark, have been enjoyed by wool growers this year.

But subdued demand from buyers had calmed prices across most wool types at the last few wool auctions.

Last month’s auction at Hawke’s Bay’s last remaining wool auction house, Kells Wool in Napier, was a “tough day” because of buyer interest and fewer orders affecting prices, the firm said.

But owner Richard Kells said prices firmed at this week’s auction on Tuesday, with long wool types attracting the greatest competition.

The average greasy price hit 375 cents versus 488c clean, with the average price per bale reaching $562.87.

This compared to the same time last year when the average greasy price was 285c, 342c clean, with the average bale nabbing $417.72, Kells said.

“We had a big turnout, a full bench of buyers and the bidding was brisk, so they all wanted some wool,” he said.

“That’s what gives us confidence that we’ve seen the worst of this correction.”

Kells said there was some reluctance from Chinese buyers in particular to pay top dollar again, but he expected the bottom had been hit.

“We’ve gone through a very sharp peak, but we’re still ahead of last year,” he said.

“The prices at our auction equalled the national sale in Christchurch.

“In fact, the fleece and the occupents were slightly firmer.

“So we think the bottom of the slide has been reached and we can look forward to some improvement in the coming months.”

Prices for second shear, crossbred fleeces and oddments were particularly hit at PGG Wrightson’s last national auction in Christchurch last week.

Here, 95c fell off the strong wool indicator and only 69% of the offering sold.

Its national auction manager, Dave Burridge, said although the market had eased considerably, the fundamentals of reduced wool supply into the next few months remained unchanged.

“Exporters have struggled to secure new sales following the elevated buying levels seen at the end of the season in June, while many overseas buyers are waiting for prices to stabilise before re-entering the market,” he said in PGG’s latest wool market report.

Kells said this week’s wool supply was “more of a dribble” than a flow, disrupted by cold and wet weather and time of year on farm.

He said ewe wool was effectively finished, and with lambing beginning for some, it was now down to trading lambs for the next couple of months.

Meanwhile, PGG said it was expecting tighter supplies to support the market, though it forecast price volatility to continue.

Its next auction will be held in Ōtautahi on August 13, with the Napier auction scheduled for August 28.

Ballentynes Fashion Central to shut its doors after serving Kiwis for more than 50 years

New Zealand Herald August 06, 2026

Ballentynes Fashion Central clothing department giant is set to close after more than 50 years. Photo / Google Maps

Ballentynes Fashion Central has announced it is closing down after operating more than 50 years.

The clothing chain’s 23 stores will be closing down progressively from next Saturday.

“On behalf of the Ballentyne family - including our incredible team of staff in the stores and in our warehouse, we would like to thank you for your support and shopping with us over the years,” a notice on the company’s website reads.

Thirteen stores will close completely, with 10 reopening as Caroline Eve Fashion.

The stores that will reopen, listed on the company website, will be in Blenheim, Richmond, Whanganui, Feilding, Palmerston North, Paraparaumu, Hāwera, Levin, Lower Hutt and Masterton.

Gift vouchers can continue to be used in-store and will be honoured at relevant Caroline Eve for six months after handover.

Faulty items can also be returned to Caroline Eve or to Ballentynes Fashion Central head office.

The clothing chain is different to the Ballantynes Department Store in Christchurch which in November faced staff cuts due to “severe recession”.

New $206m Tauranga courthouse work began without consent

New Zealand Herald August 06, 2026

Some structural steel on the new Tauranga courthouse was placed without consent approval. Photo / Sandra Conchie

Part of the new $206 million Tauranga courthouse was constructed without building consent.

Construction is underway on a new building for the Tauranga High and District Court on the corner of McLean, Willow, and Monmouth streets.

However, work began on a portion of the build before a consent had been issued, Tauranga City Council has confirmed.

The 8300sq m project would provide 12 courtrooms across the new courthouse and McLean House, which would be connected via a pedestrian bridge.

It was expected to be completed and operational in late 2028.

Hawkins Limited was contracted for the construction.

The consenting issue was discovered on June 23, according to the Ministry of Justice.

Tauranga City Council head of building services Denise Whelan said some structural steel was placed without consent approval.

“The works were only partially commenced before being identified and paused.”

She said the project team was instructed to stop works in the area where consent had not been granted.

Whelan said the $30m consent – which related to the structural, facade and roof works – was later issued on July 14.

“Where a project is on a larger scale such as this one, there can be multiple consents in place.

“From time to time, some challenges with staging can occur, and works that are not quite at consent issue start inadvertently, albeit not frequently.”

Whelan said no deconstruction or remedial risk assessments were required and there were no safety concerns.

“The project team are in daily contact with the council to ensure things progress as planned moving forward.”

The current Cameron Rd courthouse, which was described by the Ministry of Justice as leaky and not cost-effective to fix, would be decommissioned.

Cabinet approved funding to redevelop the courthouse in July 2023.

The project was initially set for completion in 2026 but was put under review in February 2023 following inflationary cost pressures post Covid-19.

Full project completion, including demolition of the old building, was expected in early 2030.

Hawkins said in a statement that consent had since been issued and all work undertaken was “consented and compliant”.

“There have been no site safety concerns at any point.”

The statement said the project involved a complex, multi-phase consenting process.

New Zealand Taxpayers’ Union head of communications Tory Relf said government departments should be held to the same standard as taxpayers and private developers.

“It is extraordinary that the Ministry of Justice, of all agencies, began work without the proper legal approval.”

He said calling the consenting issue a miscommunication was not good enough.

“The Ministry must explain who authorised the work, why its internal checks failed and how much the stoppage will cost taxpayers.

“There is no evidence yet that officials deliberately cut corners to recover earlier delays, but the possibility must be investigated.”

Relf said every day of stopped work risked contractor claims, remobilisation costs, and further delays on a project costing taxpayers more than $200m.

Ministry of Justice property general manager Ruth Currie said a miscommunication led to the consenting issue.

She said Tauranga City Council building inspectors identified the issue on June 23 and works stopped once the ministry was notified.

“It is common for the approval of building consents on complex projects like this to be sequenced.”

She said there were no additional costs or changes to the delivery schedule, and work continued as normal in other site areas.

Currie said the ministry’s project team and the council worked closely to process the consent.

“The affected works have been re-sequenced to ensure overall delivery timeline for the new courthouse remains on track.”

Bijou Johnson is a multimedia journalist based in Bay of Plenty. A passionate writer and reader, she grew up in Tauranga and developed a love for journalism while exploring various disciplines at university. She holds a Bachelor of Arts in Classical Studies from Massey University.

Weather forecast: Cold and frosty start ahead of warmer, wetter weekend

New Zealand Herald August 06, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

New Zealand was hit with another cold and frosty start this morning, with parts of the country experiencing temperatures as low as -10C.

More cold weather is expected today but conditions could start to warm over the weekend.

According to MetService, Desert Rd was the coldest place in the country today at a freezing -10.6C.

Twizel was the next coldest at -8C, while Taupo Airport and Taumarunui fell to -7C. Temperatures were slightly warmer further north, with Auckland Airport hitting a low of 1C, but some Aucklanders still woke up to frosty conditions.

However, conditions are expected to remain calm, with MetService meteorologist Braydon White expecting ideal weather for the Warriors fixture against the Penrith Panthers in Auckland tonight.

“Clear skies and light winds mean a banger day for the game,” White said.

“Conditions will still feel a bit chilly once the sun goes down, so be sure to bring a jacket.”

Warmer and wetter weather is forecast for the weekend, with rain spreading over the South Island tomorrow, with western parts bearing the brunt of it.

The rain will gradually move north, and most of the North Island is expected to experience wet weather at some point on Sunday.

The rain also means warmer and frost-free nights for the North Island, but the South Island is expected to stay cooler, with frosty conditions inland.

Another area of high pressure will then move in, creating mild temperatures on Monday and causing remaining showers to move away, but more rain is expected on Tuesday.

This forecast is a departure from the chilly mornings much of New Zealand felt this week, which included Auckland experiencing its coldest temperatures since July 2021, with readings of 1.5C at the airport and -1.7C at Whenuapai.

Taumarunui recorded its second-coldest temperature of -6.4C, only slightly warmer than the record of -6.8C set in 2010, while Mt Cook Aerodrome was the coldest location in the country at -10.1C. Twizel was the second coldest at -9.4C.

The cold meant Wednesday’s electricity peak was the highest power use ever, according to Transpower, with a warning of a potential energy shortfall today.

The polar blast wreaked havoc with travel plans in parts of the South Island, with police asking people in Dunedin to avoid travelling unless necessary and Wellingtonians also recording snow flurries from their windows.

A person has reportedly been stabbed on a central Auckland street in the early hours of this morning.

The incident happened near the 77 Convenience Store on Victoria St West, close to the Sky Tower.

An employee at the 24-hour store known as Seven Mart told the Herald he’d swapped with his graveyard shift colleague shortly after police arrived at the scene.

He was informed by the worker and police that there had been an alleged altercation on the footpath outside the 24-hour convenience store, involving two individuals believed to be known to each other, and one of them had been stabbed.

“It happened just round the corner,” he said.

The Herald has requested comment from police.

The worker said there were typically people sleeping rough in the area, but it was uncharacteristically quiet this morning when he arrived.

Two police vehicles – one marked and another unmarked – were stationed outside the shop on the corner of Victoria St West and Federal St early this morning.

Just before 7am, three officers were still on the scene. One could be seen speaking to the shopkeeper before two workers showed police something on the shop’s computer.

Police have since left the scene of the incident.

A Hato Hone St John spokesman earlier said the ambulance service was called at 5.43am and sent a critical care unit and a transporting ambulance.

Local government reforms: Western Bay rejects Tauranga merger proposal

New Zealand Herald August 06, 2026

Western Bay of Plenty Mayor James Denyer (left) and Tauranga Mayor Mahé Drysdale supported the councils working together on forming a new subregional unitary authority, but the Western Bay council voted overall to reject the plan. Photo / Ayla Yeoman

Tauranga City Council has been left at the altar by its proposed amalgamation partner, the Western Bay of Plenty District Council.

But resistance to the union may prove futile, with Tauranga agreeing to push ahead with a proposal without its neighbour’s support.

The two councils held a five-hour joint meeting in the Western Bay chambers yesterday to discuss submitting an outline proposal through the Government’s Head Start local government reform process.

The application deadline is Sunday.

Tauranga councillors first voted in favour of pursuing the creation of a new joint unitary authority covering the Tauranga and Western Bay areas, as part of a wider Bay of Plenty application.

A unitary authority includes district/city and regional council functions.

Their Western Bay counterparts then voted 6-4 against this, opting instead for the Government-led Backstop reform process.

Tauranga reconfirmed, in an 8-2 vote, that it would stick with its plan.

Tauranga Mayor Mahé Drysdale said the city would join other Bay of Plenty councils in proposing to create three new subregional unitary authorities: Eastern Bay (Whakatāne, Kawerau and Ōpōtiki); Western Bay (Tauranga and Western Bay); and Rotorua.

“As of today, five of the six councils support that, and Western Bay will be dragged into it,” Drysdale told the Bay of Plenty Times.

He said it was always going to be a close vote for Western Bay: “That’s democracy for you”.

Drysdale believed forming a unitary council was the right thing for the subregion and would “deliver significant benefits for all that live here”.

He understood Bay of Plenty was the first region to find a solution that “works for everyone” and expected the application would be well-received by Cabinet.

Western Bay Mayor James Denyer and Deputy Mayor Margaret Murray-Benge backed the proposal.

Denyer told Local Democracy Reporting he was disappointed his council’s vote ultimately went the other way.

“It is inevitable that we’ll end up with Tauranga in one way or another.”

Murray-Benge told the meeting she deeply regretted “that it has come to this”.

“This is a complete failure on the part of Western Bay.”

Steve Morris said not coming to an agreement and going with Backstop would fail the community.

Drysdale said the application was “a start line”.

“Let’s redesign it, let’s build it from the ground up.”

Hemi Rolleston said it was an opportunity to “build a new whare” and create something new together rather than focusing on merging.

Glen Crowther abstained from the initial vote on merging to see what the Western Bay decided.

He said the two councils did not trust each other.

Crowther and Kevin Schuler later voted against going ahead without Western Bay’s support.

Rodney Joyce said forming an arrangement has been painful, comparing it to “laying an egg”.

He said the Government’s 90-day Head Start application deadline was too short, adding “we don’t know what the Backstop would bring”.

Graeme Elvin said he wore a black suit to show his concern for the demise of democracy.

He said he favoured amalgamation but not how the Government was doing it.

He did not support agreeing to form a partnership now and figuring out the details later on.

“The devil is in the detail. I want to sit down and work out the issues.”

Murray-Benge said she wanted to see the councils build trust in each other.

“We’re all equal round this table.”

Standing to address the two councils, she said this was the most important decision they would make.

“We have a responsibility to our ratepayers.”

Denyer said the community supported a subregional unitary authority.

He believed the biggest issues, debt and representation, could be resolved.

He preferred the councils to be in charge of their own destiny.

Tracey Coxhead said she was not comfortable with feedback she had heard or the city council’s high debt levels, and was concerned smaller communities would lose their voices.

“Our two councils are not entirely aligned in our values and objectives.”

Shane Beech said the 90 days was not long enough to do meaningful community engagement.

He said the two councils had differing priorities, including urban versus rural priorities.

“I do not believe the council should be making decisions out of fear of government intervention.”

Laura Rae said she struggled to see how a merger benefited ratepayers.

“Bigger doesn’t always mean better.”

Allan Sole said he did not agree with shaping an organisation then trying to make all the details fit.

He said the two areas had little in common “besides geographically”.

“We need to dot a few more i’s and cross a few more t’s. Honestly, I think we’re so damn close.”

Darlene Dinsdale said she would vote in favour as it set a plan and direction.

Kawerau, Whakatāne, Ōpōtiki district councils each voted this week to pursue creating an Eastern Bay subregional unitary council – though with reluctance.

Rotorua Lakes Council will meet today to finalise its approach, but has backed the three-unitary model.

Bay of Plenty Regional Council cannot participate in a Head Start application.

It was set to discuss its response to local councils’ plans in a meeting yesterday, but elected to wait for the Tauranga/Western Bay meeting to finish.

Cabinet will assess Head Start applications and announce which ones will progress next month.

Final proposals would be due March 2027, with subsequent decisions expected in May.

If proposals were declined or a council opted for the Backstop pathway, this process would begin after the 2028 local elections.

New evidence immigration minister was kept in dark about major budget blowout

New Zealand Herald August 06, 2026

Immigration Minister Erica Stanford. Photo / RNZ, Samuel Rillstone

By Jo Moir of RNZ

Immigration Minister Erica Stanford has fresh concerns her senior officials may have deliberately withheld information, with new evidence suggesting she was kept in the dark about a significant budget blowout.

Stanford has released information to RNZ that includes two reports summarising the state of play of the now-canned biometric capability upgrade (BCU) that gave markedly different accounts of what was going on with the project.

One report was delivered to then-Immigration Minister Andrew Little in 2023 and another – covering the same period of time, with no mention of ballooning costs – was handed to Stanford a year later.

Stanford’s concerns prompted her to pass the two conflicting reports on to the inquiry into Immigration NZ, led by Michael Heron KC.

Senior immigration officials repeatedly ignored requests from the minister’s office and progressed work on the project, despite Stanford never agreeing to extra funding.

The now-abandoned BCU wasted at least $40 million of taxpayers’ money, before being scrapped by Immigration NZ.

Public Service Commissioner Sir Brian Roche tasked Heron with looking into “integrity concerns” within the department, after Stanford revealed officials “deliberately withheld” information from both her and the previous Government.

Last week, the chief executive of the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, which immigration sits within, fronted the Privileges Committee to explain to MPs why he hadn’t alerted Parliament sooner that the project had been canned.

The issue was raised as a matter of privilege by Labour’s Phil Twyford, after chief executive Nic Blakely fronted the Education and Workforce committee in March, and was asked about the key risks and milestones in the project’s implementation, but at no point told MPs it had been terminated.

Speaking at the privileges committee last Tuesday evening, Blakely admitted “we got it wrong – I accept that – and we should have said differently”.

Blakely said he had a “genuinely held belief” there were budget and commercial sensitivities limiting what he could say publicly.

That appearance and some of his answers caught the attention of Stanford’s office, and led to her telling media the following day that it was now clear at least another $6m had been wasted on the project, bringing the total to more than $40m.

Stanford referred that new information to Heron to consider as part of his inquiry, after Blakely confirmed to the minister “he cannot be confident this further $6m represents the full extent of expenditure ... and he has made the decision to commission an independent financial audit”.

In addition to concerns about the ministry’s financial controls, Stanford has now alerted Heron to another instance where it appears officials were trying to withhold further information from the minister.

One of the two weekly reports in question appears to have been summarised in a more positive light, without any mention of cost blowouts, when provided to Stanford.

In March 2024, Stanford’s office had started asking questions about the project and requested additional information about BCU, including any advice provided previously to Little.

Among other things, Stanford received an update on BCU’s progress covering the week August 2-8 of the previous year – before she was minister.

The update was signed off by immigration risk and border general manager Richard Owen, and noted the project reached a “major milestone” on July 24, “following satisfactory security assurance testing”.

While the current go-live date was set down for mid-November 2023, the update said “this remains at risk” and depended on tests, finalisation of commercial negotiations and visa processing peaks.

“Further updates will be provided, as each of these aspects is completed and worked through – with a back-up go-live date in early 2024, if required”, but a later report received by Stanford painted a different picture.

Last month, when the ministry sent Stanford’s office a package of documents it was planning to proactively release, the original weekly report sent to Little and his associate minister, Rachel Brooking, surfaced.

That report was put together by deputy chief operating officer Simon Sanders, and deputy secretary Alison McDonald and general manager Jivan Grewal were also included in the correspondence.

In that 2023 update, it also said BCU had passed a “major project milestone”, but noted delivery in mid-November 2023 looked unlikely and “it has now become evident that this date is no longer feasible nor possible, and a new go-live date of March 2024 is proposed”.

It noted, as the project duration had extended, both the vendor and ministry had suffered increased costs.

“These delays and also a review of the whole of life cost of the project has meant that the budget will now exceed the previously agreed cost of $35m that the Minister of Immigration recently approved. It is evident that the whole-of-life costs will now more likely be in the region of $45m.

“Given the new cost exceeds ministerial delegation, this will now require cabinet approval to proceed.”

The update went on to say the ministry was “in the process of preparing a paper for the minister to summarise the current state of the project and in parallel, will prepare a paper for the minister to take to cabinet as well, if the minister is supportive of this approach”.

None of the information about the cost blowouts had been passed on to Stanford, when her office requested all advice and documents related to the project.

Both reports have now been passed on to Heron to investigate further and determine whether the information had been deliberately kept from Stanford.

Stanford had nothing further to say about the matter, when RNZ asked whether this had further shaken her confidence in both her ministry officials and the chief executive.

Likewise, the ministry would not comment, while the inquiry was underway.

Wild goats on Napier’s Hospital Hill have been catching the attention of passing motorists and the plants of nearby residents, leading to questions about what to do with them.

Hospital Hill is a residential area close to central Napier.

Along with thousands of residents, the council has recently been made aware of four wild goats residing on the hill.

In recent months, the animals have been spotted roaming along a steep bank above the busy Pandora Rd and Hyderabad Rd roundabout.

Residents have also noticed them around their properties.

“We do get calls about them. We are exploring potential solutions,” a Napier City Council spokeswoman said.

She did not expand on what those solutions could be, but said the council’s animal control team and parks team were both involved.

In 2009, more than a dozen wild goats were moved from a bushy area of Napier Hill (which incorporates Bluff Hill and Hospital Hill) to Waimārama.

Hawke’s Bay Today reported, at the time, that the move ended an almost century-old association with wild goats on the hill.

But now they’re back, with appearances on Hospital Hill beginning roughly a year ago.

A truck driver, who preferred not to be named, said he’d driven past the hill for about 20 years and hadn’t noticed wild goats before - until recently.

Hospital Hill resident Ali McCarthy has lived in her home there for 13 years.

She also hadn’t seen or heard of any wild goats in the area, but that changed about 18 months ago.

She said about six or seven goats started roaming in the neighbourhood, including eating fruit and vegetables on residents’ properties.

She said, in some cases, they would wander down people’s driveways.

She said the council got involved and, around late last year, a contractor was brought in to reduce the numbers.

In recent months, she said a small number of wild goats had - once again - started appearing.

She said, as far as she could tell, they were based in the bushy gorge behind Main St.

“That is where you see most of them.”

She said it was unclear how they came to be there, but most people she’d spoken to thought they had been dumped in the gorge.

Enviropest offers pest control services across the North Island, including for wild goats.

Owner Mick Berian said in small numbers - like four - wild goats wouldn’t cause many problems, other than perhaps getting into someone’s garden.

However, he said they were a pest in larger numbers.

“The problem is, for example, if you have three nannies [adult females] and a billy [adult male], well those four goats probably, realistically, turn into seven or eight next year, the following year you have probably got 10 or 12, then from there it just starts getting silly unless you control them.” He said it was common for goats to have twins.

Berian said goats have a strong digestive system and eat plants and food other animals don’t.

He said that can be “quite detrimental” for native bush, and can even cause erosion.

With larger populations, wild goats can also pose a risk for motorists, as they can potentially walk in front of a vehicle.

“They can be quite a problem on the side of any public road.”

In July, more than 200 wild goats were culled near Cromwell, following a NZ Transport Agency Waka Kotahi-contracted operation to reduce the number of wild goats next to State Highway 8.

Napier City Council’s Animal Control Bylaw 2021 does not prohibit goats as pets, but does include strict restrictions around the responsible keeping of animals.

The Department of Conservation (DoC) manages wild goat populations in parts of New Zealand, but is not involved with any programmes around Hospital Hill.

According to DoC, goats were introduced to New Zealand by European settlers for food and also for weed control.

Goats that escaped or were released thrived in the country’s grass hills, forests and scrubland areas.

Rotorua black ice: SH30 crashes leave farmer traumatised and repeatedly repairing fences

New Zealand Herald August 06, 2026

Nathan Moore has a haunting memory of finding two people dead in his driveway.

Now a series of vehicles skidding on black ice amid Rotorua’s recent cold snap, in which temperatures plunged to -4C overnight, has brought back the “terrible sight”.

The two-vehicle crash that “really shook” Moore occurred early in the morning on January 15.

Moore found Gisborne man Saul Rerekura, 42, and Rotorua woman Taukirangi Hewitt, 32, dead in their vehicles.

“[It’s] something I can’t ever forget ...

“Now, whenever it’s icy on the roads ... I have trouble sleeping ...

“I worry what I’m gonna find out there,” he said.

Moore said six vehicles had skidded off the stretch of State Highway 30 outside Titoki Tihi Farm in the past two weeks.

Thankfully, only one person was injured in the crashes.

Every winter brings more crashes along the length of the farm. Moore estimated a “minimum” of 20 since he started living and working there eight years ago.

His 21-year-old son, who works alongside him, had also witnessed his share.

The experience has turned Moore into an unwitting first responder. Many times, he has rushed to help motorists and has pulled their vehicles from the farm fence with his tractor.

Moore said the highway was a “reasonably straight piece of road” where drivers could safely travel at 100km/h in normal conditions.

The speed limit increases from 80km/h just past Hell’s Gate Geothermal Reserve and Mud Spa, a tourist attraction about 2km before the farm.

“It’s just on those cold mornings when there’s ice there; that’s when people need to just slow down ... have their wits about them,” Moore said.

Moore drove the stretch of road regularly and said he had only noticed ice and grit warning signs in the past few weeks.

Farm co-owner Jon Marshall said the property was often a “few degrees cooler” than Rotorua town.

A forestry block across the road kept part of the highway in shade, allowing ice to remain on the road late into the morning on some days.

Jon and his wife, Debbie, split their time between the farm and Auckland, where they run a business, returning to the property every second week.

They have also become accustomed to rushing out to check on motorists when crashes happen.

Debbie had considered refreshing her first aid training so she knew exactly what to do if waiting for an ambulance.

But Moore was the one most affected, they said. Finding Rerekura and Hewitt had been “traumatic” for him.

Jon said Moore was left “freaking out” when crashes occurred, worried he would again find “something he doesn’t want to see”. The following days were spent repairing damaged fences to prevent livestock wandering on to the road and causing further crashes.

Some crashes in past years had happened in the middle of the night. The couple only knew when they found a section of damaged fence the next day.

The majority of motorists who had caused damage had not paid any compensation, Jon said. Claiming insurance was “hardly worth it”.

The process was lengthy and the excess could cost almost as much as repairing the fence, he said.

The Marshalls and Moore said they had asked police to install warning signs alerting motorists to icy conditions.

In the past week, a civil construction service had spread grit on the road to improve grip in icy conditions, Jon said.

He believed gritting needed to occur more often as it wore away quickly.

An NZ Transport Agency Waka Kotahi spokesperson said the agency “actively monitors and treats” the section of SH30 during winter.

Permanent ice and grit warning signs have been in place for “many years”. They were unfolded to be on display during winter when icy conditions are possible and folded away over summer.

The spokesperson said crews spread grit on the road on eight days in July and again on August 2 and 3.

Gritting was guided by weather forecasts, site inspections and ongoing assessments, and was carried out when ice posed a risk to motorists.

“We are continuing to assess conditions on this section of SH30 and will review whether any additional measures are appropriate,” the spokesperson said.

Drivers travelling on cold winter mornings should reduce their speed, increase following distances and take extra care, the spokesperson said.

“Black ice can form quickly and is often difficult for drivers to see.”

Rotorua road policing manager John Stapleford urged motorists not to brake harshly in icy conditions.

It was safer to lose speed by decelerating, Stapleford said.

He urged people stopping to help after a crash to remain visible, avoid blocking the road and stay clear of any downed power lines.

“Call emergency services, don’t assume someone else has called ... call 111 so the appropriate service can attend,” Stapleford said.

A police spokesperson said local police could definitely attribute one crash outside the farm in recent weeks to black ice.

The local police did not believe the stretch was more prone to black ice than other roads.

They said it was possible other crashes during the same period may have gone unreported.

Annabel Reid is a multimedia journalist for the Bay of Plenty Times and the Rotorua Daily Post, based in Rotorua. Originally from Hawke’s Bay, she has a Bachelor of Communications from the University of Canterbury.

The worst girl in America? More like the best story in pop music

Sydney Morning Herald August 07, 2026

An “overnight success 10 years in the making”, breakout pop sensation Slayyyter is finally slaying.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

The line between dedication and desperation is razor-thin. For almost a decade, emails about Slayyyter’s “unapologetic new video” or “raucous new club banger” peppered my inbox like the April rains: persistent, relentless, dank.

While playing on the same smart-dumb hyperpop eccentricity of PC Music and 100 Gecs, early singles like Daddy AF and Throatzillaaa were so outrageous that, for years, I marked Slayyyter as a tacky provocateur and publicist’s emails went unread. (Look, I’m a prude.)

Then, midway through last year, came Beat Up Chanel$. The single, somewhere between Y2K-era ghettotech and nu-rave, grabbed everyone’s attention. Its video – filled with booze, guns and trucker hats – set off a wave of unexpected anticipation around Slayyyter’s third album, Wor$t Girl in America. Not to mention a personal reckoning: was I wrong about Slayyyter?

A comment under an online review of the album sums up its appeal: “This album made me realise I am awesome and hot.” Wor$t Girl in America is validation for the pyjamas-and-slides to the mall set. It is hangover music for a generation that can’t see its future. If ever a set of songs existed for double-fisting pre-mixed tinnies at a boggy festival, this is it. Add in a viral Coachella set that highlighted its communal rush, and finally Slayyyter had her breakout moment after years of artistic hustle.

“I was pretty shocked. I just wasn’t expecting people to connect with it so much,” the 29-year-old, born Catherine Grace Garner, says of the album’s success. “I think people see a lot of themselves in it, or see a lot of their own hometowns. I feel everyone can feel the pain and aggression in a lot of the music. It’s a therapeutic thing to scream at the top of your lungs. A lot of people are resonating with it, which is funny and nice.”

Slayyyter’s speaking over Zoom from her hometown – St Louis, Missouri – following a triumphant homecoming to launch her Wor$t Girl in the World Tour, which hits Australia this month. Her persona might be pure trashbag – see her hedonist’s anthem Crank (“I get so gay off that tequila!” ) – but Slayyyter doesn’t live like that.

“My music is so angsty and aggressive, but I try to keep a very calm environment around myself on tour,” she says. “I don’t really, like, go out. I’m on vocal rest a lot, and it’s a lot more chill. I kind of just rest and take care of myself and try to give the best shows possible.”

More than a wild phenomenon, Wor$t Girl in America was a career resurrection. As the New York Times noted, Slayyyter is “an overnight success 10 years in the making”. She dropped her first mixtape in 2019 and has hustled ever since. When popheads online banished her to the “Khia asylum” – a disparaging grouping of mid-tier pop stars, named for the one-hit wonder of My Neck, My Back (Lick It) – Slayyyter persevered.

“I’ve always been comfortable with where I am,” she says. “I try not to expect anything more than what I’m receiving in life, and I don’t really think about the way [my music’s] received. As a little girl I always dreamed that I would have big stardom, I guess, but as I’ve gotten older it’s more just about making things I really love.”

Barely two years ago, she was on the verge of stopping altogether. In interviews, she’s discussed losing money on tours and merchandise to the point the project felt unsustainable. Wor$t Girl’s closer Brittanny Murphy – a song about depression and suicidal ideation – doubles as a meta farewell to the chase for musical relevancy (“Do you notice all I’ve done? Do you know it’s all I want?” ).

“I was planning to quit music,” says Slayyyter. “I would have probably kept doing it just as a hobby but I wanted to put a halt to doing it professionally, or even as Slayyyter, and just go back to doing it as a side project and do other things.”

What was she thinking she’d do had she given up on music? “I’m not sure. I don’t really have a college degree, so I guess we’ll never know,” she laughs. “It would have had to have been something creative, or something in music but just on the other side of things. But I guess the universe had different plans, which is nice.”

Slayyyter’s last album Starf---er – a moody mélange of Italo-disco, Gagaisms and Pino Donaggio’s scores for Brian De Palma’s films – earned enough of a push online that Columbia Records (a subsidiary of Sony Music) took a gamble on the singer for what she’d imagined would be her last album. With nothing to lose, she went all out.

What’s most remarkable about Slayyyter’s breakthrough is that it has come from the most raw and abrasive music of her career. Revisiting sounds she grew up listening to on her iPod, tracks evoke early-’00s “electroclash”, the era of Justice and Soulwax, Bang Gang parties and Flickr galleries of sweaty clubgoers. Her writing – most notably on Gas Station, a song that segues movingly from a bad romance to her relationship with her estranged father – added a more vulnerable edge.

“I think it was definitely born out of wanting it to be the last project I would leave behind and what I would feel if it was the last thing I ever released,” Slayyyter says of Wor$t Girl. “I wanted to make something I was very fulfilled by and that felt like it was right for me to say, ‘This is my last piece of art’, or the last imprint I will have on the world to leave behind. I went into every studio session treating it like the last thing I would ever do.”

Six months since its coronation, she’s started hinting at what follows: an “inverse album” – a playful spin on the deluxe album treatment that she’s calling a “brother album or a part two” – titled Wor$t Man in the World. New single Brand New Chanel$ – the Chanels are no longer beat up – connects The Killers and Balearic dance. It’s anthemic as ever, but airier than anything on Wor$t Girl.

“Instead of a typical deluxe album or a remix album, I wanted to make more music – and new music that feels inspired by the album that came before it,” she says. “I’ve had more life experiences and a different perspective after this album took off – going through personal life issues and thinking more about family things and wanting to lead more with forgiveness in my heart – so I wanted to make music that felt like a flip to the album. It’s a little lighter and less aggressive, more soft and sad.”

After almost stopping, she’s now contending with a different sort of pressure that comes after the success of Wor$t Girl in America. “I’m trying not to put pressure on anything and not get in my head too much,” she says. “I feel like anything I make is what I’m meant to make, and it’s more about a release or an expression. I’m not really worried about what it does afterwards. I just make what I want to listen to. Everything I do is just what I love and what I want to hear or what I feel like I’m not hearing in the world.”

When she looks back at her journey, can she understand why it took such a circuitous route or why the other albums didn’t take off to this level? “I think it’s just timing and that it just wasn’t meant to be, you know?” she says. “I feel that way about a lot of things. You can’t force things. I think [those albums] just weren’t right and I hadn’t really reached inside myself or I hadn’t really hit my stride yet with the visuals and music. And I think this one hit off because I finally found it. I unlocked it.”

Slayyyter’s new single Brand New Chanel$ is out now. Her Wor$t Girl in the World Tour plays at Sydney’s Enmore Theatre on August 9-10, Brisbane’s Fortitude Music Hall on August 14, and Forum Melbourne on August 17-18.

Are you part of Brisbane’s missing 20 per cent? How much foot traffic has dropped

Sydney Morning Herald August 07, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Since the coronavirus pandemic changed the way we work – and where we work – almost 60,000 fewer people walk through Brisbane’s Queen Street Mall on average each day.

Foot traffic in Queen Street Mall has not returned to pre-pandemic levels, falling nearly 20 per cent.

The trend is playing out across the CBD, as working from home changes the rhythm of the River City.

In December 2019, the last festive shopping period before COVID, 317,811 people on average walked through the mall each day, compared with 255,928 post-pandemic in December 2025.

Pedestrian movements through Queen Street Mall are recorded by six council sensors positioned in key areas, including the Albert, Edward and George street entrances, as well as Burnett Lane and the stage area near the long-standing Oasis Juice stand.

The sensors record movements, rather than individual pedestrians, so a person who walks over the same sensor five times is counted multiple times.

Analysis of the foot traffic data debunks the myth that Brisbane, which did not endure extended COVID lockdowns like Sydney and Melbourne, emerged unscathed from the pandemic.

The virus changed Brisbane permanently, particularly the CBD.

Working from home – or hybrid working – is the biggest contributor to plummeting pedestrian numbers in the city, says Gary Mortimer, a professor of consumer behaviour and retail marketing at QUT.

The Queen Street Mall has also been beset by the loss of Myer in July 2023, which created a five-level retail hole in the heart of the city.

Also in 2023, two Queen Street Mall venues – the Pig ‘N’ Whistle and Milano – were demolished as part of a Brisbane City Council plan to improve connectivity between the CBD and South Bank.

The Wintergarden has closed and parts of the building, including its distinctive butterfly exterior, will soon be demolished to make way for a new office tower, as well as the redevelopment of the former Hilton Hotel, now branded as Intercontinental Brisbane.

Despite the introduction of Brisbane City Markets every Wednesday in Reddacliff Place, the top end of the mall, near George Street, has been notoriously subdued and marred by vacant shopfronts.

Retail vacancy rates in Brisbane’s CBD remain the second-highest in the country, behind Perth. According to commercial real estate agency CBRE, 17.5 per cent of shops in Brisbane’s CBD were empty in February.

Mortimer says that figure reflects broader retail trends, as fewer people choose to shop in the city over the likes of suburban Westfields in Carindale, Mount Gravatt and Chermside.

Darlia Argyris, 36, who works in the energy industry, is rarely in her CBD office more than three days a week.

“I love it,” she says of hybrid working. “I can’t see myself going back [to the office] full-time.

“I am now able to use my before and after work time and even lunch breaks to head to appointments without having to take leave, or leave work early, prepare dinner, catch up on housework and exercise.

“At times there are more distractions in the office, especially when all of us are hybrid [workers] and on different schedules … so you may not have seen a particular co-worker for a number of weeks, so at times my office days can become very social.”

According to figures from CBRE, however, Brisbane’s CBD is flush with office workers compared with Sydney and Melbourne.

“The Brisbane office market has actually been one of the better performers in the Asia-Pacific region since the pandemic,” CBRE head of office research Tom Broderick says.

“Office vacancy in the CBD peaked at 15.4 per cent in late 2021 and is likely to be under 10 per cent by the end of 2026.

“Our estimate is office attendance in Brisbane is at 92 per cent of pre-COVID levels compared to the national average of 81 per cent.”

But traders in the mall and its adjoining arcades are experiencing the drop in pedestrian traffic firsthand, and have been forced to accept consumer behaviour has changed radically.

Fridays are typically the busiest day in Queen Street Mall by a small margin, followed by Tuesdays and Wednesdays, according to the council’s data.

On weekdays, foot traffic unsurprisingly peaks around lunchtime as office workers venture outside for food.

Michael Makras, owner of Italian cafe Marchetti, is not sure Brisbane will ever return to being a “five-day-a-week city” and feels the CBD is yet to find its new rhythm.

“Friday used to be the biggest day for us, undoubtedly. But post-COVID, there is no pattern. Sometimes Monday is the biggest day, sometimes Tuesday. It’s very unpredictable,” he says.

“We’re just ready for any day now, which makes staffing a bit more challenging.”

An optometrist by trade, Makras is in a unique position to observe changes in trends across the city, having owned businesses in the CBD and on James Street in New Farm.

The highly curated James Street precinct has seized upon changing consumer preferences for local, unique shopping experiences.

“Having a business in the city and having a business in the James Street precinct, I’ve noticed the shift,” Makras says. “The business in James Street was growing faster than the one in the city.”

His cafe is arguably at the “right” end of Queen Street Mall, near Edward Street, an area dominated by luxury retailers and dubbed by some as the “Paris end” of the city.

It is located in the 100-year-old Tattersall’s Arcade, which features marble floors and intricate plaster horse friezes by prominent sculptor Daphne Mayo above the shop doors.

“It feels like you’re coming into this romantic little hidden spot,” he says.

Similarly, The Pen Shoppe owner and handwriting expert Barbara Nichol says her bespoke offering in the historic setting of the Brisbane Arcade is key to the survival and growth of her business.

Nichol has watched the Queen Street Mall grow, shrink and change over nearly five consecutive decades in business.

“There was a time when I used to see everybody with a Zara [shopping] bag, but I’ve noticed that’s really not a thing so much any more,” she says. “Less people are carrying shopping bags, that’s for sure.”

Not only did COVID change the working week, it cemented online shopping habits for all generations, she says.

The success of her business is reliant on her loyal customer base built over 47 years, as well as her workshops in penmanship and handwriting.

Gone are the days when businesses could rely on CBD positioning, quality products and steady foot traffic to guarantee success, Nichol laments.

Big changes are on the horizon for Queen Street Mall, chiefly its expansion into Albert Street once the new Cross River Rail station opens in 2029.

Griffith University is transforming the old Treasury Casino into a law, business and IT campus, which is expected to host more than 6000 students and staff from 2027.

Vicinity Centres, which now wholly owns Uptown, as well as QueensPlaza, says it intends to spend about $350 million transforming Uptown by 2029 into a shopping centre similar to the Emporium in Melbourne’s CBD.

The redevelopment of the Wintergarden, and the neighbouring hotel, by IFM Investors, is also expected to be completed by then.

University of Queensland urban planning expert Stephanie Wyeth says the opening of the Cross River Rail station on Albert Street will be the “real game changer” because the position of Central Station at the top of the hill on Edward Street makes it so inaccessible.

“The next evolution of Brisbane will be about how all our different destinations across the inner city connect and complement each other: Howard Smith Wharves, South Bank, the [QPAC] cultural precinct, the mall, Eagle Street, Roma Street Parklands, and down to the Valley,” she says.

“If the mall is going to work, we have to reimagine what it is and what piece of the puzzle it is fulfilling for the city because we’re not going back to it just being purely a retail precinct.”

Wyeth says there is a lot to be learnt from the transformation of the Treasury building into a university campus.

Mortimer agrees there is not enough market demand to sustain more retail in the mall. He has repeatedly suggested Uptown, with its numerous levels of underground parking and its position above the Queen Street bus station, become a medical hub, ideal for specialists who currently practise from the difficult-to-access Wickham Terrace.

Both suggested the CBD could evolve into a new form – a walkable neighbourhood for a large number of local residents, attracted by the ability to live near where they work and be surrounded by nightlife options.

Makras is optimistic the city can evolve and adapt.

“I’ve always loved the city – I do love the city,” he says.

He fondly remembers when the city was an exciting destination, a place where you were in the thick of things; where there was always something new to be discovered.

“I loved it as a kid in the ’80s, going out in the city and meeting your friends. The Valley wasn’t a thing then, and meeting in the city was so exciting. There was always a new opening, a new bar,” he says.

“I’m really looking forward to seeing what happens next.”
