Overshadowed by its trendier neighbours, this eat street is a casual dining cornucopia

Sydney Morning Herald August 07, 2026

To dismiss Station Street in Fairfield as just a locals’ strip or a traffic thoroughfare is to deny the deliciousness it has to offer. It’s got A-plus chicken burgs, upmarket Indian and Lebanese, and a recent injection of fresh energy.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

When it comes to dining out, Fairfield – six kilometres north-east of the CBD – has long lived in the shadows of neighbouring suburbs. It doesn’t have the standard-setting hatted restaurants of Kew, or the once “coolest street in the world” claim to fame of High Street, stretching north from nearby Northcote.

Fairfield’s main drag, Station Street, is often overlooked as somewhat of a thoroughfare, a vein connecting the north and the east. But what is it really? A casual dining cornucopia, bolstered by a brigade of new openings, that deserves more attention.

By no means is it undiscovered, though. “It’s crawling with people, but it’s more of a locals’ strip versus a destination,” says Lily Stuckings, who chose it for her second Gelato Papa location in late 2020, attracted by the “old-school village vibe”. “It’s high quality, though,” she says of the food offering. “Not like it’s been left behind in the ’90s.”

Publican Daniel El-Fahkri had seen many seasons of Station Street before he bought the Grandview Hotel at the Heidelberg Road intersection in 2000. “I grew up on this strip,” he says. His first job in the late ’60s was delivering for a chemist, for 25 cents an hour.

“Back then, it was a shopping strip filled with banks, butcher shops and fruit shops, and a couple of milk bars,” he says. “There was no such thing as a cafe or restaurant [here].”

Much has changed. “My pub used to do a rip-roaring trade in food because there was not a lot else around,” El-Fahkri says. But over 26 years that has lessened, with a snowballing number of new eateries – mostly drop-in, daytime-only spots – further up the street.

Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox.

“If you don’t reinvent, you don’t catch up,” he says. So, masterminded by his daughter Norah, who’s a co-owner in the business, the El-Fahkris recently flipped the pub’s typical bistro into Lebanese restaurant Sama, heroing their family’s heritage.

“Fairfield has a lot to offer, but it doesn’t have that proper dinner location,” says Norah.

Introducing more polished nighttime dining to the street – alongside fellow new arrival Thaali, serving modern Indian cuisine – Sama is working to fill that gap in the market.

“The amount of people who have come [to Sama] who might never have come [to the Grandview] before has been a lot,” says Norah. “They would judge the tired, old facade.”

For Theo Liolios, owner of decades-old chicken shop Rooster Bar, investment in the area from big players – whether locals Oasis and Niko’s, or national chain Guzman y Gomez – has helped build momentum. “It’s slowly evolved into a food hub,” he says.

“From what we’ve seen, general trade has picked up,” Liolios continues. “I’ve been all over Melbourne, and I think [Station Street] is up there with the busiest streets for its size.”

Stuckings sees untapped potential. “Unless you’d been going to [iconic Station Street butcher] Brenta Meats for 20 years ... or you had prior knowledge of the strip, I don’t know that you’d purposefully stop in Fairfield. But there are so many reasons to.”

Station Street is a thoroughfare with thoroughly good fare. Here’s where to stop and snack along the Fairfield strip, starting at its Heidelberg Road end and working your way north, dipping into a couple of side streets along the way.

There’s a new lure at longstanding Heidelberg Road pub the Grandview. The 50-seat bistro has been transformed into a soulful Lebanese restaurant drawing on its owners’ roots. Family photos make it homey, but linen-draped tables and a tradition-tweaking menu make Samaone of the area’s more occasion-worthy diners. Tabbouleh comes in lettuce cups; crisp whitebait mingles with pita crisps and tahini yoghurt, remixing the popular Middle Eastern dish of fatteh; and charcoal-grilled proteins are a centrepiece. And cocktails? Try an anise-tinged raspberry number with arak. So popular is Sama that the family are working on a 30-seat wine bar, Sama Meze, which will open mid-October in a room that once housed the pub’s pokies.

429 Heidelberg Road, Fairfield, grandviewhotelfairfield. com/sama

It’s in the name: expect off-the-charts crunch factor at this new Korean fried chicken shop, just down from the train line. There are few airs and graces to the space, but it lets the chook do the talking. Wings and thighs are double-dredged and flavoured to your liking. But the burgers are where it’s at, built on squishy Martin’s potato rolls, anchored by incredibly crisp and craggy KFC and either house-made dill ranch or spicy mayo. Crunch time continues with all the sides: chips, onion rings and mini hash browns.

2/83 Station Street, Fairfield, instagram. com/kcrunch_fairfield

Step off the train at Fairfield Station and straight into Treble, a new player in the suburb’s cafe game. Locals eagerly awaited the opening and it’s already proving a crowd-pleaser, with a menu as sprawling as the benchtop of freshly baked goods (cinnamon scroll alert). Traditionalists can get their avo smashed, or eggs Benedict-ed one of three ways. But there’s also a dedicated vegan menu, plus curveball items like chimichurri-coated steak and eggs for a protein hit in the leafy courtyard.

21-23 Railway Place, Fairfield, treblefairfield. com. au

Fairfield’s busiest bar and bottle-o is best enjoyed at golden hour in the new parklet, with a front-row seat to the neighbourhood’s cutest dogs and your whistle wet with a dirty vermouth and tonic (like a briny martini, but more weeknight-friendly). Wines of the world line the walls and fridges, providing hundreds of budget and blowout options to take home or crack open right there with a flat $20 corkage fee. If your hunger calls for more than fancy cheese and chips, order a pizza from Flour + Salt across the road.

28 Railway Place, Fairfield, instagram. com/rocketwinestore

Seasonal, small-batch specials mean that every visit to the suburb’s go-to gelateria is a lucky dip. The shiny, stainless-steel pozzetti hold limited-edition flavours like prickly pear or hot cross bun, alongside permanent fixtures like the standout honeycomb choc-chip (tip: add extra honeycomb). Flavours are all natural, made from scratch and even go into elaborate gelato cakes – vegan bombe Alaska, anyone?

72A Station Street, Fairfield, gelatopapa. com. au

We’re 20 kilometres from Melbourne’s Greek heartland, where the 40-year-old Niko’s cake shop has become an Oakleigh institution. But, happily for northsiders, seven years ago it also sprouted this microcosm of the original.

Tucked off Station Street, the all-day eatery heaves with early morning frappe-sippers through to late-night dessert-seekers, with a frontage that completely retracts to let the outside in on balmy days. The offering is vast and varied, but highlights include triangular slabs of spanakopita (one of many house-baked pies) and classic Greek biscuits, stars of a sweets cabinet that stretches the width of the store.

254-262 Wingrove Street, Fairfield, nikoscakes. com. au

It’s shopping up front and snacking out back at two-pronged pasta paradise Allegria. Right on the footpath is an L-shaped, open-air shopfront selling handmade pastas and sauces to take home; the family-sized ragu lasagne is an easy weeknight win. Connected to the shop is an al fresco cafe for coffees and quick lunchtime pastas in the sunshine.

86 Station Street, Fairfield, allegriapasta. com. au

Perhaps Station Street’s most enduring drawcard is Brenta, a butcher shop whose clientele travels from near and far. House-made sausages are a specialty (the pork and fennel are stellar), as are spit roasts, plus your preferred protein can be deboned, rolled or seasoned as you like. Find Brenta’s own cured meats in the back fridge with cheeses and other antipasti, next to a whole wall of Italian dry goods. Service is so refreshingly old-school that your butcher might hold the door open for you as you leave.

103 Station Street, Fairfield, brentameats. com

There’s more than meets the eye at compact, waste-conscious wine shop Oak & Young. Beyond the bottles – and behind the counter – are 20 taps pouring small-batch wines that come in refillable bottles for $24. There are even cocktails like a limoncello spritz. Once you’re done, just rinse the bottle and return to get a refill for $19. It’s a reward for leaning into the sustainable ethos. The shop also stocks some bigger-ticket French and Italian varieties, a handful of bittersweet amari, and craft beer tinnies in the fridge.

107 Station Street, Fairfield, oakandyoung. com. au

Is there a bigger name than Oasis for Middle Eastern groceries in Melbourne? Even if you’ve never shopped at its family-run Fairfield or Murrumbeena locations, you’ve likely seen its branded creations (dips, breads, spices et al.) in indie supermarkets. Go direct to the source on Station Street, where an airy cafe deals in breakfast mezze platters and falafel wraps, and the adjoining grocer is made for overspending and overindulging, its aisles flush with mostly – but not strictly – Middle Eastern products.

92-96 Station Street, Fairfield, oasisonline. com. au

Believe the slogan emblazoned on the facade of this souvlaki shop: “Grouse Greek, No Malakies” (which loosely translates to “no nonsense” in Greek). Souvas are stuffed to within an inch of their lives with charry meats and hand-cut chips; the mixed grill is piled high with the likes of biftekia (rissoles) and loukaniko (sausage); and loukomades – either honey- or Nutella-drizzled doughnuts – are a sweet finisher. Spitaki does a roaring takeaway trade, but if you dine there Greek live music might soundtrack your meal.

115 Station Street, Fairfield, spitakisouvlaki. com

This good-for-groups Korean joint allows you to choose your own adventure. In the mood to DIY? Order a premium wagyu set, fire up the barbecue and grill to your heart’s content, sharing a variety of banchan, the small side dishes that are included in the price. Or go hands off, with traditional stews and sizzling plates from the kitchen. Either road will likely detour to Korean fried chicken. Mix-and-match flavours including snow butter, which is sprinkled with a garlic seasoning.

106 Station Street, Fairfield, instagram. com/assa_koreanbbq_fairfield

First as Organic Gertrude and now as Harvest Food Store, this site has been all about organics for more than two decades. The welcoming, family-run spot is part cafe, part grocer. Pull up a seat for produce-driven brekkie plates that encourage you to eat the rainbow, then peruse the shelves and fridges throughout the slender space. They’re stocked with seasonal fruit and veg, upmarket pantry staples and organic meats.

108 Station Street, Fairfield, harvestfoodstore. com. au

An offshoot of Carlton North’s Natural Tucker, which claims to be “Melbourne’s oldest traditional sourdough bakery”, Kneadful Things flies the flag in Fairfield. Breads of all shapes and sizes blanket the back wall, with daily specials from jalapeno and cheese to spiced carrot and walnut. Definitely get a loaf to go, but don’t go past the pie warmer, layered with flaky house-made classics (sausage rolls included) that give the sourdough a run for its money. Also for sale: locally made Jam Lady jams, such as sherry and onion.

116 Station Street, Fairfield, instagram. com/naturaltuckerbakeries

At this modern Indian newcomer (one of the strip’s few upscale diners), the menu is substantial but the namesake thali offers a deliciously shareable snapshot. A tray so large it needs its own table is filled with a chef’s selection of curries from across India, rice and naan, assorted condiments, and more. Veering from tradition are starters like the burrata-topped naan, and inventive cocktails including a vodka-spiked version of aam panna, an Indian drink made of unripe mangoes and spiced with cumin. If the street-facing dining room is full, slip down the side into a colourful, weatherproofed courtyard.

120 Station Street, Fairfield, instagram. com/thaaliaus

The sheer volume of the music – and the size of the crowd enjoying it – might have you thinking: impromptu DJ set? Not quite. Middle Eastern bakery Nouha’s serves vibes as good as its bakes from a street-side coffee window that’s always staffed by a friendly face, and an inside display that’s always packed to the rafters. What’ll it be: triple-cheese pie, sujuk and egg boat, lamb-kofta foldover, all of the above? Decision fatigue is real, with a range that includes everything from brekkie wraps to well-priced pizzas.

122 Station Street, Fairfield, nouhasbakery. com

What this charcoal-powered chicken shop lacks in frills, it makes up for in thrills. You can smell it before you see it, as whole chooks are flame-licked on a rotisserie in the front window. But, surprisingly, another menu item rules the roost. Most of the masses are there for the bestselling chicken-fillet burger. At $11.50, it’s a steal. But it’s also a masterclass in simplicity: just a juicy breast fillet, lettuce and mayo in a pudgy pita-esque roll. Its schnitzel counterpart is also worth your time, as are the hot chips.

128 Station Street, Fairfield, roosterbar. com. au

Passionate Italian pizzaiolo Andrea Cozzolino has channelled his hometown of Naples – and decades of pizza-making – into a pizzeria with two locations: one in Fairfield, another in nearby Ivanhoe. The least involved pizzas are often the most impressive, like the cheese-free marinara, simply topped with San Marzano tomatoes, garlic and oregano. There’s some very casual seating for those wanting to eat their leopard-spotted pizza fresh out the oven, or takeaways are slid into signature pink boxes.

145B Station Street, Fairfield, littlenaples. pizza

This banh mi shop is so vegan-friendly that it makes its tofu in-house, spices it with lemongrass and stuffs it into shatteringly crisp tiger rolls. But Tasty Banh Mi doesn’t just cater to the plant-based population; the headlining crispy pork is thick-cut, crackling-encrusted and consistently appeases the queues of teens and tradies. A new drinks list goes hard on the green stuff, featuring a matcha made “dirty” with espresso.

146B Station Street, Fairfield, instagram. com/tasty_banh_mi

Catch a train or nab a park in our secret spot, then start at the shopping centre for Good Food’s guide to noodles, mini banh mi and a retro Cantonese restaurant.

The 25 astonishing man-made attractions every traveller should see

Sydney Morning Herald August 07, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

We inherited quite a few good ideas from the ancient Greeks: democracy, theatre, the Olympic Games. One idea that tends to get overlooked is, in effect, the travel bucket list. Hellenic writers created the original list of the wonders of the world, a selection of see-them-before-you-die monuments.

From the Hanging Gardens of Babylon and the lighthouse of Alexandria to the 33-metre statue known as the Colossus of Rhodes, most of these ancient marvels have disappeared.

But in the intervening millennia, humans have created plenty of other awesome attractions, from which we have drawn a must-see list of our own.

In compiling this list, we had to keep it manageable, we had to exclude whole categories – museums, for instance, which, generally, tend to be more compelling for their collections than their construction.

Sign up for the Traveller Deals newsletter

Get exclusive travel deals delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up now.

We have ranged freely across the globe and also across the centuries. Some of our picks are ancient, while the newest is just a few decades old, but all of them are worth seeing at least once.

Contoured to follow the rise and fall of the mountains, the terraced rice paddies of Ifugao Province on the Philippine island of Luzon, are an arresting sight. Dating back 2000 years, these terraces were built using mud and stone walls which have been carefully maintained over generations by farmers who harvest water from the high mountain forests to keep their crops alive. Examples can be found throughout the province, but the rice terraces at Banaue are the most famous. See philippinetourism. co

Twenty years after they stopped mining salt at Wieliczka, near Krakow, thousands of people a day descend into the depths – not to work, but for sightseeing. Across 700 years, miners excavated 240 kilometres of tunnels and chambers, creating some stunning set pieces along the way. There is a chapel with a bas-relief of The Last Supper chiselled into the wall, and chambers decorated with statues and chandeliers, all carved out of salt. You don’t need to take our word for it – licking the walls is encouraged. See wieliczka-saltmine. com

The Empire State Building is taller. The Chrysler Building is prettier. But when you walk the streets of Manhattan, it is the Flatiron Building that arrests your eye. One of the world’s earliest steel-frame skyscrapers was groundbreaking when it was built in 1902, towering a record 22 storeys above the street, but even to this day the Flatiron Building’s wedge shape is distinctive. See nyctourism. com

In a city like Kyoto, with 1600 Buddhist temples and more than 400 Shinto shrines, it takes a lot to stand out, so the fact that Fushimi Inari-taisha has become Kyoto’s most famous sight is saying something.

This is a modal window.

0:43

Timelapse: Kyoto's Fushimi Inari Shrine

Take a high-speed tour of Fushimi Inari Shrine in Kyoto. This important site is famous for its thousands of bright red torii gates over trails through a beautiful hillside setting. Video: Craig Platt

Its thousands of orange torii gates form virtual tunnels leading up the mountain – each of the gates is donated by an individual or business hoping for success or wealth. The best time to marvel at this heavily visited attraction is early morning, before 7am, or in the evening after 6pm. See kyoto. travel

It is not often that political conflict leads to an architectural masterpiece, but that is what unfolded in New Caledonia in the 1990s. During peace talks following violent conflict between the local Kanaks and the French colonial rulers, the French agreed to build a cultural centre celebrating Kanak culture. Architect Renzo Piano was inspired by the traditional form of Kanak chieftains’ huts in creating the Tjibaou Cultural Centre’s 10 soaring arrowhead towers, which are about 12 kilometres from the centre of Noumea, the capital of New Caledonia. See centretjibaou. nc

Chichen Itza, one of the largest cities in the Mayan world, thrived for almost 1000 years, and even today its soaring structures are imposing. These ruins on Mexico’s Yucatan Peninsula also demonstrate the ingenuity and know-how of the Mayan culture, from the remarkable acoustics to the arresting spectacle that takes place on the equinox, when the shadow of the sun on the mighty Temple of Kukulkan resembles a slithering serpent. See visitmexico. com; smartraveller. gov. au

It may be the world’s largest Buddhist temple, built over six decades by the Sailendra dynasty of central Java, but its size isn’t the most impressive thing about Borobudur. What really draws you in is the rings of Buddha statues on the temple’s top tiers, as well as the intricate narrative panels chiselled along the monument’s six terraces. They bring Buddhist texts to life with vivid depictions of dancing girls and musicians, kings and warriors, and plenty of elephants. See indonesia. travel

There are plenty of grand railway stations around the world, but Mumbai’s Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus – better known by its old name, Victoria Terminus – may be the only one with a dedicated viewing platform to keep snap-happy visitors safe from the traffic. The building’s extraordinary architecture blends Gothic features – gargoyles, arches and flying buttresses – and traditional Indian designs. Avoid sightseeing at peak hour, as 3 million commuters pass through this station daily. See incredibleindia. gov. in

No, it’s still not finished. Structural work on this Barcelona church may have recently been completed – a century after the death of Antoni Gaudi, the architect who conceived this extraordinary building – but work on the interior continues. Even so, Sagrada Familia remains a must-see, not only for its eye-catching exterior but for the organically inspired interior that makes you feel like you are wandering through a stone forest. See sagradafamilia. org/en

The six minarets flanking its domes make its silhouette instantly identifiable on the Istanbul skyline, but it isn’t until you step inside the Blue Mosque that you understand why this 17th-century building is so famous. Light pours in through more than 200 stained-glass windows and falls onto the gleaming tiles – more than 20,000 of them – decorated with designs featuring tulips, roses and lilies. It all gives the Blue Mosque a sense of serenity, despite its vast size. See goturkiye. com

Ethiopia is home to no fewer than 10 UNESCO World Heritage sites including the Simien Mountains, the ancient ruins at Aksum and the fortified town of Harar Jugol. But the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela are definitely the star attraction. Instead of building these 11 churches from the ground upwards, the 12th-century King Gebre Meskel Lalibela had them carved out of the mountains like statues, with workers chipping away until the building form was revealed. The church of Bet Giyorgis (Church of St George), with its distinctive cruciform shape, is the standout. Bet Maryam, with its vividly coloured decorations, is also a highlight. Note that at the time of writing the federal government’s Smartraveller travel advisory site has a “reconsider your need to travel warning” for Ethiopia. See visitethiopia. et; smartraveller. gov. au

Due respect to Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, the visionary designers of Australia’s bush capital, Canberra, but if you were tasked with creating a national capital from nothing, Brasilia is the city that might most inspire you. Built in just three years in the 1950s, with three shifts of workers labouring 24 hours a day, modernist architect Oscar Niemeyer’s designs were not just unexpected but also occasionally surreal – check out the parliament building in the shape of a giant saucer. The true showpiece, however, is the Catedral Metropolitana, which rejected geometric lines and standard building materials in favour of huge glass panels set between sweeping concrete columns. Passing from the dark entry tunnel into the light-filled interior is a breathtaking experience. See visitbrasil. com

The Alhambra in Granada may just be the ultimate slow travel destination. A power centre for six centuries under Muslim and then Christian rulers, this southern Spanish site has layers of history woven through it. Starting in the 13th century, it has served as a military fort, a royal residence and even a small city, and exploring it properly takes several hours. Don’t rush as you work your way through the essential sights, which include the Nasrid palaces, the cooling water features and the terraced orchards. The power of this place lies in the beauty of its details, so take time to drink in the carved stucco walls, honeycombed ceilings and glazed tiles, especially in the show-stopping Hall of the Ambassadors. See tickets. alhambra-patronato. es

You could argue that the entire city of Venice is a monument, a triumph of engineering – all those wooden pylons beneath the waves keeping the palazzos aloft – as well as aesthetics. But if you have to choose just one building to highlight, it is always going to be St Mark’s Cathedral, standing watch over the city’s main square. Its design reflects Venice’s historical role as intermediary between East and West, piling together Greek columns, Roman arches, Gothic pinnacles and Islamic domes in a way that shouldn’t work, yet does. And that is just the exterior. The inside is just as astonishing, with marble inlaid floors, a dazzling altarpiece studded with emeralds, rubies and pearls, and golden mosaics inside each dome. See basilicasanmarco. it

Travel the world long enough, and you will soon notice something peculiar: more often than not, locals are a little dismissive of the landmarks that intrigue international visitors. The Sydney Opera House is an exception. Sydneysiders love it, whether they jog past it, drink cocktails alongside it, admire it from a passing ferry or step inside to catch a concert, a play or an opera. This remarkably sculptural building sits perfectly in its surroundings – on breezy days, the massive shells echo the shape of the billowing sails on the yachts racing past – and the way it appears different from every angle, means you never tire of looking at it. It more than deserves its position as the country’s most famous building. See sydneyoperahouse. com

You never forget your first sight of the Colosseum. A ruined building so vast, it makes the traffic circling it look insignificant, this ancient relic refuses to be cowed by the modern city that has sprung up around it. Even in a place as packed with monuments as Rome, the Colosseum impresses, even if you never set foot inside. And if you do step inside, the Colosseum puts you in touch with ancient Rome in a way that all those old temples and palaces don’t. The Colosseum is about the sweaty masses upon whose backs Rome was built, the crowds that lived for gladiatorial combat and vicious fights between wild animals. Walking through the arena – past trapdoors and animal cages and the seats, where 50,000 spectators crammed in – is a visceral form of time travel. See ticketing. colosseo. it

There is something paradoxical about the Eiffel Tower. It is Paris’ most inescapable building, one that almost seems to follow you around town playing hide and seek, yet 7 million visitors a year pay an entry fee to get even closer to it. Its total weight is nearly 10,000 tonnes, yet its latticed form appears lightweight, almost fragile. It has become a timeless symbol of Paris yet when it was built in 1889, it was steeped in controversy. The tallest structure in the world for four decades, it was a triumph of both engineering and physics, its distinctive curved form designed to resist wind shear. It was also the building that transformed iron from a mere structural support to an aesthetic element in its own right. Originally decried as an eyesore, it is now synonymous with Paris. Not bad for a building that was only supposed to stand for 20 years. See toureiffel. paris

What did the rulers of the now-vanished Incan empire have in common with real estate agents? They knew a good location when they saw one. There are many reasons why the Incan citadel of Machu Picchu has become South America’s most famous attraction, but its spectacular location – on a remote, mist-draped mountain ridge – is definitely one of them. The journey there, whether you opt for the scenic train ride or the challenging multi-day hike, is part of the adventure. Ultimately, it is Machu Picchu’s ruined royal palaces, sacred temples and agricultural terracing that are the real draw. The advanced building techniques are impressive – working without mortar, the Incas fitted the granite blocks together so seamlessly that not even a piece of paper can slip between them – while the carved ritual stone called Intihuatana reveals the Incan understanding of astronomy. See machupicchu. gob. pe

All the world loves a lover, and countless visitors have been swept away by the romance of the Taj Mahal’s backstory: Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, bereft at the death of his favourite wife, Mumtaz Mahal, vowed to commemorate her with a stunning monument. He delivered on that promise: among the many masterpieces of Mughal architecture, the Taj Mahal is considered the high point, distinguished by its sense of harmony and symmetry, and the way its white walls change with the hours, blushing a soft pink at dawn and glittering in the moonlight. Not that Shah Jahan had much time to enjoy it. Even as the Taj Mahal was under construction, the emperor was also building a brand-new capital, today known as Old Delhi, where he spent the rest of his reign until he was overthrown by his son. See tajmahal. gov. in

Harrison Ford must take some of the blame. Almost 40 years ago, Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade hit the cinemas and suddenly, everyone wanted to visit the ancient Nabataean city of Petra, riding through the narrow Siq gorge that opens out dramatically to reveal the 2000-year-old city carved into the sandstone cliffs. These days Petra in peak season is overcrowded and exhausting, but choose your travel time well and this remarkable desert city is still mesmerising. Stay for a couple of days to explore beyond the famous buildings along the main street: Petra covers more than 260 square kilometres, with more than 800 registered sites. A guide can take you along less-visited trails such as the walk to the High Place of Sacrifice, passing a number of eye-catching tombs. Note that at the time of writing the federal government’s Smartraveller travel advisory site has a “reconsider your need to travel warning” for Jordan. See visitpetra. jo/en; smartraveller. gov. au

The Timurids knew a thing or two about warfare. Timur, the founder of the Central Asian dynasty, was one of history’s most bloodthirsty warlords, a nomadic conqueror who built an empire that stretched as far as Afghanistan and Iran. His successors were equally ruthless but the Timurids weren’t just about death and destruction – they also loved art and learning, and developed a unique style of Islamic art. Their unlikely showpiece is the Shah-i-Zinda necropolis in Samarkand, an avenue lined with eye-catching mausoleums built between the 11th and the 15th centuries. Every building is covered with tiles glazed in astonishing shades of blue, from azure to cobalt, cerulean to turquoise. Embellished with accents of yellow, green and white, with dizzying patterns that are variously geometric, floral and even calligraphic, the entire thing shimmers in the sunlight like a precious jewel. See uzbekistan. travel

It is just not something most countries do. The US flag doesn’t feature the White House, the Greek flag doesn’t feature the Parthenon. But look at Cambodia’s flag and there, against a background of blue and red stripes, you will see Angkor Wat, the most famous of a collection of temples that have become Cambodia’s signature sight. That tells you something about the esteem in which the Cambodian people hold these temples, erected by the Khmer Empire over 700 years, right until its fall in the 15th century. Aside from Angkor Wat, the best-known are Bayon, where more than 200 stone faces gaze down on you serenely, and Ta Prohm, where centuries-old strangler figs appear to grip the ancient stones. Just a little further afield are largely ignored sites such as Banteay Srei, built of pink and yellow sandstone blocks, and Koh Ker, with its seven-tiered step pyramid. See ctb. gov. kh

Can we all agree that, when visiting China’s Great Wall, a toboggan ride is a little unnecessary? The most-visited sections of this historic fortification, places such as Badaling and Mutianyu near Beijing, have become something akin to theme parks, packed with crowd-pleasing activities that really don’t belong at one of the world’s greatest monuments. To properly appreciate the incredible effort, extending back more than 2000 years, that went into this defensive barrier, head for one of the more rugged, less-visited sections such as Simatai or Jinshanling, where you can trace the wall’s sinuous path over ridge lines and down into valleys, all the way to the horizon. If you love to get active, the unrestored section starting at Jiankou makes for a memorable hike. See cnto. org. au

Nowhere can match Egypt’s collection of ancient monuments, and the pyramids of Giza justly get top billing. It’s not just about size, although the Great Pyramid of Khufu – the sole survivor of the Greeks’ wonders of the world – was the tallest man-made structure in the world for more than 3800 years. They are so old even the ancient Romans were impressed by their antiquity: when Augustus visited in 30 BC, before he became emperor, they were already about 2500 years old. How these monuments were constructed was for many years a mystery. It is only recently that researchers determined that a workforce of between 20,000 and 30,000 people hauled the immense blocks of stone up ramps using sledges. A new visitor centre and the opening of the nearby Grand Egyptian Museum have made this an even more compelling experience. See egymonuments. com

Rapa Nui is not a large place. Also known as Easter Island, this scrap of land is just 24 kilometres long, and five hours’ flight away from the nearest land mass, South America. Yet the people who lived here created some of the most distinctive statues ever created, the impressive moai that never cease to astonish visitors. The first surprise is how many of these giant statues there are – more than 800. Some are incomplete and never made it out of Rano Raraku, the volcanic crater used as a quarry. Others stand tall, such as the 15 moai on a platform at Ahu Tongariki, their backs to the sea, gazing protectively across the land. And when we say tall, we are not exaggerating – some of these stand up to 14 metres and weigh up to 60 tonnes. Perhaps the most surprising thing about Rapa Nui’s moai is that, just like snowflakes, no two are alike. All of them feature prominent ears and noses but beyond that, their expressions vary. Some look disdainful, others calm, and some even seem about to crack a cheerful smile. See rapanuinationalpark. com

‘It is British life’: No 10 vows to stop councils trying to limit standing in pubs

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 21:07:15 GMT

Westminster council has recommended banning ‘vertical drinking’ or ordering at the bar in new draft licensing policy

No 10 has vowed to confiscate powers from local councils which try to restrict customers from standing up while drinking in pubs or ordering at the bar.

It comes after the Guardian revealed on Thursday that Westminster council in central London recommended not allowing “vertical drinking” or ordering at the bar in its new draft licensing policy.

The draft document, now out for consultation, recommends that pubs applying for new licences allow only table service rather than bar ordering. It also suggests new pubs in popular nightlife areas including Soho call last orders at 10pm, to reduce noise and disturbance.

A Downing Street spokesperson said: “Busy pubs full of people talking to each other is not a public nuisance, it is British life, and it is thousands of jobs.

“The government is devolving new licensing powers to the mayor [of London] to help support pubs and nightlife. Soho did not become world famous by taking last orders early, switching the lights off at 10 o’clock.

“The prime minister encourages local leaders to work with the industry so that pubs can continue to thrive.”

The government is due to grant new powers to the London mayor, Sadiq Khan, allowing him to “call in” local council decisions he opposes.

Khan said of the proposals on X: “You can’t run a world-famous nightlife district with a village-hall mindset.”

A spokesperson for the mayor previously said he was against “restrictive and anti-growth policies” and said he hoped to use new powers to be granted to him by the government to stop councils from overreaching.

The draft policy says pubs should “discourage excessive drunkenness and encourage the provision of more seating in premises that serve alcohol for people to sit and enjoy a drink and order food by table service in place of open bar space that caters for high-volume vertical drinking”.

It goes on to recommend that sales of alcohol and food should be “by waiter or waitress service only”.

Operators of pubs and bars in Soho have criticised what they see as overly restrictive licensing policies and said the proposals could kill off West End nightlife.

Responding to Khan’s criticism, he said: “We don’t need lectures from city hall on backing hospitality when they have directed the police to object to every new licence application as their solution to curbing crime in the West End.”

Possession review – a nightmarish plantation drama with a divisive paranormal twist

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 21:00:08 GMT

Gugu Mbatha-Raw is a lawyer sent to Jamaica to get to the bottom of a mystery about an inheritance. What unfolds is an evocative story packed with horrors, past injustices – and a supernatural element that you will rate or hate

What do you do when a client worth £50m – thanks to family ownership of a Jamaican sugar plantation upon which a modern fortune was built – pops his clogs and is unexpectedly revealed to have cut his only child out of his will, leaving the lot to a hitherto unknown “African national” called Cudjoe East? Why, you call in your firm’s (likely only) biracial lawyer, Claudia (Gugu Mbatha-Raw), to go over to Kingston, find him and discredit him as soon as possible. “Sounds like a job for a partner, really,” replies Claudia and, promotion thus secured, duly heads out for her mother’s homeland. She may wish, before we are very far in, that she had gone for senior partnership instead.

The planter’s house is one that has been appearing to her in recent nightmares that have been full of fires, terrified figures and strange symbols. But! She is a woman of the law, not superstition, so she sets the screaming Afro-gothic warnings aside and gets on with searching the house for anything that could suggest the pro-Cudjoe will is invalid and questioning the locals for any clue as to where Cudjoe himself might be. Her late client’s driver Angelo (Jeff Crossley) tells her that he introduced the pair about six months ago when his boss wanted to learn more about local history. Angelo assures her that she will not be able to talk Cudjoe into giving up his legacy.

Soon Oliver (Jonny Lee Miller, in posh, nervy mode), the disinherited son, has joined her so that they can investigate and – he is divorced as well as disinherited – build sexual tension together.

What follows is a dual-timeline mystery. One story unfolds in the present, another 300 years ago when the estate was staffed by enslaved people, overseen by increasingly cruel members of Oliver’s ancestral line and facing the series of rebellions known as Tacky’s War – with a supernatural inflection that allows the two increasingly to mesh. Claudia’s nightmares increase, populated perhaps by spectral members of other ancestral lines. Images and objects that appear in the dream world turn up in the house, along with documents that make the abstract horrors of colonialism concrete. The spirits with which the local people think the house, their land, their culture is infused become increasingly restless. If you believe in that kind of thing, of course – but it does become much harder to deny once Oliver has been levitated and bounced off the ceiling by an unseen force.

When Claudia meets Cudjoe (Sheldon Shepherd), he is as unmoving as Angelo promised, but also claims to be nearly 300 years old – the surviving, or surviving incarnation of, Matthew, the illegitimate son (which is to say, a child conceived by the rape of an enslaved woman) of the then landowner. Matthew was promised his freedom and the estate by his father, but was denied it by Charlotte (Bel Powley), their father’s legitimate daughter. Who may or may not have hastened her father’s death from tongue cancer – strangely contracted after he cut out Matthew’s grandmother’s tongue as a punishment for possible involvement in an abortive uprising.

So the past’s injustices, sufferings and legacies work themselves into and through the present. Possession is the first full-length work from Karla Crome, so far best known for her acting roles in Misfits, You, Me and the Apocalypse and most recently in Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen. It is a potent conjuring of the pervasive, enduring evils and toxicities of colonialism. It’s a powerful look at how unadmitted sins and guilt manifest themselves and whether justice for some crimes – such sprawling, normalised, heinous crimes that you begin almost to warm to those who act out of simple depravity and malevolence – can ever be done. Are reparations possible? Where does responsibility begin and end? What is better: ancestral spirit vengeance being visited upon the guilty’s descendants, or the parlaying of a boss’s modern exploitation of your skin colour for “optics” into money and promotion?

For some the accumulating paranormal-mystical element will add to the dread and horror. For others, there is a danger that it obscures the truth of the story and the suffering. Where you land, I suppose, largely depends on whether you feel that ghosts and spirits are capable of thinking up and delivering any worse experiences than man seems able to conjure and visit on his fellow man. Part of me always feels that recourse to the diabolic or ineffable is a cop-out, but that is undoubtedly a vast failure of imagination on my part.

But either way, Possession is a well-textured, evocative tale touching on many important questions, if never quite digging down far enough into any of them to be truly satisfying.

Possession aired on Sky Atlantic and is available on Now.

Dons call for Cambridge leaders to take blame for Jason Arday appointment

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 19:54:47 GMT

Exclusive: Academics call for inquiry, saying university must be held accountable for ‘grotesque racism unleashed’

The University of Cambridge’s leaders deserve blame for the “grotesque racism unleashed” by Jason Arday’s appointment as professor, according to academics calling for the university to hold an independent inquiry.

The Guardian understands that senior dons at Cambridge are circulating a joint letter calling for an inquiry into the processes and circumstances around Arday being given the position, with many suggesting the university wanted a “quick fix” to improve the diversity of its staff.

Arday was appointed as professor of sociology of education in 2023 at the relatively young age of 37 and despite a slim track record of research and publications compared with those appointed to similar chairs at Cambridge.

Arday resigned on Wednesday after more than a week of public questions involving plagiarism in his PhD thesis and other publications, allegations of exaggerating his academic appointments, mounting controversy over his claims to have raised millions of pounds for charity, and lurid statements involving masked attackers and even a pig’s head delivered to his parents’ home in London.

Arday is preparing to publish his memoir in the US and UK in the coming days and told the Guardian that its publisher, Simon & Schuster, is to pay him “1.4 million” for his extraordinary backstory, which includes being unable to speak until he was 11 years old.

The group of Cambridge academics want any inquiry to include external members and be given independent status. They point to concerns over the appointment committee for Arday’s post, and to previous disputes within the university’s faculty of education where Arday was based.

Priyamvada Gopal, professor of postcolonial studies at Cambridge’s English faculty and one of the group organising the letter, said: “An independent investigation must scrutinise how such an early-career appointment to a very senior and prestigious professorial chair was made and what both the faculty of education and university management may have got very badly wrong.”

She added: “Whatever the results of any investigation, the university bears no little responsibility for the grotesque racism which this whole business has unleashed, and for the harm done both to the individual in the line of fire, to Black academics as a group, and the broader field of critical race studies.

“This requires accountability now from those responsible, not a cover-up.”

Other academics who spoke to the Guardian said they had been surprised by Arday’s appointment in 2023, with one sociologist admitting to never having heard of Arday before: “When it was announced I looked for his body of work, and it was disappointing to say the least.”

Gopal said Cambridge had been too tempted to “cut corners on the hard work of fostering equality and inclusion” by opting for a media-friendly appointment.

“The extent to which this appointment was paraded in the media by the university … raises questions about whether the university sought public kudos for itself rather than teaching and research from this appointment.

“It is highly unusual, to say the least, to appoint such an early-career academic to a very senior post,” Gopal said.

“Academic misconduct also needs more robust and transparent procedures in place, as more than one case at Cambridge indicates.

“The university must also pay attention to the consequences of putting young people of colour in highly visible places to carry the burden of representation before they are ready to withstand scrutiny.”

When the controversy first erupted, the university briefed journalists that it stood by its appointment process, and publicly defended Arday as “the victim of a vile campaign” to discredit him.

But on Wednesday night the university abruptly announced that it would open a fresh investigation after receiving “new information” about his qualifications and appointments.

Shortly afterwards Arday said he would resign, adding: “I no longer wish to feel as though I am living under a constant spotlight, where every aspect of my life is subject to public examination and judgment.”

The university and other organisations have since distanced themselves from Arday by deleting webpages and excising references, which one academic described as “wiping away the traces”.

Jesus College, Cambridge, and the university’s faculty of education have taken down Arday’s staff profiles.

Arday had signed up to speakers’ bureaus and, since his Cambridge appointment, has addressed a number of commercial organisations, including the annual conference of the Association of British Insurers in 2025.

Simon & Schuster’s speakers bureau lists Arday as “an internationally sought-after speaker for industry conferences, corporate events, university lectures, and more, and has travelled across the United States for speaking engagements”.

In 2024 Arday was a keynote speaker at US National Association of Funeral Directors international convention in New Orleans. His subsequent appearances, however, may dry up: an appearance in Arizona promised for October this year has also been removed.

High-profile examples of such transfer standoffs have been seen in men’s football, but incidents in the women’s game have been comparatively rare.

Trump administration to pay German firm $1.22bn to cut offshore wind leases

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 18:20:49 GMT

Agreement with RWE is fifth deal Trump team has made with energy companies, offering payouts to give up projects

The German energy company RWE has reached a $1.22bn deal with the US government to relinquish its offshore wind leases and instead redirect funds towards fossil fuel investments.

The agreement marks the fifth deal the Donald Trump administration has struck with energy companies, offering payouts in exchange for abandoning renewable energy projects and redirecting investment towards fossil fuels.

This latest deal takes it to almost $4bn of taxpayer money spent on killing offshore wind projects.

Announcing the deal with the US interior department on Thursday, RWE said it had agreed to give up its offshore wind leases off the coasts of New York, California and Louisiana.

“After careful consideration, it was determined there is no path forward to permit these projects in the US for the foreseeable future,” the company said, referring to the leases it initially secured with a “long-term commitment to develop offshore wind capacity”.

RWE paid $1.1bn for its New York lease in a 2022 auction held by the Joe Biden administration, while its leases in Louisiana and California cost a combined $163m, Reuters reports.

“The settlement resolves RWE US Offshore’s legal claims and provides $1.22 billion in settlement funds,” RWE continued, adding that the deal would allow it to “direct resources toward energy projects that can be advanced with certainty.”

As part of the agreement, RWE will spend $900m to acquire a 16% stake in an unnamed Louisiana liquified natural gas (LNG) project. The company said the settlement proceeds would be used to fund construction of the terminal.

RWE has also signed a $300m turbine reservation agreement under which it will develop a pipeline of 15 natural gas peaker plants across the country.

The interior secretary, Doug Burgum, hailed the deal, saying on Thursday: “We welcome RWE’s agreement and voluntary investment in projects that strengthen our nation’s energy security, provide dependable baseload power, and help keep electricity affordable for hardworking Americans today while supporting our country’s long-term energy future.”

The RWE agreement appears to be the largest deal the Trump administration has struck with an energy company to kill clean energy projects. Earlier agreements with other companies, including TotalEnergies and Duke Energy, amounted to $2.7bn in taxpayer money.

Following the Trump administration’s $928m deal with French energy company TotalEnergies to cancel its offshore wind lease off the coast of New York, seven states, including New York, sued the administration over what the New York attorney general, Letitia James, described as a “sham deal” and “illegal agreement”.

The administration has also spent up to $1.1bn to boost coal, a move critics argue is “fattening the wallets of his cronies” while raising working Americans’ energy bills, particularly as the US’s war on Iran drives up fuel prices.

At the same time, the federal government is seeking to slash public input periods for fossil fuel drilling on federal lands while shifting more of the financial risks of cleanup to taxpayers.

Meanwhile, a report released last fall by the Environmental Integrity Project found that every fully operational LNG facility in the US had violated federal pollution limits in recent years.

According to the non-profit research organization, violations included the discharge of illegal amounts of bacteria, zinc, oil and other pollutants into waterways, as well as failures of terminal managers to submit monitoring reports for waterway discharge.

Safety fears as scientists make first viruses designed by AI

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 18:00:04 GMT

Researchers say breakthrough offers hope for new medicines but also raises urgent biosecurity questions

Scientists have made the first viruses designed by artificial intelligence in a milestone that raises hopes for new medicines but also concerns over how to ensure the technology remains safe.

The viruses are specific kinds known as bacteriophages, which only infect bacteria and are used around the world to treat patients with persistent infections. In lab tests, a cocktail of the AI-designed viruses killed E coli bugs that were resistant to natural bacteriophages.

Dr Brian Hie, a chemical engineer at Stanford University in California, used genome language models, the genetic equivalent of the large language models behind AI chatbots, to design functioning genomes for bacteriophages. The viruses were then made in the laboratory and pitted against E coli in a dish.

The ability to “rapidly design” genomes and tune them for specific bugs while overcoming resistance could “transform phage therapy” and “expand biotechnological toolkits”, the researchers wrote in the journal Science.

But beyond the potential benefits, the scientists said the work raised “important biosafety, biocontainment and biosecurity considerations” and urged others who were designing whole genomes to “consult both safety and security professionals throughout the project”.

In an accompanying article, Prof Tom Inglesby and Dr Moritz Hanke at the Center for Health Security at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, reinforced the warning, writing: “Although this is promising for life sciences applications, it also raises urgent biosafety and biosecurity questions. The ability to compose viral genomes using generative AI now exists; the governance to safely steer it does not.”

Hie and his colleagues used AI models called Evo1 and Evo2 to design the new viral genomes. The models were trained on genetic data from 2 million bacteriophages. The genetic code for viruses that can infect plants, humans or other animals was intentionally excluded from the AI’s training to reduce the risk of it designing dangerous viruses.

The AI generated thousands of potential genomes from which the researchers selected nearly 300 to make in the lab. These were dropped into bacteria, which read the genetic code and churned out the new bacteriophages. The process was not efficient: only 16 bacteriophages proved to be viable, but a cocktail of them swiftly overcame resistance in two different strains of E coli.

Bacteriophage genomes are tiny, but Inglesby and Hanke said the work nevertheless proved that generative AI could create functioning viral genomes. Whether the same approach could be applied to other viruses was unknown, but they said work on pathogens that could infect humans, animals or plants should not be pursued.

“Such genomes might encode new pathogens that … cannot be contained by existing countermeasures,” they wrote.

Tom Ellis, a professor of synthetic genome engineering at Imperial College London, said the work was impressive, but revealed how hard it would be to make more complex genomes. “This is literally the smallest and easiest genome to make,” he said.

An AI trained on the genetic code of dangerous bugs could be used to design more harmful viruses, Ellis said, but controlling access to genetic data and having restrictions on making genomes that look dangerous would help. “Governments are working hard to do this already,” he added.

“But honestly,” he said, “the threat from full AI design and writing of a genome of a virus or bacteria is very overblown when we consider that just taking existing pathogens and making gain-of-function changes to their genomes is so much easier and much more likely to be a real pathogenic threat.”

Dr Filippa Lentzos, a reader in science and international security at King’s College London, said the most important point to intervene at the moment was when DNA was being manufactured. “It’s important to see the bigger governance picture and not focus regulation solely on the AI model,” she said. “A layered approach makes more sense: safeguards around model development and access, responsible research review, synthesis screening, and established laboratory biosafety and biosecurity.”

Tour de France Femmes: Reusser stays ahead as Le Court savours stage win

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 17:50:48 GMT

Mauritian rider outsprints Kerbaol and Pieterse

‘Winning a stage in a Tour de France is very special’

Marlen Reusser retained the overall lead in the Tour de France Femmes from rival Demi Vollering after another broiling stage through central France saw Kim Le Court take the second Tour stage win of her career in Tournon-sur-Rhone.

The Mauritian rider Le Court recovered from a mechanical problem earlier in the stage on the climb of the Col de Lalouvesc to join the day’s breakaway group and outsprint Cédrine Kerbaol of France, and Queen of the Mountains classification leader, Puck Pieterse.

“I was on the limit,” Le Court said of her winning sprint. “I can’t believe I still had the legs to sprint. It was really hard, this close, before I could give up. I will never give up after the big effort my team did.”

Le Court had originally been considered a contender for final victory but lost ground after Tuesday’s individual time trial. “I’ve been really struggling since the time trial day but I think this really makes our Tour,” she said.

“We’ve still got ambitions for the general classification, but winning a stage in a Tour de France is very special. People don’t really remember top 10 or top five riders in Tour, but they do remember stage winners.”

Le Court’s success is a popular one, after a difficult season in which she has dealt with serial injuries. But she has also shown considerable sportsmanship, stopping to help Kasia Niewiadoma after the 2024 Tour Femmes winner crashed heavily in Milan-San Remo.

Despite missing out on the stage victory, it was a successful day for Pieterse as she now has 47 points in the mountain classification, the highest total ever recorded in the history of the Tour de France Femmes.

“I wanted to win the stage of course,” Pieterse said, “but I think I did everything else today. I decided to gamble, but Kim was still the strongest in the sprint, so I don’t think I can be too sad.”

As the heatwave continued, the peloton raced over six classified climbs into the Ardeche, with Friday’s ascent of Mont Ventoux now very much in their thoughts.

After three days she will want to forget, defending champion Pauline Ferrand-Prevot arrested the decline in her form and finished the stage in the group of favourites alongside Reusser, Vollering and Niewiadoma. She is still languishing in 15th place overall, five minutes behind race leader Reusser, and on Wednesday had conceded that: “It’s over.”

However, while her deficit seems almost insurmountable, her rivals will have taken note of her improved performance and of her experience of the Ventoux, which she first rode in 2021.

“I think it’s the most iconic climb in France,” Ferrand-Prevot said of the Provençal mountain. “Everyone knows about it, even if you’re not a cyclist.”

The inclusion of the Ventoux in the Tour de France Femmes is the latest indicator of a race growing in stature, year by year.

“We try to align with the most mythical summits,” Tour de France Femmes director Marion Rousse said. “They’re part of the history of the Tour and the history of the sport.”

Both Vollering and Niewiadoma have prior experience of the mountain, but not at this level of racing, and only from the less demanding north side, rather than the more daunting southern ascent. However, there is no doubt that the ascent of the Ventoux, by a women’s peloton that only a few years ago was derided by some for its abilities, will be a Rubicon moment.

One rider who never shared those doubts is current race leader Reusser. “It’s proof that human beings aren’t always such a smart species,” she said of those who had disparaged the women’s peloton.

In terms of past exploits by women on the “Giant of Provence” Nicole Cooke’s solo attack over the Ventoux, which took her to overall victory in the 2006 Grande Boucle Feminine, is perhaps the most memorable.

“I don’t suppose anybody wanted to chase me all the way up the Ventoux,” Cooke recalled. “The heat was a big factor. People don’t want to chase on a day when the heat is so debilitating.”

Cooke won the stage by four minutes and the race overall by more than six. “After the finish, we went to a cafe and had ice-creams,” she said. “It was one of the special days.”

At that time, women’s cycling had little profile and media coverage was almost nonexistent. Cooke’s achievement never really got the recognition it deserved, due to what she considered to be media’s preoccupation with the prevalence of doping in men’s cycling. The rebirth of the Tour de France Femmes however has dramatically reversed that trend. The heat will also be big factor in toFriday’s stage to the Ventoux, 20 years after Cooke’s own moment in the sun. But the inclusion of a climb that the French still call the “killer mountain”, is a total vindication of the quantum leap achieved by the women’s peloton.

The Guardian view on mental health: the new secretary of state should make it a priority

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 17:30:06 GMT

Parity for people with physical and psychological ailments has been promised for years. New neighbourhood clinics are a step in the right direction

The rise in children and young people with mental health problems makes this week’s announcement of a new network of community clinics in England particularly welcome. A&E departments have recorded an increase in difficult-to-manage symptoms including aggression and hallucinations. New specialist walk-in mental health services should take some of the pressure off. The bringing forward of a deadline for ending out-of-area acute placements, and a pledge to reduce waiting times for children, are also positive.

Declining mental health was among the key themes of Alan Milburn’s interim report on young people and work. It is a big factor behind the rise in claims for illness and disability benefits. Children’s anxiety and other psychological difficulties are also among the many challenges facing schools. Recent years have seen steep rises in emotionally based school avoidance, as well as in autism and neurodiversity.

But while concerns about mental health are shared across government, they have not been prominent in policies put forward by the department where you might expect them to feature most: health. Partly, that is due to other pressing issues including social care and enormous hospital waiting-lists. Partly, it is because ministers have been waiting for a review led by Prof Peter Fonagy into mental health conditions, ADHD and autism. Its recommendations are expected soon, and will feed into an upcoming strategy. In her first interview with the Guardian as health secretary, Yvette Cooper focused on maternity services and the need to prepare for future heatwaves. But the commitment to expand community mental health points to a welcome recognition that this should be an area of focus too.

Parity between mental and physical healthcare became a policy goal in 2011, with the launch of a No Health Without Mental Health initiative. Efforts to stress the importance of psychological wellbeing, and its interconnectedness with physical health, long predate that. The commitment made in last year’s 10-year health strategy to shift resources gradually away from acute hospitals and towards community services would seem to dovetail with this balanced, holistic outlook. But one year on from its launch, experts including Siva Anandaciva, of the King’s Fund, have raised doubts about “whether the NHS really will be committed to the fundamental shift away from hospital care that the health plan proposed”. This week it was revealed that one mental health trust, in east London, is planning to make £230m of cuts. Mental health is not ringfenced within NHS budgets, and as a proportion of overall health spending fell from 9.0% of the total in 2023/24 to 8.78% in 2024/25.

The reasons for the lower priority placed on mental health, compared with physical diseases and injuries, are complex, and reflect cultural as well as structural factors to do with the way that the NHS is organised. Socioeconomic determinants of poor mental health including incomes, work and housing, are outside Ms Cooper’s remit. But the disparities in access to treatment are irrational and unjust. Severe depression and anxiety are highly debilitating conditions. Expectations about waiting times and treatment options need to be clarified.

There are no easy fixes in a system as complicated as the NHS. It is not clear where the new neighbourhood centres fit in existing plans – or who will staff them. But providing that further details are produced in due course, the shift in focus that they signal should be supported.

The controversy sent the book into the bestseller charts, and its author was suspended for bringing the army into disrepute.

A year out from Italy’s next general election, Mr Vannacci is a problem not for the military but for the country’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni. Now a member of the European parliament, in February he exploited his notoriety to found National Future, a political party which argues that Ms Meloni’s coalition government has sold out its far-right supporters through not being extreme enough. The “true right”, according to the former paratrooper – who once served as a military attache in Moscow – should be pro-Putin and anti-Ukraine, anti-EU, and committed to restoring the “cultural homogeneity” of Italy through the expulsion of immigrants and their descendants.

Shockingly, polls are now placing National Future just behind Forza Italia, the second-biggest party in Ms Meloni’s hard-right coalition, and ahead of its third main component, Matteo Salvini’s League. For Ms Meloni, Mr Vannacci’s rapid rise now threatens to become a major dilemma. To beat the combined forces of the left next year she may require the support of a party that does not disguise its sympathy with Italy’s fascist past. But to seek it would give the lie to efforts to present her own Brothers of Italy party (which retains a neo-fascist political symbol in its logo) as part of the mainstream conservative tradition.

The rest of Europe should sit up and take notice of Mr Vannacci’s rise. At a time when Russian influence on the far right is already a cause for concern, he has declared himself open to the idea of funding from Moscow and also Beijing. More broadly, the emergence of National Future confirms that as well as dragging mainstream politics towards more extreme positions on immigration, the continent’s far right is itself radicalising.

Here, the equivalent can be found in Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain party, which has been exerting a rightwards gravitational pull on Reform UK. Poland’s nationalist and Eurosceptic Law and Justice party has embarked on a similar trajectory, in order to compete with two newish and growing far-right parties. In Germany, Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) stands on the brink of a historic breakthrough in state elections in eastern Germany, and leads in national polls.

The ominous political consequences were on display last week in the panicked overreaction of leaders to the crisis in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. With one eye over her right shoulder, Ms Meloni was at the forefront of divisive early calls for action to be taken against Spain following an incursion by irregular migrants. For his part, Mr Vannacci used the incident to amplify his calls for a Europe-wide “remigration” strategy.

Mr Vannacci’s repugnant politics are beyond the pale. In Germany, the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, continues to rule out any form of national alliance with the AfD. Were Ms Meloni to countenance any form of accommodation with Italy’s rogue general, it would demolish her fragile claims to mainstream respectability.

Trump’s legal team sought to stop the discovery order that would have given the BBC access to the president’s financial records in the multibillion-dollar case.

Last month, a Miami-based judge ruled that Trump would have to begin producing extensive financial records by 6 August, including information covering the hundreds of businesses held by the Trump family trust.

On Wednesday, Trump’s attorneys asked the court to temporarily suspend that order, arguing the BBC had demanded a “shockingly broad amount of information based on clearly political motivations”.

In a four-page order signed on Wednesday and released on Thursday, Altman said Trump’s effort to remove his claims that the documentary damaged his brand and businesses could reduce the BBC’s need to obtain his financial records. Trump’s lawyers are seeking to narrow the claim to alleged reputational harm.

The BBC has argued that Trump’s business value remains relevant because his public reputation was closely linked to his success as a businessman.

The broadcaster’s lawyers also pointed out that Trump’s proposed amended complaint, which has not yet been made public, still seeks $10bn in damages. They contend that amount would be difficult to support if the case was based only on reputational harm.

At the center of the lawsuit is a scene from the BBC documentary Trump: A Second Chance, which edited together portions of Trump’s 6 January 2021 speech in a way that made it appear he directly encouraged supporters to attack the US Capitol. The lawsuit is part of a series of legal actions Trump has launched against media organizations over coverage he says is defamatory or unfair.

In a separate case, Trump’s attorneys argued that his $10bn defamation lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal should proceed to trial after the newspaper reported on a “bawdy” letter the president was said to have contributed to a birthday book for Jeffrey Epstein in 2003.

Catholic or not, many of us share Andy Burnham’s beliefs

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 16:46:10 GMT

Readers respond to an article by Julian Coman on Andy Burnham’s faith and the influence of Catholic social teaching on his work

Julian Coman’s article about Andy Burnham resonated with me, as I share his belief in compassion, social responsibility and concern for those who are struggling (Like Burnham, I was an altar boy. His Catholic upbringing is shaping the way he governs, 1 August). Where I differ is in the suggestion that these values are rooted primarily in Catholicism.

I grew up in inner-city Manchester during the Thatcher years, in a low socioeconomic working-class community facing unemployment, poverty and drug misuse. My parents were not religious, but they instilled in me a humanist outlook based on empathy, fairness and our shared responsibilities to one another.

The same values were reinforced at my primary school. In a diverse inner-city neighbourhood, children from different backgrounds learned side by side. Looking back, religion barely featured in our day-to-day lives at school. Faith was generally considered a private matter. What united us was a simple understanding that everyone deserved respect, fairness and kindness. We learned to see one another not as representatives of different beliefs, but as fellow human beings with a shared stake in our community and society.

It was an inclusive environment that left me comfortable and confident in Britain as a diverse society. Through our families, teachers and local community, we came to appreciate the secular institutions that bound us together: the NHS, social housing and the welfare state. Children whose families had lived here for generations learned alongside those whose families had arrived more recently, but there was a shared understanding that these institutions represented something valuable, something to be respected, strengthened and improved. Civic responsibility, inclusivity and social justice were not religious lessons; they were human lessons.

Those values shaped me, too, but they came from a secular humanist upbringing, my community, and Britain’s civic institutions. The compassion that Coman admires in Burnham may well have been strengthened by his Catholic upbringing, but compassion, solidarity and social responsibility are not the preserve of any one faith or worldview. If there is a moral tradition worth celebrating, it’s the broader human one: the belief that we flourish not alone, but through our obligations to one another, regardless of faith. Lorna PetersManchester

Julian Coman’s article was encouraging. The faith communities I know are all deeply involved in politics, justice, homelessness work and much more. At a recent local Labour party meeting, there were two Methodists (I was one), several Catholics and a couple of Quakers.

Coman mentions the Methodist worldview that Margaret Thatcher inherited from her father. But Mrs Thatcher didn’t know her Methodist roots. Our founder, John Wesley, said: “The gospel of Christ knows of no religion, but social; no holiness but social holiness.” So when she said “there is no such thing as society”, she was denying her Methodist roots. Much worse, though, was that she was wrong and set in train the rise of individualism. Rev Richard ParkesNewcastle-under-Lyme, Staffordshire

Julian Coman has it pretty much spot-on. “The problem with Christianity is that no one has ever really tried it,” as my wise mother, Peggy Brown, always said.

While I continue to disappoint myself in that regard, perhaps Andy Burnham will succeed in being the first to preserve integrity and hope in the fire of political separatism and selfishness. John BrownHartford, Cheshire

Andy Burnham is Britain’s first lifelong Roman Catholic prime minister. Tony Blair converted to Catholicism while in office and Boris Johnson, though baptised a Catholic as a baby, converted to Anglicanism at a later stage in his life.

For hundreds of years – after the Protestant Reformation in the 16th century, until the Repeal of the Penal Laws in the early 19th century – Roman Catholics in Britain were stripped of economic, political and religious power. They could not hold civil or military office. They could not get educated, vote or practice a profession. Until 2013, a British royal could not marry a Catholic and, in fact, the monarch today still cannot be a Catholic.

But now, in 2026, we have a Catholic prime minister, who has said his Catholic upbringing means a lot to him. If this upbringing is shaping the way he is governing, we might see a focus on the common good and the influence of the social teachings of the Catholic church, including the need to put the poor and vulnerable first, the dignity of the human person, the dignity of work, the worker and the rights of workers, the call to the family and community, the work towards peace and solidarity in the world, and the care for the stewardship of God’s creation.

Let us wish Andy Burnham luck in his endeavour to create a just and equitable society. Julia O’SheaKilcummin, County Kerry, Ireland

Early release is a sign of a broken prison system

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 16:46:00 GMT

Readers respond to Andy Burnham’s review of controversial measures for the early release of thousands of prisoners to free up space in jails

There is something deeply incongruous about a penal system centred on incarceration having to release prisoners early because it has run out of room to incarcerate them (PM to tighten early release rules but men jailed over PC Harper’s death can be freed, 4 August).

The government’s latest early-release measures may be necessary to prevent our prisons from becoming completely overwhelmed, but they are surely a symptom of a much deeper failure. We appear to be operating a revolving-door policy: tougher sentencing fills the prisons, overcrowding forces early release, public concern produces calls for tougher sentencing, and the cycle begins again. It is rather like baling water out of a sinking boat without ever fixing the hole.

The question we should be asking is not simply how many prisoners we can accommodate, but what imprisonment is actually intended to achieve. If the purpose is punishment, routinely cutting sentences undermines the principle. If it is public protection, we should concentrate prison places on those who pose the greatest risk. And if rehabilitation is the objective, we should question the wisdom of short custodial sentences when properly supervised community sentences can sometimes produce better outcomes.

Early release may therefore be an unavoidable short-term expedient. But it cannot sensibly become a permanent method of managing a prison system whose fundamental assumptions have never been properly examined. Name and address supplied

If the current early-release policy puts women at risk from violent men, and most women in prison have no history of violence, doesn’t it follow that early release should be focused primarily on women prisoners? With a little reorganisation, and resources redirected towards mental health services, whole prisons could presumably be freed up. Marcia SaundersLondon

Lloyds Bank should publish the human cost of its AI savings

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 16:45:49 GMT

Banks should factor in the time spent by humans checking invented facts, writes Dr Gleb Tsipursky

Your report (Lloyds Bank to cut £2bn in costs as part of AI-powered strategy, 30 July) raises a question that financial targets alone cannot answer: who absorbs the work when automation fails?

Banks often count the minutes saved by the employee who uses an AI tool. They should also count the time colleagues spend checking invented facts, repairing customer messages, explaining rejected applications and escalating errors. A system can make one team look more productive while moving risk and effort elsewhere.

Lloyds should publish a simple scorecard for each consequential AI workflow: total time saved across the process, error and rework rates, customer complaints, successful human interventions and changes to entry-level roles. It should also name the executive with authority to pause a system when the evidence turns negative.

The bank’s relationship managers and customers need a clear route to challenge automated recommendations. Staff must be able to report weak outputs without being branded resistant to innovation.

AI may shorten mortgage decisions and improve advice. Those gains will deserve trust only when Lloyds measures the whole workflow and shows that £2bn in savings did not become hidden costs for workers and customers. Dr Gleb TsipurskyBehavioural scientist, Columbus, Ohio, US
