Baby safely delivered 30 minutes after mother died in nine-storey fall

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 16:13:36 GMT

Emma Atkinson, 38, was seven months pregnant when she fell from window of flat in Leeds tower block, inquest told

A pregnant woman who died from a nine-storey fall had her baby safely delivered 30 minutes after her death, an inquest has heard.

Emma Atkinson, 38, was seven months pregnant when she fell from the window of her father’s flat in Shakespeare Towers in the Burmantofts area of Leeds, on 22 October 2024.

Wakefield coroner’s court heard on Thursday that Atkinson was pronounced dead by paramedics who arrived at the scene shortly after she fell at 10.20am. Atkinson’s body was taken to Leeds general infirmary, where an emergency caesarean section was performed.

The baby girl was born soon after arriving at the hospital. She sustained some injuries from the fall, including a punctured lung and fractured tibia, requiring her to remain in intensive care for the first weeks of her life, but has since recovered. The girl, who is now 21 months old, is reportedly “being raised happily” by family members.

In a narrative verdict, the inquest ruled that Atkinson had “deliberately propelled herself” from the window of the tower block, but was unable to decide if she had done so with the intention of ending her own life.

The coroner Naomi McLoughlin said that while “the deliberate act of removing the safety catches from the window” and “the manner of her falling, captured by the CCTV” was significant, other evidence such as the lack of concerning signs in the weeks prior, and the fact she had made plans beyond that day with her family, meant she could not conclusively say Atkinson meant to die when she fell.

The court heard that at the time of her death, Atkinson was suffering from poor mental health and was worried about the possibility of being incarcerated after failing to attend a court date for a shoplifting offence.

Her father, David Atkinson, told the inquest via a summarised statement that his daughter had come to visit him at his flat that morning. While there, she began to smoke a cigarette in front of a window in his living room, which she then opened fully after removing the safety catches.

Atkinson said that he asked his daughter what she was doing, to which she told him “not to worry (as) she was just getting some fresh air”, before she said “I’m off” and fell through the window head first. He also said he believed his daughter had intended to end her own life that morning.

Other members of her family who attended the inquest said Atkinson would not have intentionally taken her own life, stating that she “would never have left her kids” and that her “life revolved around her children”.

The University of Greater Manchester’s embattled vice-chancellor has had his contract terminated by the university’s governing body, ending a period of uncertainty over the university’s leadership.

Sir George Holmes, who had led the university for two decades, was initially suspended last year over allegations involving financial mismanagement and other misconduct.

On Wednesday afternoon staff and students were told that Holmes was no longer employed by the institution, which was previously known as the University of Bolton.

An email to staff said: “Dr George Holmes’s contract as vice-chancellor has been ended by the governing body of the university. Dr Holmes is therefore no longer an employee of the university.”

His position had been under pressure after a series of investigations published by Manchester’s the Mill, which revealed a string of allegations by whistleblowers involving bullying, racism and fraud.

In response, Holmes said he was determined to clear his name and hold the university’s current management to account.

Holmes, 65, said: “The decision of the university’s governing board to terminate my contract in this way after over 20 years of loyal service to the University of Greater Manchester is a travesty.

“I have been denied natural justice, due process and the right to be presumed innocent of all that I have been accused of.”

A spokesperson for the university said Holmes’s employment had been ended earlier this week. Holmes was suspended in May last year following the results of an external investigation commissioned by the university.

The development was welcomed by Phil Brickell, the MP for Bolton West, who had been calling for a resolution to protect the university from further fallout during the vital student recruitment period this autumn.

Brickell said: “Now that we know that George Holmes is no longer the vice-chancellor of the university, it is vital that the institution focuses on restoring confidence, ensuring strong governance and maintaining its commitment to students, staff and the wider community.

“There is an ongoing police investigation but once concluded the university should seek to draw a line under this affair, learn any lessons arising from it and move forward in a way that delivers the best outcomes for its staff, students and the people of Bolton.

“Stability, transparency and a clear focus on educational excellence will be essential in the period ahead.”

The university said the current acting vice-chancellor, Greg Walker, would remain in place and the governing body would “meet in due course to consider the process and timelines for appointing a permanent head of the institution”.

Last year, Greater Manchester police (GMP) said detectives and investigators from its major incident team had been looking into “suspected fraud and bribery” relating to the case and searched seven properties in Greater Manchester and the south of England to seize evidence.

In July this year, three people were arrested as part of the investigation, with GMP saying it was “exploring evidence” of more than £1m in alleged fraudulent activity between 2014 and 2025 involving 60 transactions and more than 1m emails.

GMP carried out arrest warrants at two addresses in Bolton and three others in Lancashire, Humberside and West Yorkshire, arresting two men in their 60s and a woman in her 50s.

All three were arrested on suspicion of money laundering, while both men were also arrested on suspicion of fraud and one of them on suspicion of bribery.

The three people arrested have been released on bail without being charged.

Andy Burnham’s government is “urgently” identifying any grooming gang perpetrators who may still be eligible for early prison release after concerns were raised about a potential loophole in the system.

The prime minister has “personally intervened” after men convicted of assaulting children in Bradford were expected to be freed from prison early despite a promise earlier this week that they would remain behind bars.

In a statement, No 10 said it would ensure that “everything possible is being done so that vile groomers are dealt with in the way their victims deserve”.

About 5,000 people are expected to be released early under sentencing changes in England and Wales, down from 6,000 after ministers excluded grooming gang members, rapists and “serious” child sex offenders from the scheme designed to reduce overcrowding in jails.

Critics have questioned the scope of the exemptions after reports that some men convicted in relation to historical grooming gang cases could be among those freed.

Some of the offending took place before sexual abuse laws were changed in 2003 and the perpetrators were charged with crimes such as indecent assault, which do not fall within the exclusions to the scheme starting in October.

A spokesperson for Burnham said: “As part of the review of sentences, the prime minister asked the Ministry of Justice to conduct an in-depth review of cases to ensure that grooming cases were identified.

“This work is happening urgently. This is extremely important to the PM and he has personally intervened to ensure everything possible is being done so that vile groomers are dealt with in the way their victims deserve.”

Burnham suspended the scheme in his second week as prime minister after coming under intense pressure from MPs, victims, campaigners and frontline prison officers to halt the early release of serious sexual and violent offenders.

Prisons have become a major point of political contention, with Labour blaming the Conservatives for creating the overcrowding crisis between 2010 and 2024 by increasing sentences while failing to build enough jails.

The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, wrote to Burnham on Thursday demanding to know which offences would be eligible for early release and accusing the government of “yet another betrayal of the victims”.

As first disclosed by the Times, there are a number of instances where men convicted of assaulting children in Bradford as part of historical investigations into Asian grooming gangs were not excluded from the early release scheme.

As many of the assaults took place before anti-grooming laws were introduced in 2003, the men were charged with indecent assault, which does not fall within the exemptions announced by the prime minister this week.

The government has also resisted pressure to exempt two of PC Andrew Harper’s killers from early release as the boss of his former force considers joining a potential legal challenge over the plans.

Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers could be freed halfway through their 13-year sentences for manslaughter after the officer’s death in 2019.

Harper sustained fatal injuries after getting caught in a strap attached to the back of a car and being dragged down a country road as the killers fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Sulhamstead, Berkshire. The driver of the vehicle, Henry Long, received a 16-year sentence for manslaughter and will not be eligible for release under the scheme.

The Thames Valley police chief constable, Jason Hogg, said he was receiving legal advice on whether the force could join a legal challenge mooted by the local Police Federation chief, Aileen O’Connor, to prevent Cole and Bowers being freed.

The prime minister has said he wanted to “go further” with the exemptions, but this was “not possible without the prison system reaching capacity and collapsing”.

Those released will face tougher probation conditions, including electronic monitoring, random drug testing and possible bans from driving, pubs and events such as football matches.

The changes were part of the Sentencing Act passed earlier this year, which cut the minimum amount of time many offenders would have to spend in prison.

The social media algorithm has left me behind. I’m unc and I’m chopped – and that’s OK

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 15:00:05 GMT

If you have to Google an internet or Gen Z/alpha slang term, you absolutely shouldn’t be using it. I’m accepting this milestone with quiet dignity

I’ve recently reached an important adult milestone in my life. Getting married? No. Having a baby? No. Buying a house? Don’t be ridiculous, I’m a writer in Australia. This milestone was small, but important: I finally had to Google a Gen Z slang term.

I know this may be something many of you have passed already, along with your houses and babies, but it’s only recently started looming on the horizon for me. I am someone who has been online for a long time. It’s been necessary for my career, but it’s also my favourite hobby: going on the internet.

I never needed to research slang, not because I use the terms, or have a specific interest in the youth of today, but because spending a lot of time on the internet meant I absorbed them through osmosis. It’s science! I would see a post start popping off in a far flung corner of the world and watch as it migrated platforms. I knew the context. I knew who was using it. I knew when it should be used. I knew when it was already embarrassing to use it. I wasn’t speaking the language, but I was fluent. Now, I’m joining the ranks of the bamboozled elderly and Googling “quiet on the creek”.

My parents might have been able to keep up with slang back when people my age were doing it, but the craziest we got was “roflcopter” and “pwned”. The internet was less fragmented. There was a time when someone terminally online could feel as if they had a rough map of the place, and knew where all the cultural hubs were.

Today’s internet has no centre.

Instead of one internet, there are endless overlapping internet microcultures, each with their own language evolving independently. Reddit, Discord, twitch, TikTok, streaming culture, gaming culture – they all experience an endless flow of changing language. It’s no longer possible to understand everything, even if you wanted to. Technology and culture is moving so fast, all the time, it makes sense that young people are constantly coming up with new terms.

There are pedants and young people haters out there who get het up about the slang and the memes and the 6-7 of it all, but generally, I love it. Some slang terms, the ones that trickle down from streaming or “incel” culture, can be ugly or negative. Many of the more creative or sticky terms originate in POC or queer culture. A lot of what makes it to the mainstream is clever, or funny, or right. For example, it’s already probably outdated now, but “rizz” for “charisma” is delightful.

I appreciate the rapid evolution of language, the inventive wordplay, even if it does get annoying at times. Some of it will stick, some will get left behind. But now I no longer have a front row seat. The algorithm has left me behind. That’s OK, it has to be that way. As you can see, I am accepting this with quiet dignity. Others should follow my example – if you have to Google a slang term, you absolutely shouldn’t be using it. If you are a politician or police PR person, please avoid using slang to try to appeal to young people. It will never work, it will only ever embarrass you, and in some cases kill the poor term dead in its tracks.

I’m personally still going to keep finding out what slang means for my own interest, and to ensure I can make some sense of what the kids in my life are trying to communicate, but I know my limits. I’m no longer absorbing the language just by being online; I am studying it. I’m unc and chopped – and that’s OK.

Rebecca Shaw is a writer based in Sydney

BBC hires 26-year-old entrepreneur to help reach younger audiences

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 15:00:04 GMT

Brandon Relph, who founded first company at 13, joins strategy team in ‘much-needed step’ for the broadcaster

A 26-year-old business prodigy and self-styled gen Z whisperer has been drafted in by the BBC as it battles to reach young audiences increasingly choosing content creators on YouTube and TikTok over traditional broadcasters.

Brandon Relph, who founded his first company aged 13, and has been praised by Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak, has joined the BBC’s strategy team to help counter the existential threat of falling audiences among young people.

Relph has jokingly described himself as “the go-to guy who knows the youth” and has already had a dizzying career. He made his first £10,000 before the age of 16 with a company based around the Minecraft video game and founded several other tech and marketing companies as a teenager.

The BBC, along with all broadcasters, is facing a huge generational shift in the way young audiences consume media. While 78% of the over-75s still watch live TV on a television in the course of a month, less than half of 16 to 24-year-olds do so, turning instead to content creators on digital platforms such as YouTube.

Matt Brittin, the new director general brought in for his experience in the tech world, has pledged to reshape the BBC as part of the renewal of its royal charter, which is being negotiated with ministers.

Prioritising digital content will be reflected in the major cuts being made across the BBC’s services. The corporation is already trying to adapt, recently announcing a deal to produce bespoke YouTube content.

Relph, who previously claimed the title of the UK’s youngest ever chief executive, has specialised in talking to executives about marketing to young audiences, stating his businesses have been “built on people’s lack of understanding of our generation”.

His exploits have included building a large online audience for live video gameshows, while his company also built a Minecraft version of a Tesla after he and his business partner met Elon Musk at a convention.

Those familiar with his past entrepreneurial efforts said he had encountered resistance within the media industry to embrace online content creators, which he sees as necessary to reach young audiences. That resistance is now melting away.

Another of his projects, touted as a “Netflix for the creator generation”, could not find the venture capital needed. Relph was subsequently hired by the consulting firm Accenture, from where he joined the BBC.

Relph has already started in the BBC’s strategy team, with insiders praising his gen Z focus. Previous colleagues described him as a “special case”, stating he was popular with his teams and willing to politely question senior executives over their strategy despite his young age.

His appointment has been praised by figures pushing the BBC to take a radically different approach to reaching young audiences, but they also said it needed to reflect a wider effort.

“Brandon looks great – he’s somebody who’s had a very successful career, done brilliant work and is obviously very talented,” said Jordan Schwarzenberger, the manager of the Sidemen YouTube collective. “He’s clearly an entrepreneur at heart.

“The BBC’s challenge is a bigger issue than one hire. They need to address that institutional media, distributed traditionally, can’t reach an audience who have simply gone to other places. Young audiences are not watching linear. And the BBC is pretty much built upon its linear broadcasting foundation.”

Relph has previously criticised the iPlayer over its user experience and said that the “BBC won’t have a long term future” without a greater focus on younger people.

Some in the BBC argue its efforts to adapt to young audiences are already well under way. It is the only UK brand in the top five most used media for the 16-34 age group, alongside YouTube, Instagram, Facebook and Netflix. It still reaches 63% of the age group on average, each week. However, BBC figures are acutely aware of the scale of the challenge.

“Brandon’s appointment is a much-needed step,” said Jo Redfern, a former BBC insider and digital media expert. “Anyone tasked with making the BBC indispensable to the under-24s requires a momentum internally and externally because there’s an urgency.

By day five of my labour, I didn’t want an ‘ideal birth’. I only wanted to survive

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 15:00:03 GMT

Yvette Cooper’s maternity reforms must change a system that too often fails women when they’re at their most vulnerable

On the third day of being in labour with my first child, I entered a new state of being. It was time to dig deep. This is what I had learned in all the childbirth classes. As long as I remained calm, breathed as instructed, moaned through the pain, things would happen as they were meant to. My body knew what it was doing. Only, it didn’t.

On the fourth day, I started to beg. This wasn’t right. Despite contraction after relentless contraction, I wasn’t dilating. I hadn’t slept, I couldn’t even sit down. I needed help. And still, they waited. For what, I never understood.

When Yvette Cooper told the Guardian this week that women must not “feel pressurised” to have “an ideal birth experience”, it was a relief to hear her name this all-too-common phenomenon in which maternity staff are reluctant – or refusing – to escalate. But Cooper’s characterisation of the problem is not the full picture. The harm here is not just in women being nudged towards a certain kind of birth experience, but in a culture that can completely override women’s physical and psychological safety in favour of a low-intervention ideal.

Half of Britain’s maternal deaths are considered preventable, and low-intervention births are the ideal for a reason. Midwife-led care usually results in better outcomes for healthy women with straightforward pregnancies – lower risk of infection and severe bleeds, and quicker recovery. In 2024-25, 45% of all hospital deliveries in England (542,235 total births) were performed via caesarean section – it was the first time C-sections outnumbered unassisted natural vaginal births. (Another 11% needed extra support through instruments such as forceps.) There is a natural, and warranted, cautiousness about the over-medicalisation of birth, which can lead to avoidable complications, and leave women who would prefer a natural birth feeling pressured to take a different route. But we can’t ignore that there are also structural forces at play here: lower intervention also translates to lower cost for an overstretched, under-resourced system. One midwife told me explicitly that they would have admitted me to the labour ward earlier if there had been a bed.

Of course most first-time mothers would choose the lowest possible intervention if they could. I had hoped to float blissfully in a birthing pool under the soft glow of fairy lights. But when it comes to the messy, unpredictable, dangerous act of bringing new life into the world, the concept of choice can quickly be revealed as a fallacy. By day five of my labour, I was not thinking about my birth plan. I was not thinking about very much at all. My only focus was survival.

The demographic of people giving birth today looks nothing like it did 30 years ago. The average age of a mother in England and Wales is now 31, a figure that has been creeping up since records began. There is something deeply flawed about a system that pushes quite so strongly for low-intervention births despite the fact that mothers over 30 are more likely to require a higher level of medical involvement. Almost half of UK women aged 30-39 have caesareans, and for those over 40, it is now the most common way to give birth. Yet the narrative of an “ideal birth” persists, leaving women who end up needing more help wondering where they went wrong. Maternity practices must reflect this reality, or risk perpetuating a cycle that leaves women at risk and then pushes the blame back on to them.

After the best part of a week, I was eventually wheeled down for an emergency C-section. Even then, it wasn’t the desperate pleas from my husband and me that finally spurred action, it was the fact that my baby started showing signs of distress. The doctors who greeted us displayed clear consternation that I had been left in that state for so long, a factor that probably played a part in my child developing an irregular heartbeat. The ideal birth narrative – that low-intervention, midwife-led care is always best – has hardened into institutional bias, amid a system in which women’s choices about their medical care are too often sidelined.

In one of her first acts as health secretary, Cooper said she intends to reintroduce binding national maternity standards. They will include ending the postcode lottery for levels of care, and tackling racial inequalities that have meant worse outcomes for poorer and for black and Asian women. Her promises sound reassuring, but we have heard similar things before. What’s needed is a fundamental cultural shift so that women’s voices are treated as clinical evidence, not background noise.

There is a deep-rooted disconnect in NHS maternity units. Between the needs of patients and the people treating them, and between different parts of the system itself. When midwife-led care and obstetric intervention are positioned in opposition, rather than as complementary approaches, escalation can be perceived as failure instead of necessary care. And in that gap, women at their most vulnerable have their pain minimised and their instincts questioned, sometimes to the point that risk becomes life-threatening.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Trauma is a brutal introduction to motherhood, and one that is all too common. For me and thousands of other mothers, our births could have gone so differently if we had only been heard. My ideal birth is not defined by candlelight or calm breathing. It is one where I am listened to, believed and responded to in time. One that both my baby and I survive at any cost.

Natalie Morris is the author of Mixed/Other: Explorations of Multiraciality in Modern Britain

E-scooters far more dangerous than motorbikes or cycles, analysis suggests

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 15:00:03 GMT

Study of accidents in England and Wales shows e-scooter riders three times more likely to suffer traumatic brain injury than bikers

Electric scooter riders are three times more likely to suffer traumatic brain injuries than motorcyclists, according to an analysis of accidents in England and Wales – which found women were particularly at risk of serious harm.

Brain injuries accounted for more than a third of adult injuries on e-scooters, but riders also sustained more internal organ and blood vessel damage than did motorcyclists or pedal cyclists, the study found.

The government has backed trials of rental e-scooters in England since 2020, but an additional 1m or so e-scooters are privately owned in the UK. These cannot legally be used on public roads, paths or cycle lanes, but police forces across the country have confiscated thousands because their owners were breaking the law.

The accident analysis reveals that women were involved in about a third more collisions than men – and were more than twice as likely to report severe injuries. Children were also at risk with, 16% of e-scooter injuries in under 18s.

The findings have led to calls to make e-scooters more stable and safer, especially for women who suffer more chest injuries because the handlebars are typically set at a height for men. Mandatory safety training and making helmets compulsory would also help, experts said.

David Bodansky, a consultant hand, trauma and orthopaedic surgeon at Chelsea and Westminster hospital NHS foundation trust, turned to the national major trauma registry to analyse injuries from e-scooter, motorbike and bicycle collisions in 18 cities in England and Wales between 2020 and 2022.

He found e-scooter riders were more than three times as likely to suffer traumatic brain injury or blood vessel damage and 1.5 times more likely to injure internal organs than motorbike riders, and they fared worse than cyclists for these injuries. Their risk of bone fractures was lower, however, than cyclists or motorcyclists.

The data shed no light on why e-scooters are involved in so many accidents, but Bodansky believes that design is a factor. “They’ve got very small wheels and it’s very easy to jam one of those into a pothole. You’ll then go head over heels over the front and land on your head,” he said. Less than 6% of e-scooter riders reported wearing a helmet, according to the study, in Scientific Reports.

While some previous work found women were more likely to ride e-scooters on the pavement, other research saw no sex differences. In a 2024 study, Dr Petya Ventsislavova, senior lecturer in transport psychology at Nottingham Trent University, found more than half of e-scooter riders rode on pavements, and with another person at the same time, while men reported using their phones and shooting red lights more than did women.

“These figures highlight the urgent need for comprehensive legislation governing private e-scooters,” said Ventsislavova. The legislation should clarify not only where and how e-scooters can be used but also include mandatory safety training, she said.

“Unlike cars and motorcycles, e-scooters were introduced without any requirement for formal training, despite being motorised vehicles,” she said. “E-scooters handle very differently from bicycles. Riders stand upright, have a higher centre of gravity, use more sensitive steering, and are more vulnerable to sudden stops caused by small wheels striking kerbs, potholes or road debris. These characteristics make them inherently less stable and contribute to the severity of injuries when crashes occur.”

A Department for Transport spokesperson said: “These are concerning findings, and our thoughts are with anyone who has been injured on our roads. Road safety is our top priority, which is why our e-scooter trials are testing their use in a controlled environment now, before updating the law to ensure they can be used safely more widely.”

‘James Dean has got nothing on that kid’: River Phoenix films – ranked!

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 14:35:22 GMT

As Stand By Me is re-released for its 40th anniversary, we look at the late actor’s most intense, enduring roles – from a goofball boffin to a narcoleptic hustler

Issue-of-the-week TV movie about elder abuse, with Tuesday Weld as a harried mum taking out her frustrations on her own ageing mother. Phoenix slaps on the hair gel as the essentially decent son who blasts his music too loud, lets his rowdy if unusually spiffy pals put their feet on the furniture and resents the new house guest: “Grandma is really getting on my nerves!”

Sam Shepard’s turgid western premiered at Sundance in early 1993, then sat on the shelf for a year. As with his unfinished final film, Dark Blood, Phoenix plays a desert-dwelling widower gone mad with grief. In this case, his father (Richard Harris) steals a second wife for him from the travelling showman (Alan Bates) who sold him his first. Nuance is not required from Phoenix here, just doleful, brooding twitchiness. A family connection: his brother Joaquin later played Harris’s son, too, in Gladiator.

Directed by Peter Bogdanovich, this was the last film Phoenix completed. Samantha Mathis (his then girlfriend), Dermot Mulroney and a pre-fame Sandra Bullock are aspiring country-and-western musicians convening in Nashville, but their warm, lively work only underlines how ill at ease Phoenix seems on screen. As the most gifted performer of the bunch, he is remote in ways that can’t easily be explained away as acting choices. “He looks ill,” observed the critic Roger Ebert, who thought the performance “should have been seen by someone as a cry for help”.

Espionage for dummies. Phoenix is the all-American high-schooler Jeff, who has no inkling that he is really Nikita, son of Russian sleeper agents. That’s until undercover FBI man Sidney Poitier cosies up to him and spills the beans. Both deserve better than this minefield of spy-movie cliches, but you’ll never catch Phoenix coasting. He delivers the line “Truth has no meaning in this house!” with all the conviction of James Dean in Rebel Without a Cause screaming, “You’re tearing me apart!”

Despite a strong cast (Ellen Burstyn, Molly Ringwald, Paul Sorvino) and direction by British television veteran Waris Hussein (Doctor Who, Henry VIII and His Six Wives), this TV movie about a teen suicide pact is mostly soapy and simplistic. Phoenix is affectingly uninhibited, though, as the grieving sibling: “Boy, he must have hated us,” he weeps after the death of his beloved older brother. He won a Young Artist award for his troubles, beating his co-star, Poltergeist poppet Heather O’Rourke, who died three years later at the age of 12.

A little more than half of Phoenix’s final movie was in the can when he died of a drug overdose on 31 October 1993. Director George Sluizer stole the footage to prevent it being destroyed, then used stills and narration to plug the gaps in a patchwork cut which premiered in 2012, two years before his own death. Phoenix plays a widowed recluse who rescues a married couple (Jonathan Pryce and Judy Davis) after their Bentley breaks down near his desert shack; Knife in the Water-style thriller dynamics ensue. Phoenix is a haunted, enigmatic presence but only Davis’s performance truly coheres. On-set tensions were rife between her and Sluizer; he accused her of giving Phoenix hell, though producer Stephen Woolley recalls the young actor kissing Davis’s feet.

Broad, wacky comedy about a wronged wife (Tracey Ullman) plotting to murder her philandering husband (Kevin Kline, whose performance in A Fish Called Wanda beat Phoenix to the best supporting actor Oscar in 1989). She is encouraged and assisted by, variously, her own mother (Joan Plowright), who sets the plan in motion; an earnest hippy (Phoenix), whom the couple employ at their pizza joint, and who has his own reasons for wanting the husband out of the way; and a pair of stoned amateur hit-men (William Hurt and Keanu Reeves). Phoenix denied that his character, with his crystals, beads and mysticism, bore any resemblance to himself (“Nope, no similarities whatsoever”) but he feels at the very least like a riff on the actor’s persona.

According to Esquire magazine, Phoenix was embarrassed by the commercialism of this engaging code-breaking caper, and even advised his friends not to watch it. Admittedly, there isn’t a whole lot for him to do on screen, but at least he and Poitier, previously paired in Little Nikita, get to participate in a superior espionage adventure this time around. They’re part of the eccentric tech-security team headed by Robert Redford (who had just picked Brad Pitt for the lead role coveted by Phoenix in the fly-fishing drama A River Runs Through It). The rest of Redford’s crew includes David Strathairn and Dan Aykroyd, who in one scene is wearing a T-shirt advertising Aleka’s Attic, the jangly folk-pop outfit fronted by Phoenix.

Phoenix was a reluctant heartthrob, so it follows that his one bona fide teen movie would be unorthodox and melancholy. As Jimmy, a slick, priapic but troubled young poet whose sexual partners include one of his mother’s friends, Phoenix flirts with the dislikable and unsympathetic. In one scene, he loses interest during his girlfriend’s elaborate masked-intruder sex fantasy: “I don’t feel like Jack the Ripper today.” In another, he is scolded by his best pal (a pre-Friends Matthew Perry), who tells him: “Your goddam pecker leads you around like a mule chasing a carrot.” Twentieth Century Fox re-edited the movie as a splashy comedy; director William Richert’s cut, retitled Aren’t You Even Gonna Kiss Me Goodbye? after his original novel, is the classier version. He and Phoenix were reunited when Richert played the Falstaffian vagabond Bob in My Own Private Idaho. Richert died in 2022; his website still advertises a crowd-funding campaign to pay for “deepface [sic] technology” that would insert Phoenix into the director’s version of The Man with the Iron Mask.

The most delirious part of this threequel is its breakneck, origin-story prologue, with Phoenix (who was recommended for the role by his Mosquito Coast co-star Harrison Ford) showing how the young Indiana Jones acquired his bullwhip, battered fedora, chin scar and ophidiophobia. It’s such a hoot that only a spoilsport would ask why a strictly-parented Boy Scout in 1912 Utah sports the unruly surfer-dude fringe of a 1980s teen idol.

Joe Dante used his Gremlins clout to make this charming goofball fantasy starring Phoenix and Ethan Hawke, both 14, as friends who build and pilot a rinky-dink spaceship. Making his movie debut after several years of TV work, Phoenix was already on course to be a teen pin-up but was cast against type as the boffin Wolfgang. Hawke recalls seeing his co-star for the first time walking back and forth outside their motel: “[I] asked him what he was doing, and he said he was trying to figure out how Wolfgang walked … from that moment forward he was always ahead of me.” Next to him, said Hawke, “I never felt more ordinary in my life.”

Peter Weir’s dogged, Paul Schrader-scripted adaptation of Paul Theroux’s novel about a ranting, idealistic inventor who drags his family off to live in the Central American rainforests is dominated by Harrison Ford’s oppressive performance. The rest of the cast, including Helen Mirren as his wife, scarcely get a look-in, though Phoenix makes a strong impression as the adoring eldest son whose idolatry gives way to mounting horror at his father’s murderous insanity. Phoenix’s then-girlfriend, Martha Plimpton, has a memorable scene in which she speaks for his thousands of teenage fans by admitting: “I think of you when I go to the bathroom.”

Hot from his Oscar nomination for Running on Empty, Phoenix was granted director approval for this drama about a group of callous young Marines competing in a “dogfight” to find the ugliest date during their last night before being shipped off to Okinawa, and then to Vietnam. He wisely chose the film-maker Nancy Savoca, who brings a complex tenderness to the emotional tussles between Eddie (Phoenix) and his prey, the shy waitress and amateur balladeer Rose (Lili Taylor), who turns out to be nobody’s fool. Phoenix doesn’t soft-pedal Eddie’s cruelty, which makes his pangs of conscience even more resonant. “How did we get to be so full of shit?” he asks his fellow Marines the morning after the dogfight before. “How did we become these fucking idiots?”

If modern audiences want to know why Phoenix was so loved, said Ethan Hawke in 2014, “Go watch Stand By Me … James Dean has got nothing on that kid.” As the toughest but most complicated of the 12-year-old friends who trek into the woods to find a corpse in the late Rob Reiner’s film of Stephen King’s novella The Body, Phoenix evokes vividly the boy’s inner tensions, his hurt at the unfairness of his bad reputation; “I’d like to go some place where nobody knows me,” he sobs. Then there’s his exit. Each of the actor’s three greatest films gives him a killer final shot which has only gained in poignancy since his death. But it is his silent farewell in Stand by Me – waving at the camera, then plodding away and literally dissolving into thin air as the voiceover reveals that his character died prematurely – that hits the hardest.

Phoenix received his only Oscar nomination for this fine drama about a pair of former radicals (Christine Lahti and Judd Hirsch) wanted by the FBI for their involvement in a bombing years earlier. He plays their eldest son, a sensitive piano prodigy who has learned never to let down his guard, which causes complications when he falls for his music teacher’s daughter (Plimpton). Under the direction of veteran auteur Sidney Lumet, who declared that Phoenix “couldn’t be ordinary if he tried”, the actor is achingly sad and true as the boy unfairly shouldering his parents’ burdens. It’s striking, too, that even in his short career, Phoenix starred in so many portraits of mysterious, idealistic and/ or itinerant families not unlike his own. This one, though, is the best.

Three decades ago, queer parts for straight-identifying actors were still thought of largely as awards bids (see William Hurt’s transparently covetous performance in Kiss of the Spider Woman) or career-killers (even at the end of the 1990s, Matt Damon, Brad Pitt and Leonardo DiCaprio all turned down Brokeback Mountain). In that context, the boldness of Phoenix and Keanu Reeves in unselfconsciously playing sex workers in My Own Private Idaho, a kind of Midnight Cowboy cross-pollinated with Shakespeare’s Henry plays, should not be underestimated.

But the narcoleptic hustler Mike, who turns tricks while searching for his mother, was no ordinary job for Phoenix. “He was already this amazing actor,” said writer-director Gus Van Sant, “but with this film, he was able to have an effect on what the film was becoming … He was very excited he could control the destiny of his character.” The most obvious example is the campfire confession in which Mike admits his true feelings for Scott, the Prince Hal figure played by Reeves. The dialogue was scripted by Phoenix himself and scribbled on napkins, the scene moved to the end of the shoot so that he could build up to it emotionally. “The character I wrote was blasé and noncommittal,” said Van Sant. “River made him gay and committal; he redeemed him with emotions.”

He did the same for the film, too. Van Sant’s innovative touches – shirtless studs coming to life on the covers of porn magazines, or the eerie pseudo-freeze-framed sex scenes – are cunning and cool, but it is Phoenix’s performance, from his opening orgasm to his final collapse on a deserted country road, that gives the movie its heart and its kick.

Farmer who killed lodger and hid body in concrete in South Yorkshire jailed for life

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 14:33:16 GMT

Christopher Wright, 73, who shot Richard Dyson and dismembered his remains, given 35-year minimum term

A man who killed his lodger and concealed his dismembered body in a barrel filled with concrete for more than five years has been jailed for a minimum of 35 years.

Christopher Wright, a 73-year-old farmer from South Yorkshire, was convicted in July in Sheffield crown court of murdering Richard Dyson, 55, in 2019.

Dyson had been living in his car on Wright’s farm in Hoyland and had been doing jobs for the then 67-year-old when the pair had a falling out.

Wright, an antique firearms collector who was described as a “weapons fanatic” during his trial, suspected Dyson of stealing some of his prized possessions and selling them.

The court heard that when Wright confronted Dyson with his suspicions in November 2019 an argument broke out that ended with Dyson being shot in the chest and arm with a shotgun, killing him.

Wright, a former butcher, dismembered Dyson’s body over the course of several days, then placed the remains in a barrel which he filled with concrete. He then placed the barrel in a trailer and asked an unsuspecting neighbour to keep the vehicle on their property.

Wright was aided in covering up his crime by Karl Schwalbe, a lifelong friend who received a three-year sentence for conspiracy to pervert the course of justice.

Dyson’s disappearance was initially treated as a missing person inquiry and his remains went undiscovered for more than five and a half years.

While South Yorkshire police were aware that he had been on Wright’s land in the days leading up to his disappearance, they could not find evidence implicating the farmer, who denied any knowledge of Dyson’s whereabouts.

Dyson remained missing until July 2025 when police, driven by new evidence that showed Wright had contacted a local farmer about storing a vehicle on his property in the days after Dyson disappeared, searched the farm and found a barrel containing concrete and human remains, which were later identified as Dyson’s.

Speaking after sentencing him on Thursday, Mr Justice Cotter told Wright he would probably die in prison and said the killer’s experience as a butcher made him “skilled enough to do such a terrible thing, something few ordinary people would have the stomach for”.

Dyson’s daughter Bethany Dainty, who filed a missing person report in the days after her father was murdered, read a victim impact statement in court detailing how hard it had been not knowing her father’s fate: “I couldn’t grieve because I did not know the truth.”

She added: “While I cried myself to sleep, while I begged for answers, while I prayed my dad would walk through the door again, someone already knew where he was. Someone watched me suffer for years and said nothing. That level of cruelty is impossible for me to understand.”

After the sentencing, DCI Andy Knowles praised Dyson’s family for the strength they showed during a “long, complex and emotionally draining” investigation.

Knowles said: “Wright and Schwalbe knew what happened to Richard and even with the evidence against them, they continued to deny accountability, making Richard’s family endure a trial, listen to harrowing evidence and distressing testimonies.

“The strength and dignity in confronting each moment of this process has been nothing short of extraordinary.”

The Ugandan parliament observed a minute of silence in Owori’s honour on Wednesday.

In June Sydney Gongodyo, a Ugandan rugby international, ​died after a mob attacked him in Kampala, mistaking him for a thief, police said.

Uganda’s National Council of Sports said: “Sadly, ​Ugandan sport has been hit with many such ​tragedies lately, and we hope for justice and a lasting solution.”

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 14:30:00 GMT

Their parents were Womack & Womack, Uncle Bobby was a superstar and so was their grandfather, Sam Cooke. The trio explain how, after driving Ubers and being told soul was dead, they joined the family business

Backstage at a London festival, on a Sunday afternoon, the Womack Sisters are assembling themselves on a sofa, still clad in the clothes they were wearing on stage a few minutes ago. They look very stylish in their black dresses, tights and high heels, but they are not, it has to be said, dressed appropriately for the weather, which is sweltering. “You don’t feel anything on stage,” says Zeimani with a shrug. “You just feel amazing, like you’re floating.”

“And we’re committed,” nods her sister BG. “You know, we were taught by professionals.”

Indeed they were. BG, Zeimani and Kucha Womack’s father was Cecil Womack: he wrote Teddy Pendergrass’s oft-sampled classic Love TKO, as well as hits for the O’Jays, the Four Tops and Patti LaBelle, and was one half of Womack and Womack, of Love Wars and Teardrops fame. The other half was their mother, Linda Womack, the daughter of “king of soul” Sam Cooke. Their uncle was Bobby Womack, who initially performed with Cecil in early-60s band the Valentinos – their most famous song was It’s All Over Now, later covered by the Rolling Stones – before going on to record a string of classics that earned him the unofficial soubriquet The Greatest Soul Singer in the World: from Across 110th Street to If You Think You’re Lonely Now to the triumphant final album he made before his death in 2014, The Bravest Man in the Universe. Their half-brother’s mum, meanwhile, was Mary “My Guy” Wells.

Given their heritage, Zeimani says her father thought a career in anything other than music was a waste of time: when she approached him with the idea that she might go to medical school, he reacted with something approaching horror. “He said, ‘Just go in the studio and make music.’ I told him I needed to have a Plan B. He was like, ‘Plan B? Do Plan A, go hard, get on it.’”

In fairness, the Womack Sisters had long been apprenticed in the family business. They had spent their childhood travelling the world with their parents: Compass Point Studios in the Bahamas or Bob Marley’s studio in Jamaica; homes in Bangkok, Phuket, Johannesburg, London and, slightly less glamorously, Southend-on-Sea. “We were raised between London, Thailand, Paris and Amsterdam, but mostly here in London,” recalls Kucha. Their mum and dad didn’t just take the kids along with them, they got them involved “in everything they did, in the studio, on stage, in meetings. They wanted to make sure that we knew what they were doing with their time, so they communicated with us a lot.”

BG says that if I had interviewed her parents back then, “We would have been in the interview. If they went on a television show, we were on the couch with them.”

Zeimani made her first public appearance as a baby, in her mother’s arms on the cover of Womack and Womack’s Conscience, the 1988 album featuring Teardrops. The sisters made their recording debut, alongside their four other siblings, on the 1993 album Transformation to the House of Zekkariyas. “We opened their shows,” remembers Zeimani. “And it was the start of us realising that we could be a group, because before, we were just sisters. ‘Yo, actually this is a good feeling, I could do this for the rest of my life.’”

But still, she says, “we didn’t take our dad’s advice”. They decided they did need a Plan B. “We were a little hard-headed. We wanted to go out and explore.”

The three sisters moved to Los Angeles and attempted to balance regular jobs with getting a musical career off the ground. There was a cleaning company, and a brief stint, as Zeimani puts it, of “selling drugs”, which turns out to mean they ran a marijuana dispensary. But it wasn’t as easy as they had hoped. “We kept getting fired,” says BG. “I got fired from Zara for trying to take a couple of trips out of town for shows.” The sisters also drove Uber taxis. “Uber was a lifesaver! I swear, without it I would have been turning tricks,” BG laughs.

To compound their problems, there was the music industry’s attitude towards them. The group “always had soul in mind,” says Zeimani – they were huge fans of Amy Winehouse – but the labels they met with kept pushing them towards pop. “We would go to them with our demos and tell them what we would like to accomplish, with a live band, an orchestra, everything. They were just like, ‘Soul’s not what’s happening right now, here in the States, particularly for brown artists.’ So for years we were trying other things. We dabbled in R&B. They even had us rapping a couple of times.”

Hang on – are you saying you were told that Black artists shouldn’t make soul music?

“Yeah, I know,” nods BG, rolling her eyes. “They told our manager that, and he didn’t want to tell us, he was so embarrassed. Eventually, we just put our foot down and said, ‘We’re not doing anything else.’ Couldn’t get anyone to invest in what we were doing, so we funded our own thing.”

Happily, their own thing caught the attention of Daptone Records, home to Jalen Ngonda, Thee Sacred Souls and the late Sharon Jones, whose house band the Dap-Kings are best known for backing Winehouse on her Back to Black album. “An instant connection!” enthuses BG of their meeting with the label’s co-founder, Bosco Mann, who now plays bass in their backing band. “We just hung out and listened to music for a year before we actually recorded anything. So when we finally came down to it, it just rolled, it flowed, the music was just pouring out.”

The result was a string of acclaimed singles, among them Chauffeur – which details the downsides of the sisters’ period as Uber drivers, including realising that you’re invisible to the “fine-looking” man you just picked up – and If I Let You, which last month enjoyed a burst of social media virality after support from a startling array of luminaries: SZA, Timbaland, Ghostface Killah, Pharrell Williams, Erykah Badu and Questlove. One suspects the stars were drawn by the Womack Sisters’ fusion of traditional and modern: the music on their upcoming debut album is as deeply rooted in soul’s past as you’d expect (“We are,” as Kucha puts it, “so familiar with these streets”), but it never feels self-consciously retro.

But it does feel strikingly raw, racked with very real emotion. “We crafted it from our hearts,” says Zeimani. “I wouldn’t say that we had a lot of sorrow to get off our chests, but there is a lot of relationship drama in our family, you know? Our father passed away, our Uncle Bob passed away shortly afterwards. Our aunt, our Uncle Jude’s wife, there was a car accident and she didn’t make it. I lost my husband in Atlanta in 2020 – he was robbed, he got shot, he didn’t survive. You find love, there’s nothing that impacts you more, and to lose it before you can fully experience it – like, we were married but we were about to start a family … I had a really hard time moving through that.

“You know how when we were in the pandemic, we couldn’t do anything? That’s really what you need to do to reset from loss – stop doing everything, just love on yourself, go to the beach, find a reason to smile again.”

Their live shows, meanwhile, are proving triumphant. At the London festival, their set featured a roaring take on Teardrops, their parents’ most enduring hit. No, they say, they aren’t intimidated by their family’s legacy. “We’re proud of them, but they exist in their own right. The time they came up in and the things they faced – segregation, things we can’t even imagine – they saw that,” says Zeimani.

“If you can imagine, our mother came up behind Sam Cooke – and we saw her win Grammys,” nods Kucha. “So I’m just like, well, she did it.”

“She focused on herself – that was her advice to us,” says Zeimani. “And Uncle Bob’s career was piping hot at the same time as my dad’s career was piping hot, so we saw that we could coexist without competing, because they were very different from one another. They always told us: you’re not us and you don’t have to be. You’re you, and there’ll never be anyone like you. We took that seriously.”

The Womack Sisters is released 14 August via Daptone

Throwing Muses frontwoman Kristin Hersh: ‘I was compelled to make music after cracking my skull open’

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 14:00:49 GMT

The alt-rock veteran answers your questions on Buddhist time travel techniques, duetting with Michael Stipe, and her autobiographical new album

Do you think Throwing Muses would have sounded different were it not for your bicycle accident? [Hersh was struck by a car when she was 16, resulting in a concussion that changed the way she heard sound.] Bhafc99Yes. I think people might have liked us more, but we would have been more forgettable. Our songs were not very marketable. They came from a place of such utter honesty that it was difficult for us to become a band with an image, ambition or direction, which plays well on a human level, but not on a corporate one. Some people hate our music; they can’t deal with it because it’s triggering [emotionally], which I get.

I was compelled to make music after cracking my skull open and then my life was very upsetting. But at the same time, I had real listeners. If you happen to come across a song that resonates with you, then it’s yours – you can ignore the musician who played it, because they were just the messenger.

Your guitar sound and playing is so distinctive, creative and superb – do you have an influence or hero who has inspired or guided you? GoonergeofNobody. We started the Muses when I was 11, so I didn’t have time to invent a sonic vocabulary. I wish my music could be that palatable. I think there’s a place where music can touch people and not be off-putting, but I couldn’t engage in that way.

But I babysat for this music critic and, every time I put his kids to bed, I was allowed to sit in his office and listen to records that hadn’t been released. One was the Violent Femmes’ first album [in 1983]. I remember the music critic told me that the boy in the band was “the male me” and I admit when I heard it I was like: “He’s right!” They had this simple, percussive and raw sound that was very effective. [Singer] Gordon Gano sat in his adolescent-boy self and was just being very honest. That first record is a reminder that we’re all attracted to that sweet spot where we seem to be in enthusiastic agony. And it turns out to be a party!

What was the inspiration behind the song Counting Backwards? _Tiana_Time-tripping! I was raised Buddhist by hippy parents and I never thought I was made for letting go of the past, which any therapist will tell you is really unhealthy! But I felt very strongly that I could alter the present by altering the past in a dream state. And that it has to be done with kindness.

I am curious why Leslie Langston left Throwing Muses between Hunkpapa [1989] and The Real Ramona [1991]. What happened? Androo1984She has a health issue with her skin where she couldn’t play bass for decades. She didn’t play on The Real Ramona, but then she came back for our next record, Red Heaven. Leslie ended up moving to the west coast and didn’t want to tour, so Bernard [Georges] came in. Leslie’s just now starting to play bass again and she almost played on the last record. She’s a social worker and my hero; we spend a lot of time thanking each other for being on Earth. I lean on her – she’s one of my favourite people.

Any chance of you working with [her step-sister and Throwing Muses co-founder] Tanya Donelly again? ChrisOwensYes – she was on tour with us a couple of years ago. She sang on the second self-titled Muses record [2003]. And my son Ryder just stayed at her house when he flew into Boston. All doors are open: anybody who is in the musical moment with me is allowed in, but it’s a big ask. No one’s ever left the Throwing Muses, it’s more like: “You feel like playing? OK, let’s do it!”

I supported you in Dublin in 2001 and you said I reminded you of Frank Black. Have you seen Frank lately? PaulOReillyThe first time I heard the Pixies was when we were in soundcheck. A painter friend was at the bar and he said: “You should listen to this band,” which I would never normally do. I thought Charles [Thompson, AKA Frank Black] was a woman at first. I thought she was so cool – she had a shaved head and was singing about her dick. I was like: “She rocks!”

But I forgave him for not being a girl and then I said: “I’m never letting go of you. You’re playing all of our shows with us, and here’s my manager, and here’s my label, and you’re coming on tour, and we’re gonna make all of this happen.” I did it for selfish reasons, because I wanted to hear them the whole time and I didn’t want to be alone any more. That relationship lasted for years. Charles once drew a pie chart on the wall of a dressing room and said: “This is a Throwing Muses song.” It was a moment where I forgave myself for carrying my musical treasure into the hurricane of the music biz.

Your Ghost [from her debut solo album, featuring REM’s Michael Stipe] is one of the most gorgeous songs I have ever heard – two unique voices coming together on such a haunting duet. Was it written with Michael Stipe in mind and are you still in contact? Frou1967I wasn’t ever going to have a solo career; I wasn’t interested. But I had to get off Warner Brothers and breaking up the band wasn’t going to work. [In order to fulfil the recording contract, she was required to make another album.] I had this tape of leftover acoustic songs and Michael Stipe picked it up. He called me up and said: “I love this tape.” He knew I was going to fuck up the recording of it because I didn’t care. He called the studio as I was having trouble recording Your Ghost and I realised I needed his voice on it.

Not too long ago, I was in New York playing a solo show and he was in the audience and I didn’t know. When I was playing Your Ghost, apparently he was in the back singing his parts and freaking out all the people around him. But I didn’t know!

You’ve been prolific over the past decade. Is it safe to assume your EMDR nightmare is over? [Eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing is a psychotherapy technique that Hersh used to treat post-traumatic stress disorder and a dissociative disorder.] JosephKyleMy life has been so very difficult; my whole system was just confused. I reacted to the real [PTSD] triggers by passing out, vomiting and screaming. My band members knew to protect me from my triggers, but that’s hard in life. Thanks to EMDR, I can still play music, which I didn’t think I would be able to. I wouldn’t recommend it for everyone. EMDR is like psychological chemo. I would collapse every time I did it. And then you can’t stop it – it’s like a snowballing process, where all the pain you dissociated from comes back to you at once.

Your upcoming album, Sugar on Blackstone, has such an evocative title. Where did it come from? VerulamiumParkRangerMaking this album, I was back in my home town of Providence, Rhode Island, living in a street called Hope. It’s off a street called Blackstone, which has this intense path on it that’s like this ship of lost souls. So I had “Hope” on the one side and the ship of lost souls on the other. These songs are autobiographical. They are very old stories from childhood, some of them dating back to the 1970s. There is one [Dark Eyed Junco] about me and my little brother, how we were scared to go home because our stepfather was there. So we just played basketball until we couldn’t any more. The song is about how the feel of the basketball is more important than getting it in the hoop. I don’t even want to aim for the hoop.

Sugar on Blackstone is released on 18 September via Fire

London to face Rome, Munich and Nairobi after confirming 2029 World Athletics bid

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 13:48:09 GMT

Bid team reach agreement with West Ham to use stadium

Host city for event to be announced in September

London has submitted its bid for the 2029 World Athletics ­Championships after reaching an agreement with West Ham to allow it to host the event that September.

World Athletics is yet to announce the other candidate cities, but Rome, Munich and Nairobi have also ­submitted applications for 2029.

West Ham had threatened to thwart London’s bid, arguing they had ­priority for the stadium during the football season. However, the impasse has been broken after lengthy discussions with the London mayor’s office, Athletics Ventures, the joint organisation responsible for putting on major events, and the Department for Culture, Media and Sport.

If London is successful, West Ham will play no more than two consecutive away games in the Premier League or three in the EFL in the 2029-30 season.

Jack Buckner, the CEO of UK ­Athletics and co-founder of Athletics Ventures, said: “Bidding to hold the World Athletics Championships in the London Stadium, the showpiece of London 2012, was always at the centre of the UK’s Olympic legacy plans.

“We’re delighted that we have reached agreement with the London Stadium and West Ham United for the use of the London ­Stadium and our sincere thanks for their commitment in making this happen.”

Hugh Brasher, the CEO of London Marathon Events and co-founder of Athletics Ventures, said: “Our bid is not just about what happens within the London Stadium. Sport has the power to bring communities together, to change lives and to inspire the next generation. The 2029 World ­Athletics Championships in London would drive more than £400m in economic and social benefit in the capital and nationwide.”

A spokesperson for Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, also welcomed the news: “London is the sporting capital of the world and the mayor believes that hosting the World Athletics Championships at the London Stadium in 2029 would build on the city’s long history of hosting the most prestigious sporting events.”

Bombs, heists and big cats: TV’s 25 best true-crime shows ever

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 13:10:53 GMT

From mind-boggling murder investigations to decade-long scams, there’s no shortage of documentaries about real-life awfulness. We list the most incredible

Since the true-crime explosion a decade ago – kickstarted by Netflix’s Making a Murderer – audiences have been fed a steady small-screen diet of cold-case killings, catfishing scams and creepy cults. And, after years of varying results, Netflix’s latest show, A Toxic Love Story – which recounts how a California couple framed an innocent woman for stalking, intimidation and recruiting men from Craigslist to rape her ex’s new wife – is being billed as a return to true-crime form. But when it comes to similar shows worth your viewing time, what else is up there?

Here’s a selection of the genre’s 25 standout shows and where to watch them – which, let’s face it, is mainly Netflix. Let the boggle-eyed bingeing begin.

Disney+This ESPN-produced five-parter, which won an Oscar and an Emmy, is the definitive account of the fairytale rise and steep fall of the former NFL running back OJ Simpson. It chronicles the buildup to and fallout from the 1995 trial at which Simpson was accused (and acquitted) of the brutal murders of his ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ron Goldman. A stunning state-of-the-nation study of race, gender and celebrity.

Sky/Now (UK), HBO Max (UK/US/Australia), Foxtel Now (Australia)

An oldie but a goodie. The HBO series remains groundbreaking for reasons we won’t spoil. The film-maker Andrew Jarecki follows Durst, a billionaire New York real estate heir, who is suspected of three murders across 19 years. When Durst agrees to a sit-down interview, it proves to be the biggest miscalculation of his life.

Netflix

The director Skye Borgman, whose 2017 film Abducted in Plain Sight also merits a watch, keeps the victim front and centre in this jaw-dropper. In 1990, a young woman was found in critical condition at the side of an Oklahoma highway. What begins as an investigation into an apparent hit-and-run soon escalates into a harrowing tale of abduction, abuse and identity fraud.

Sky/Now (UK), HBO Max (US/Australia), YouTube TV (US)

People behind bars in Alabama used contraband phones to film the footage and make the calls from which this startling documentary was largely assembled. The result of a six-year investigation by the directors Charlotte Kaufman and Andrew Jarecki (of The Jinx pedigree), it viscerally lays bare the cruelty inflicted on prisoners as they are beaten, abused and even killed by prison guards. It’s a righteous howl of protest about systemic failures.

Netflix

In 2003, Brian Wells, a pizza delivery man, walked into a Pennsylvania bank with a bomb locked around his neck and demanded $250,000 in cash. He was killed when the device detonated before cops could disarm it. The film-makers Barbara Schroeder and Trey Borzillieri unravel the conspiracy across four episodes, until a climactic revelation flips everything on its head.

Prime Video (UK), HBO Max/YouTube TV (US)

It starts as a HBO film about clowns hired for children’s parties. It soon morphs into a haunting deep dive into the retired New York schoolteacher Arnold Friedman and his 18-year-old son, Jesse. In 1987, the pair were convicted of owning an extensive cache of child sexual abuse images and abusing local boys who took computing classes in their basement.

Netflix

In 2018, a pregnant woman, Shanann Watts, and her two toddler daughters were murdered in their Colorado home by Shanann’s husband, Chris. Only days before, he had posted smiley family snaps on social media. Via text messages, home videos, Facebook reels and police bodycam footage, the director Jenny Popplewell constructs a digital portrait of domestic tragedy.

HBO Max (UK, US, Australia), Foxtel Now (Australia)

The stranger-than-fiction story of Gypsy Rose Blanchard. From birth, the Missouri girl was in and out of hospital, diagnosed with all manner of debilitating diseases. She used a wheelchair and was tube-fed and shaven-headed due to cancer. Or so everyone thought. When Gypsy Rose learned the truth, she murdered her mother, Clauddine. This compelling film interviews her in prison. She has since been released on parole.

Netflix

A true-crime phenomenon that doesn’t involve murder. Just don’t Google it first or you may ruin the head-spinning twist. This cleverly crafted film from Skye Borgman (Girl in the Picture) follows a teen couple in small-town Michigan who are relentlessly cyberbullied by an anonymous caller. A community is torn apart by finger-pointing before the culprit is unmasked. Cue your jaw hitting the floor.

Netflix

The unsolved murder in 1969 of a nun called Catherine Cesnik is the gateway into a panoramic exposé of endemic abuse at the all-girls school in Baltimore where she taught. Was Sister Cathy killed by a priest when she tried to blow the whistle? This searing seven-parter gives voice to victims, while the lead investigators aren’t journalists but two retired former pupils, working from their kitchen tables.

Prime Video

Those who had followed the tragic case were agog last summer when Bryan Kohberger, accused of fatally stabbing four university housemates in 2022, took a plea deal to avoid the death penalty. Directors Liz Garbus and Matthew Galkin rushed to update their forensic four-parter, which follows not just the investigation but the impact of social media sleuths. A second season is in the works.

Netflix

Along with The Jinx, which was released months earlier, this is the one that began the true-crime boom. The directors Laura Ricciardi and Moira Demos spent a decade immersed in the case of Steven Avery and Brendan Dassey, Avery’s teenage nephew and alleged accomplice, to build a genre-defining masterpiece. Hard-hitting and heartbreaking, it sparked national outrage and a presidential petition demanding justice.

HBO Max (UK, US, Australia), YouTube TV (US), Foxtel Now (Australia)

The crime author Michelle McNamara spent years obsessively hunting the Golden State Killer – a nocturnal home invader responsible for at least 50 rapes and 13 murders in California in the 1970s and 1980s. This HBO series from Liz Garbus (One Night in Idaho) weaves together the manhunt with a profile of McNamara, who died before the bogeyman was caught at last.

Netflix

Another Garbus-directed banger – less a whodunnit, more a look at how the legal system values certain lives above others. She spent nearly a decade researching the Gilgo Beach killings, in which more than a dozen women, many of them sex workers, were murdered between 1993 and 2011. Garbus shows empathy for the victims and ​illustrates how those left behind built a supportive community from their shared pain. In June, Rex Heuermann pleaded guilty to seven murders and admitted to an eighth; he was sentenced to life in prison without parole.

Netflix

When the eccentric novelist Michael Peterson called 911 in 2001 and said his wife, Kathleen, had died after drunkenly falling down the stairs of their North Carolina mansion, he was soon arrested for murder. For this Canal+ (and latterly Netflix) series, the director Jean-Xavier de Lestrade was embedded with Peterson’s defence team, capturing the courtroom drama up close as he defended the charges. In 2017, Peterson entered an Alford plea to voluntary manslaughter, maintaining his innocence but agreeing there was enough evidence to result in a guilty verdict. Not to be confused with the 2022 HBO dramatisation starring Colin Firth and Toni Collette.

BBC iPlayer (UK), Britbox (US)

This BBC three-parter tells the devastating story of Jean O’Brien and her daughter Megan Bhari, who set up a charity for terminally ill children in 2012 after Bhari was diagnosed with a brain tumour at 13. Other parents started to question O’Brien’s claims about her daughter’s condition, while funds raised for Believe in Magic – including millions from the boyband One Direction – went unaccounted for.

Netflix

In 1981, the utopian Rajneesh cult – led by the Indian spiritual teacher Bhagwan Shree Rajneesh, AKA Osho – established itself on a ranch in rural Oregon. Three years later, its followers committed the first and biggest bioterrorist attack in US history. This mesmerising, Emmy-winning series interviews perplexed locals and Ma Anand Sheela, formerly a PA to Osho, who died unrepentant in 1990.

Sky/Now (UK), HBO Max (UK, US), YouTube TV (US), Binge (Australia)

In the early 90s, the serial killer Richard Rogers – AKA the Last Call Killer – murdered and dismembered four gay men on the east coast of the US. The case was covered by the media in a sensationalist, homophobic style, while the justice system failed the victims; Anthony Caronna’s infuriating but ultimately redemptive series humanises them at last. Each of the four episodes is dedicated to one of the men killed.

Netflix

We all know the enraging story by now, but this gut-punch series about the notorious sex trafficker – based on James Patterson’s book – lays bare the human tragedy behind the headlines. The director, Lisa Bryant, hears the candid testimony of survivors, including Virginia Giuffre and Maria Farmer, along with former members of Epstein’s staff and the police who investigated his exploitative empire.

Netflix

Geeta Gandbhir’s unflinching documentary investigates the fatal shooting of a Black Florida woman, Ajike Owens, by her white neighbour, Susan Louise Lorincz. Comprised mostly of police bodycam and interrogation footage, it builds into a searing indictment of community tensions, the state’s controversial “stand your ground” law and systemic racial bias.

HBO Max

In 1993, the murders and mutilation of three eight-year-old boys in Arkansas sparked a moral panic about heavy metal and satanic rituals, resulting in the wrongful arrests of three teenagers. Paradise Lost: The Child Murders at Robin Hood Hills remains the only docuseries for which Metallica have allowed their music to be used. Two sequels followed the case’s progress over the next 15 years.

HBO Max (UK, US, Australia), YouTube TV (US), Spectrum (US), Foxtel Now (Australia)

Nxivm styled itself as a global self-improvement organisation. Of course, it was a cult – one that abused, blackmailed and branded its female members. Its svengali-like leader, Keith Raniere, was ultimately convicted of charges including sex trafficking and racketeering. This unsettling HBO docuseries began filming inside Nxivm years before the FBI investigated, capturing the mechanism of manipulation in action.

Netflix

Reminiscent of the Zodiac Killer in 1960s San Francisco, Richard Ramirez terrorised Los Angeles in the summer of 1985 with a string of brutal, seemingly random murders and sexual assaults. This four-parter documents his deadly rampage through the lens of the two detectives, Gil Carrillo and Frank Salerno, who became consumed by the case and doggedly tracked him down.

Netflix

“Hey, all you cool cats and kittens.” It’s now inextricably linked with the early months of the Covid pandemic, but if this talking-point series managed to escape you, it’s worth seeing what all the fuss was about. Investigative film-making with the pull of reality trash, it follows an eccentric Oklahoma zookeeper, Joe Exotic, who allegedly hired a hitman to kill a big-cat activist, Carole Baskin.

Netflix

A twisting, turning thriller with the kicker that it’s all too real. This three-parter beggars belief as it follows Facebook sleuths who launch an amateur investigation into online videos of kitten cruelty. The armchair detectives repeatedly express their fears that the culprit will escalate to murdering more than just pets – and are proved correct.
