One potential breakout star for each Premier League club this season

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 12:13:36 GMT

A crop of young players emerges every season in the Premier League. Who will make the grade this year?

By Opta Analyst

Dowman is old news by now, so we’re going to look at someone four months older than him. Much like the fish of the same name, Salmon has risen quickly. The defender became the fourth-youngest player to represent Arsenal last season when he came off the bench against Club Brugge in the Champions League in December at the age of just 16 years and 102 days.

Salmon made four appearances for the first team last season, while also featuring 14 times for their Under-21s in Premier League 2. He won an impressive 71.8% of his duels in PL2 (56 of 78); of defenders to contest at least 50 duels, only two players had a better success rate. Salmon – who can play right-back or centre-back – has signed a pre-agreement to commit his future to the club when he turns 17 later this month, and it would not be surprising to see him given more opportunities by Mikel Arteta.

Aston Villa signed Madjo from Metz in January for about £10.5m but were not able to register him. He is available now and has been involved regularly during pre-season. The giant 17-year-old centre-forward’s movement and power are reminiscent of Erling Haaland.

He has caught the eye in Villa’s recent friendlies, scoring four times. Pre-season only counts for so much, of course, but you can only score against what’s in front of you.

After the departure of Marcos Senesi, Bournemouth have a position in the centre of defence up for grabs and Milosavljevic could be the man to claim it. Milosavljevic joined the club last summer from Red Star Belgrade. Although he didn’t feature prominently, making just seven appearances in all competitions, the 19-year-old is clearly a promising defender.

He made more clearances than any other Bournemouth player on his Premier League debut in September, before going on to make his full international debut for Serbia in October. Marco Rose may want more experience at centre-back, especially given how youthful some of Bournemouth’s other defenders are, but Milosavljevic will hope to take another step forward this season.

Milambo had a difficult introduction to English football last season. Signed from Feyenoord for around £21m last year, he suffered a season-ending ACL injury on international duty in October. He was obviously set back but will be confident he can force his way into Keith Andrews’ thinking this term.

He became Feyenoord’s youngest ever player in 2021, when he made his debut as a 16-year-old, but Milambo rose to prominence in 2024-25 as a forward-thinking, box-to-box midfielder who was technically good and could be a threat in attack. No other Eredivisie player under the age of 21 bettered his 14 goal involvements in all competitions that season. He could be a dynamic asset in the very useful midfield Andrews has built.

Yohanna will need a little patience as he’s still quite raw but, if he is given opportunities at Brighton this season, he will catch the eye. The 19-year-old Nigerian has joined from AIK for around £21.5m, a record sale for Swedish football, despite playing just 13 league games for the club. It was enough to convince Brighton, who have been impressed by his direct style and fearless dribbling.

A left-footed winger who plays on the right side of the attack, Yohanna was attempting more dribbles per 90 minutes than any other player in the Allsvenskan this year before his move was confirmed in June. He also tallied the most take-ons driving into the box (six), take-ons in the box (15) and the joint-most take-ons followed by a shot (three), despite playing significantly fewer minutes than many other players. His end product needs work, but he will get bums off seats.

Chelsea always have a conveyor belt of young talent waiting for a chance – the issue is many seem to get lost in the crowd. But, after losing Rio Ngumoha to Liverpool a couple of years ago, the club have apparently made a greater effort to keep hold of emerging homegrown talents, and one of those they were especially keen to tie down was Reggie Watson.

A towering defensive midfielder, Watson, 16, has impressive physical attributes but is also tidy on the ball, appears to have good spatial awareness and plays with considerable personality for one so young. It’s easy to see why he’s been tentatively compared with Rodri.

Xabi Alonso has also spoken about being “really impressed” with his impact in pre-season. Given the uncertainty around other midfielders – such as the fitness issues of Roméo Lavia and Dário Essugo – Watson could get minutes this season.

With survival being the name of the game for Coventry City season, giving minutes to young players may not be Frank Lampard’s top priority. There is one youngster who could force his way into Lampard’s plans, though: Andrews. The 19-year-old midfielder made 10 appearances for Coventry last season before joining Hibernian on loan.

While Andrews failed to make his mark in Scotland, he ended the campaign on a high as he made his first start for Wales in a friendly against Romania. He acquitted himself well in the match, making nine passes in the final third, the third most of any player, and winning two fouls. Andrews will need to decide whether to stay at Coventry and fight for a place or go out on loan for regular minutes.

Drakes-Thomas became Crystal Palace’s youngest Premier League player last season and will hope to play a more prominent role this campaign. The wideman made his Palace debut in the Conference League when he was just 16 years old and he shone against Finnish side KuPS. He attempted seven crosses during the match, the most of any player, and he created two chances, the joint-most. The appointment of Pierre Sage has signalled the start of a new era at Selhurst Park, and Drakes-Thomas has the ability to be a figurehead of any future success.

George looked promising at Chelsea, but his first few months at Everton after initially joining on loan in February were something of a settling-in period, as he started just one game for David Moyes’ side. With a full pre-season under his belt, George could burst into life this season.

Quick, dynamic and eager to run at full-backs, the 20-year-old could be the one to benefit most from Jack Grealish returning to Manchester City after his loan. George has started three of Everton’s four pre-season friendlies in the absence of Iliman Ndiaye, who is reportedly the subject of interest from abroad. With Grealish gone and Dwight McNeil dropping down the pecking order, George has a big opportunity.

The 19-year-old will be hoping to make his debut for Fulham this season, having already impressed for their Under-21s. He signed his first professional contract with the club last summer and went on to score 10 goals in PL2. The left winger also added seven assists, proving he can create as well as find the net himself.

Only Chelsea’s Shumaira Mheuka (19) and Liverpool’s Kieran Morrison (18) recorded more goal involvements than Ali-Wahid (17) in the PL2 last season, while just 10 players created more chances from open play than his 26. He was nominated for the PL2 Player of the Season award and the new Fulham manager, Álvaro Arbeloa, has been picking him in pre-season.

Hughes was Hull’s defensive lynchpin last season. The 22-year-old centre-back started 36 games in the Championship and played every minute of their successful playoff campaign. He has a remarkable willingness to put his body on the line. Last season, he made 1.54 blocks per 90 minutes, the most of any regular player in the Championship. He also made more clearances per 90 minutes (7.62) than any of his teammates (1,000+ mins). Hull may struggle in the Premier League, but Hughes could be a diamond in the rough.

Mendel-Idowu, who spent most of his youth development at Chelsea before a year at Anderlecht, was snapped up by Ipswich in the summer of 2024, though he is yet to make his first-team debut. The winger is an intelligent fellow; he appeared on a TV show called Child Genius when he was eight years old and went on to become a King’s Scholar at Eton College.

He has not only thrived in academia, but also on the pitch. He recorded 15 goal involvements in 17 PL2 games for the Ipswich’s Under-21s last season (nine goals, six assists); only three players managed more in the league. On top of that, only three players created more chances from open play than his 33, and just two won possession in the final third more than him (21).

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

Chances were at a premium last season for young players under Daniel Farke. The youngest player to play for Leeds was 21-year-old Facundo Buonanotte, who had already made his debut for Argentina, and even he only played a fleeting role in the second half of the season.

But Lienou may just be winning Farke’s trust. The 18-year-old defender started all but one of Leeds’ PL2 games last season and won possession 5.4 times per 90 minutes, the second most in the side. He was the only youth-team player to feature in Leeds’ first three pre-season games, and he was called into the senior Wales squad by Craig Bellamy in June, showing he is impressing coaches for both club and country.

With a new manager comes a new opportunity to impress, and Trey Nyoni has taken that chance in pre-season. The midfielder had to be patient after joining Liverpool from Leicester in 2023. Arne Slot gave him limited minutes last season, with Nyoni making 14 appearances in all competitions, only two of which were starts, both in the League Cup. With Andoni Iraola now in the dugout, the 19-year-old has been able to stake his claim and has been Liverpool’s standout midfielder in pre-season.

One of the most impressive aspects to his game is his verticality. Nyoni wants to get the ball forward as often as possible, though he’s not careless in possession. In his three friendlies this summer in the US – against Sunderland, Wrexham and Leeds United – Nyoni attempted 154 passes, completing 141 of them (92%). Just looking at forward passes, he completed an impressive 44 out of 54 (81%). With Curtis Jones potentially leaving, and most of Liverpool’s transfer funds seemingly going on attackers, the path may open up for Nyoni.

McAidoo has shone in City’s extremely competitive academy. The winger impressed in the PL2 last season, with only Reigan Heskey (15) registering more goal involvements than him (12) for City. McAidoo made his first-team debut last season, and he marked the occasion by scoring the ninth goal in City’s 10-1 drubbing of Exeter City in the FA Cup.

More recently, the 18-year-old caught the eye with his one-v-one ability in City’s pre-season friendly against Inter. He also had the second-most touches in the opposition’s box (13). Enzo Maresca raved about McAidoo’s performance, calling him “the type of winger I love”.

Gabriel is undoubtedly the biggest hope in Manchester United’s academy. He apparently nearly left at the end of the 2024-25 season until senior club figures stepped in and his reputation has only continued to grow since. Then, aged 14, he had already become the youngest player to represent United’s Under-18s, scoring twice on his debut. After turning 15 in October, he was soon involved in first-team training.

Nevertheless, his focus remained the Under-18s, for whom he scored 23 goals – a tally bettered by only one player – in the 2025-26 U18 Premier League campaign, winning the competition’s Player of the Season award.

A skilful attacker who can play out wide or through the middle, Gabriel is brave, expressive and confident. He showed these traits when he came on as a late substitute in United’s pre-season friendly against Atlético Madrid at the weekend.

The record for youngest Premier League player is out of reach, but Gabriel has a good chance of becoming United’s youngest player in the Premier League; that honour currently belongs to Angel Gomes (16 years, 263 days).

For all the good he did at Newcastle, some supporters think Eddie Howe could have done more to bring young talent through. Now he’s gone and Newcastle are in a transition period, several of their young players will fancy their chances of stepping up. Park, 19, is one of them. The South Korean left-winger was signed last summer and spent the season adapting to English football in PL2. He averaged 4.7 dribble attempts per 90 minutes in that competition and caught the eye with his energetic displays and tidy footwork.

With Anthony Gordon gone, there may well be chances available on the left flank, especially if new signing Bazoumana Touré does not get off to a flying start. Park has impressed in pre-season and a step up to top-flight football might not be far down the line.

Thompson signed for Nottingham Forest from Northern Irish club Linfield last July and, despite being 16 at the time, he went on to spend the majority of 2025-26 playing for the club’s Under-21s. The left winger was the youngest player to feature for Forest Under-21s last season and yet only four players – three of whom are now 20 – tallied more minutes than him (1,090).

The 17-year-old won the club’s scholar of the year prize at the end of the season. A tricky and purposeful player, Thompson’s 4.7 dribble attempts per 90 ranked highly in the PL2 and his six goal involvements were the most of any Forest player.

Although Angulo reportedly cost £15m in January and is already 23 years old, he just about fits into the potential breakout player category. After joining from Anderlecht, Angulo’s impact at Sunderland wasn’t exactly explosive. There were flashes of his flair but he was clearly still pretty raw.

Nevertheless, those first few months gave him time to adapt and, after a fairly encouraging World Cup with Ecuador, he’ll now hope to kick on. He has the ability and he has an athletic build which should help him once his game has been refined a little more.

Sunderland will hope the Angulo of Anderlecht comes to the fore a little more this season. Prior to his move last season, he’d attempted more dribbles (111) than any other player in the Belgian Pro League, while only Christos Tzolis (17) – now at Arsenal – bettered his 11 goal involvements. If he keeps progressing, Angulo will be a very useful weapon for Régis Le Bris.

Spurs seem to have exciting young talents breaking through every other season, and now it’s Williams-Barnett’s turn to see if he can make his mark. Williams-Barnett started last season playing Under-18s football but quickly broke into first-team contention. He made one senior appearance but featured on the bench semi-regularly throughout the campaign.

He was one of Spurs’ standout players in the PL2 despite only playing 10 games. Williams-Barnett recorded an astounding 1.25 combined goals and assists per 90 in the PL2, ranking him fourth among all players (500+ mins). The 17-year-old attacking midfielder also created 0.8 big chances per 90 last season, again ranking him fourth (500+ mins). He has featured heavily in pre-season, building great momentum which he can hopefully take into the season.

‘The first time I felt art in my nose’: why a critic missed the point when he called my exhibition meaningless

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 12:00:47 GMT

Projects like London’s Backyard Biennial East are collective endeavours aiming to reach people who feel excluded by art galleries

In 2018, on the outside wall surrounding the entrance of the National Theatre of Bangladesh, I first encountered a work by the artist Reetu Sattar. A group of musicians were perched on construction scaffolding, all dressed in white and playing a single note on the harmonium – an instrument used in Bengali classical music. Together, they produced a low hum that seemed to vibrate through everything around me. The work was called Lost Tune.

I came across the work at a time when I desperately wanted to learn a musical instrument, but music was not allowed in my house. A growing sentiment in many Bangladeshi Muslim households held that music was prohibited in Islam, despite our long histories of musical traditions. It felt as though everything we knew of the past had been locked away inside the Jadu Ghor, the “magic house” (the Bangla words for museum), quietly collecting dust.

It amazed me that an artist could gather so many people to commit themselves to an artwork when nobody around me seemed to believe art had any value at all. Until then, I had only felt art in my eyes and my mind. In Lost Tune, I felt art in my chest.

I continued following Reetu’s practice, though much of it took place abroad. Eventually, I too left Bangladesh to study art in the UK.

It was here that I discovered the work of Adam Farah Saad. At his exhibition at Camden Art Centre in London, I smelled KA soda the moment I entered the room. A fountain bubbled it endlessly. It was the first time I felt art in my nose.

It was also in London that I discovered Brick Lane’s Bengali sweet shops. There I found my father’s favourite childhood snack: one sweet and one savoury item that he always mixed together. I remembered the first time he had taken me to a sweet shop in Bangladesh. That memory has always been yellow, a display cabinet glowing beneath warm tungsten light. It is my earliest emotional memory of him.

That memory became the foundation for the work I conceived two years ago and am re-presenting in East of the Aldgate Pump, a group exhibition at London’s Whitechapel Gallery as part of a new collaborative East End arts festival, Backyard Biennial. Every day, members of the Bengali social enterprise Oitij-jo Kitchen help maintain the work, preparing and bringing the specific mixture of snacks into the gallery. Their contribution isn’t separate from the artwork. It is part of it. In many ways, that collaboration feels like a direct descendant of Lost Tune: people choosing to sustain something collectively.

A recent review in the Guardian of East of the Aldgate Pump provoked questions around where meaning in art actually resides. During conversations with the curators, I found myself thinking about the Aldgate Pump itself. For centuries it has marked the symbolic gateway to east London while witnessing continuous movement, migration and change. I thought about the geographer Doreen Massey’s idea that places are not fixed locations but meeting points of multiple journeys. Every artwork in the exhibition seemed to have travelled a different route to arrive there.

When my mother visited London in 2023, she went to Brick Lane with a friend. They came out of Aldgate East station, and her friend pointed out Whitechapel Gallery.

“Did you go in?” I asked later.

“No,” she replied. “We were scared.”

I want art spaces to become less scary to enter, for me, for my mum, for everyone. I hope, more and more, they become places where people feel that they belong.

If projects like Backyard Biennial have a purpose, it is not to provide tidy answers or singular narratives. It is to create the conditions for people to encounter one another, their histories and themselves. It is to give people an opportunity to recognise something of themselves in a space the previously may have felt closed to them. That meaning may be messy, partial and collective. But it is not meaningless.

Backyard Biennial: East is at various venues in London until 6 September

Trump’s Gaza Board of Peace issues first building contract – for a military base

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 12:00:47 GMT

Exclusive: Louisiana firm awarded tender to build rudimentary outpost to house Moroccan troops

Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, which was set up in January to oversee the reconstruction of Gaza, has finally issued its first construction contract in the devastated territory: a project to build a rudimentary 150-person military outpost to house Moroccan troops, a source familiar with the matter told the Guardian.

The contract, which has not yet been finalised, was awarded to Arkel International, a Louisiana-based firm that has previously carried out work with the US government in countries such as Iraq.

The Board of Peace is chaired by the US president and led by a team that includes his son-in-law Jared Kushner and friend Steve Witkoff.

In an email, a Board of Peace official said the board and a group of Palestinian technocrats installed to oversee Gaza “are in the final stages of preparing several contract awards. None have been finalised.” The Palestinian group is known as the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza.

The official said “one prospective contract concerns facilities to support the international stabilisation force (ISF), which will assist in implementing the roadmap’s security and governance arrangements”.

They added: “This contract will be one of many that are essential for the future of Gaza.”

The award comes just days after Trump announced that Hamas had agreed to disarm, though there are considerable questions about how the group would give up its guns. Israel has opposed the plan, and increased airstrikes in Gaza after Trump’s announcement.

The Guardian reported in July that the board’s original Gaza reconstruction had shrunk dramatically from an ambitious blueprint to rebuild the whole territory to a small pilot project in the south of the strip.

The base now being planned is just 100 metres by 120 metres and is intended to house a contingent of Moroccan troops, who would rotate from a base in Israel, the source said. It would lie in the 60% of Gaza’s territory that the Israeli army directly controls. Israeli forces have also created a buffer zone beyond that area.

The source said the base was about a mile from the Israeli border and would have a “quick extraction route” in case the small force came under attack.

The UN resolution authorising the Board of Peace had approved establishing an “international stabilisation force” for Gaza, and there have been varying reports on which country would provide these troops. Morocco has promised a small contingent, but the legal framework for the ISF has yet to be finalised, and it is not clear when the deployment would begin.

In earlier contract plans seen by the Guardian, the 150-person base was the first phase of a plan to build a 5,000-person military base in Gaza for the ISF.

This base would have included “vehicle fighting positions” and a perimeter berm – or raised defensive bank – and would have rudimentary facilities suitable for short-term deployments. The earlier contract said the first phase would consist of “tents and cots for forces to sleep, as well as chemical toilets and handwashing stations. At this phase, this is what we would consider habitable.”

Trump announced in February 2025 that the US would “take over” and “own” Gaza, although the agreement that set up the Board of Peace fell short of that.

At the board’s first meeting in January, Kushner unveiled a “master plan” to build “New Gaza” with an expansive waterfront city with gleaming mixed-use towers. “It could be a hope, it could be a destination. A lot of industry,” he said.

At least 80% of Gaza’s buildings were damaged or destroyed in the war. Ten months after the ceasefire, most of the territory’s 2 million people are still living in makeshift and unsanitary camps.

‘Do we really need huge cruise ships here?’ Fears £150m Falmouth Docks plan threatens habitats – and town itself

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 11:05:35 GMT

Plans involve dredging and expanding docks to allow larger cruise ships to visit with up to 200,000 passengers annually

Janavi Kramer had just enjoyed a swim with friends and was sitting on a bench taking in a wonderful Cornish view – headlands plunging into deep water, bobbing boats, a bustling harbour town.

“We’re lucky to have this space,” said Kramer, who is an artist and scientific illustrator. “We use it for work, recreation and pleasure and it’s so scary to think that this could all be harmed. I worry about what we may be living with soon and what we’ll be leaving for future generations.”

She is talking about a £150m plan to redevelop Falmouth Docks in south-west Cornwall. It includes expanding the docks to allow larger cruise ships to berth, which many people worry will exacerbate environmental problems and put pressure on the fabric of the town.

Hannah Cocks, a marine social scientist, who had been taking a dip with Kramer, said she wasn’t opposed to redevelopment of the docks, which have been here for more than 150 years.

“But I want it to be done in a way that is environmentally and socially just,” she said. “The community has not been adequately consulted about a decision that could have such adverse effects.

“Even now Cornish infrastructure can’t cope with the number of people who come in the summer. Do we really need these huge cruise ships here?”

The plans also involve dredging around the docks, which some fear could lead to harmful material being churned up from the seabed, such as heavy metals washed into the harbour when Cornwall was a mining superpower and toxic paints once used to protect boat hulls.

Fishers and environmentalists are warning that precious habitats could be damaged, including oyster grounds and rare maerl beds – created when rare types of red seaweeds grow into hard, twig-like lumps.

Gio Reale, a wildlife storyteller, said it had been a good summer for spotting marine wildlife. “I normally go out looking for sharks. We have seen small-spotted catsharks and nursehounds, quite a few octopuses and a lot of the usual lobsters and pipefish.

“We have maerl beds, seagrass meadows, kelp here. It’s a beautiful but fragile ecosystem and I’m concerned it could be really badly harmed.”

The UK government is supporting the redevelopment. Falmouth already hosts cruises, but ministers say the expansion will allow larger vessels – such as Excellence Class cruise ships, which are up to 345 metres (1,131ft) long, to berth.

This could help to attract up to 200,000 cruise visitors annually by 2030, it says, injecting millions of pounds into the local economy and supporting hundreds of tourism-related jobs.

Cornwall council will debate elements of the scheme in the coming weeks but much of it is going through the planning process under the government’s fast track system, designed to push complicated developments through and cut red tape.

It means developers work with a single, lead environmental body – in this case the Marine Management Organisation (MMO) – rather than what the UK government calls a “merry-go-round of overlapping regulators”.

But many in the town worry that fast-tracking may lead to a lack of scrutiny.

Jem Wallis, who runs a sauna on the waterfront, said he didn’t feel a clear case had been made for the project. And he had never had a cruise passenger visit his sauna. “It all seems a massive risk to me.”

Zoe Young, a tour guide, added: “A terminal for stinky great ships to meet stinky coaches to Land’s End – is that the best we can hope for?”

When the Guardian visited John Spargo’s souvenir shop Tall Ships Trading on Church Street, a passionate debate about the pros and cons broke out. Spargo said most cruise passengers who arrive in the town were taken by coach to other attractions such as the Eden Project. “They don’t bring as much money into the town itself as you think,” he said.

Bernie, a visitor from Kent, said she thought cruise ships were dreadful. “Other places in Europe are trying to get rid of them. Why do you want bigger ones? It’s not worth losing the character of this place for cruise ships.”

Susie, who lives in Falmouth, disagreed. “They do bring in money. They are good for many of the shops and the boat tours do well when they come. St Mawes Ferry is always packed when a cruise ship is here. The passengers say they don’t feel they are on a real boat when they’re on a cruise ship so love getting on a little one.”

The government has said the fast-track system does not mean corners are being cut. It said the MMO was reviewing information submitted during the consultation period to support a “robust” marine licensing decision.

A spokesperson said: “The lead environmental regulator model is about ensuring better coordination between developers and environmental regulators to prevent delays in the planning process without lowering environmental standards.”

Balaena, the maritime engineering and shipbuilding group that operates the docks, said the project would ensure the port remained fit for purpose, safeguard skilled jobs, create apprenticeship opportunities and support businesses across Cornwall and the wider south-west.

It said “targeted pocket dredging” was needed around the dock, which had been subject to a comprehensive environmental impact assessment. There would be no dredging in the main docks channel or wider estuary and material that is not suitable for disposal at sea would be taken to a facility inland.

Jason Pascoe, who has worked the oyster fishery for 40 years, was unconvinced. “The river systems here are very complex. Can they be sure if they dump waste out to sea it won’t find its way back here? Ironically, we’ve just had our best ever season. This feels like a horrendous threat to me.”

The American left is making strides. But can they win in November?

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 11:00:50 GMT

The left is increasingly winning within the Democratic party. But it still needs to prove that it can build general-election coalitions capable of beating Republicans

The ideological struggle within the Democratic party continued on Tuesday night with primaries in Kansas, Michigan, Missouri, Virginia and Washington. The results showed an increasingly intense conflict within the party, with high Democratic primary turnout and bruising ideological battles up and down the ballot.

The Democratic electorate is shifting, becoming more progressive and more willing to challenge party leadership, but not as quickly or uniformly as many assumed.

Progressives and socialists scored another round of victories, most notably Abdul El-Sayed for Senate, but also downballot with Donavan McKinney and Will Lawrence in congressional races, and in state legislative seats such as Chris Gilmer-Hill in Detroit. But the scale and breadth of those victories fell short of the expectations created by polling and media coverage.

A few key lessons have emerged. First, building a mass left in the United States is a slow and bruising process, and there is no single tipping point at which the party and its voters suddenly become committed leftwing partisans.

Second, the left is nonetheless growing rapidly, able to win beyond young, deep-blue urban areas where concerns about general-election viability against Republicans are relatively limited, and across an entire statewide Democratic primary electorate in a swing state.

This is a major step in the left’s development as an electoral force. Third, the left’s next and most important challenge is winning swing states and competitive seats against Republicans.

The left has enjoyed a string of notable electoral victories during the second Trump administration, beginning with Zohran Mamdani’s primary win in New York City, and continuing up through the 2026 primaries. The Democratic electorate’s attitudes are changing: party leadership has grown less popular, while democratic socialism has gained support. The left has quickly gone from an extremely marginal force, with just a handful of members of Congress, largely confined to deep-blue urban districts and a small number of favorable constituencies, to a driving force in the party. Much of the media coverage has portrayed the party as being overtaken by an ascendant left. That broader narrative, reinforced by favorable polling, created an expectation that El-Sayed would win resoundingly.

In practice, the recent wave means that a meaningful additional share of Democratic primary voters, perhaps 10-15%, is now willing to consistently support left candidates, on top of the existing leftwing base.

It does not mean that every candidate backed by the DSA or the broader progressive movement will automatically win, or every Democrat backed by Aipac will lose. The actual campaign still matters tremendously; a large share of Democratic voters remain moderate, cross-pressured or primarily candidate-driven.

Politics just doesn’t move that fast. The project of building a leftwing base and turning it into a durable majority, even within the Democratic party, is still a long-term one.

El-Sayed’s narrow victory has been described as disappointing, because of favorable polling and the expectations created by the recent wave of leftwing victories. It is anything but. The polling miss has distorted how the result is being interpreted.

Viewed against Michigan’s demographics, the left’s previous statewide performance, spending disparities, endorsements and comparable results elsewhere in the country, the victory was historically significant.

The left has not previously won a genuinely competitive statewide Democratic primary of this kind, nor has a left candidate previously assembled a winning primary coalition extending this far beyond the movement’s urban base, especially in a swing state where voters are likely to weigh general-election viability.

The left’s strategy over the past decade has been one of patience, winning seats in friendly areas, knocking doors and slowly building a base. It began by winning city council and state legislative victories and expanded more recently into successful mayoral and congressional races, all in deep blue areas.

This is the first time the left has real proof of concept that beyond urban cores with friendly demographics, it can win over a majority of Democratic voters. It also offers early evidence that a left candidate could compete seriously in a Democratic presidential primary in 2028.

The next test is November. The left has been battle-tested in primaries against moderate candidates, party institutions and well-funded outside groups such as Aipac and the crypto lobby. But a general election in a swing state is a different and less hospitable terrain.

El-Sayed, along with Francesca Hong if she advances in Wisconsin, needs to demonstrate the left can win not only a winning Democratic primary coalition, but a broad enough general-election coalition to prevail outside deep-blue territory. This matters in the near term, for Democrats to win the Senate and retain governorships; in the medium term, because presidential primary voters in 2028 will want evidence that left candidates can win competitive general elections; and in the long term, because the leftwing political project rests on being able to twin and govern with durable electoral majorities.

On Tuesday, the left continued its string of victories, activating young voters and bringing Arab and Muslim voters back into the Democratic fold. But these victories do not resolve the movement’s central challenges.

Every primary remains a brutal fight, highly contingent on candidates, organization, spending and local conditions. And the movement must now prepare for the more difficult terrain of November. The left is increasingly winning within the Democratic party, but it still needs to prove that it can build general-election coalitions capable of defeating Republicans.

Ben Davis works in political data in Washington DC. He worked on the data team for the Bernie Sanders 2020 campaign and is an active member of the Democratic Socialists of America

‘Like a jet taking off’: the cicada that can top 120 decibels and nearly break the pain threshold

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 11:00:46 GMT

The palm-sized greengrocer is bright, loud and abundant, and has long been a collectible item for Australian children

Revealed: the top 10 invertebrates of the year

Before marbles, stamps and trading cards, there were cicadas.

There are thousands of cicada species globally, but for Australian children the craze centres on one particularly collectible item: the greengrocer.

“In both Sydney and Melbourne, greengrocers come out every now and again in fairly decent numbers, and they’re coming out in leafy gardens and parks, quite close to where people are,” says the environmental consultant Dr Lindsay Popple. Searching for and collecting cicadas has become an activity firmly entrenched in children’s folklore, he says.

Most of their lives are spent as nymphs underground, but when they emerge in late spring, greengrocers are bright and abundant.

About the size of an eraser, this perfectly palm-sized minibeast comes in a variety of vividly coloured morphs, each with a nickname to match. There’s the yellow Monday, the masked devil, red warrior and chocolate soldier, and the appropriately rare, blue moon. Who wouldn’t want to collect them all?

Dom Yates, a Guardian reader from New Zealand, is a fan. “They sing joyously after living years underground so we should appreciate their happy efforts all the more,” he says.

Unlike the North American cicada, which emerges in a 17-year cycle, greengrocers materialise en masse in alternating batches, roughly at seven yearly intervals, with 2027 the next big event.

When cicada nymphs become adults, they shed their skins and grow wings, leaving behind their exoskeletons on trees and fences These are extra treasures for children to discover and stash inside lunchboxes.

Every cicada species has its own acoustic identity, Popple says, and the Australian greengrocer, found along the east coast in some of the most populated parts of the country, is one of the loudest.

Greengrocers produce two main tunes, one a continuous drone, and the other a kind of croaking pulse, using drum-like organs on either side of their bodies called tymbals, and amplifying the sound with their hollow abdomens.

Popple says the males broadcast at intervals throughout the day and often at dusk, trying to attract a mate. Its Queensland cousin, the northern greengrocer, is known as the “seven o’clock cicada” for its propensity to pipe up at dinnertime.

It’s a spectacular racket. “Close to them, it’s like being near a jet taking off, it’s really loud,” Popple says. “On a really, really, warm morning, if you get a really hot day, they can start up calling pretty early in the day, which can be a bit of a wake-up for some people.”

As the 16-year-old Guardian reader Matteo says: “They’re loud and gorgeous and they climb trees and shout. What’s not to love?” Indeed.

Greengrocer cicadas are among the loudest invertebrates on land, reportedly reaching volumes as high as 120 decibels at close range – that’s nearing the pain threshold for human hearing, according to the Australian museum.

In general, the closer you are the louder they sound.

But, perhaps luckily, if you get too close they’ll stop singing.

‘Community spaces are being taken away’: campaigners rail at rise of pay-to-play padel courts

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 11:00:45 GMT

Proposals to convert skateparks, children’s play areas and basketball courts have angered residents

Aiwa Saito and her children are among the many families who were regulars at Barking Skatepark. But after they skated here for more than five years, London’s only full-size indoor skatepark closed on Sunday – to be replaced with padel courts.

Padel is one of the UK’s fastest-growing sports, according to the Lawn Tennis Association, and the plan to convert Barking Skatepark is the latest in a series of proposals across London. However, some plans that have sought to build pay-to-play padel courts on top of existing spaces have angered residents and sparked claims of “gentrification” and community displacement.

Saito no longer feels she has a safe, indoor space in the capital to take her kids skating. “Outdoor skateparks aren’t safe for children, particularly teenage girls,” she says.

“Parents already tell their girls: ‘You have to be really careful when you go skateboarding, which park you go to. It’s not safe.’ And to take that away, with no alternative, is unacceptable.”

Saito has high hopes for her 11-year-old daughter, Toko, who is on Skateboard GB’s talent pathway programme and hopes to one day compete internationally. But after the closure of Barking Skatepark, Saito worries if she will be able to keep Toko’s ambition alive.

“To make her dreams come true, we need the right facilities,” she says. “Without an indoor park, on a wet weekend in winter, where do we go? Where can she train?”

And it is not just the parents of aspiring Olympians who worry about the closure of the park. “It’s important to the local community,” says Eleanor Dunlop, who led the campaign to save the venue. “Parents come here to socialise, they bring their kids to be active. Barking and Dagenham is one of the most deprived parts of the country, and people really need this space to be accessible.

I’ve seen panic in people’s faces when I told them that it could close, because they’re saying: ‘Where am I going to take my kids?’”

The council says that while it owns the freehold on the site, the skatepark (and wider sports complex) is run independently by a charity, GLL, which has the right to determine what sports it offers. Barking and Dagenham Council argues: “GLL has advised that the skatepark has been operating at a financial loss for a number of years and that it intends to replace it with indoor padel courts.

“It should be noted that equipment from Barking Skatepark has been distributed to skateparks in the wider area, and will be enjoyed by skateboarders for years to come.”

Part of the backlash to the “padel boom” among local residents can be explained by the cost of playing the sport, which at an average of £51 an hour for a court in London according to the racket sports app Playtomic, means that many feel they will not be the ones to benefit from new facilities.

“It’s so expensive, it just feels exclusive,” Dunlop says.

The price and popularity of padel has attracted investors and private equity firms to build lucrative courts and clubs. According to LTA figures, in the past seven years alone the number of padel courts in the UK has increased by more than 2,500%, from 68 in 2019 to more than 1,800 today.

Saito says that before taking up skating, her daughter used to attend a community gymnastics centre in Beckton. That was until the building, a designated “asset of community value”, was sold to a developer and converted into a private padel club – despite local opposition and an online petition signed by almost 10,000 people .

“One of her two sports was already taken away because of padel,” she says, explaining that while the gymnastics club moved to Newham Leisure Centre, the facilities were not as specialised as those at Beckton and her daughter’s friends all dispersed. “Now her main sport is going to be taken away. It just feels crazy.”

In Bethnal Green, meanwhile, the local council installed a £24-an-hour, pay-to-play padel court in the middle of an open, multi-use area shared by people freely roller‑skating, playing basketball and skateboarding.

“Being able to spontaneously come and go from a space like this, means one less financial restriction on how we use our free time – which in today’s world is already inhibited by just how expensive everything is,” says the campaigner Lillie Almond, who is fighting to remove the padel court.

“The padel court has obviously changed who’s now using this space, and how,” she adds. “This all results in the removal of culturally rich, diverse, long-standing communities – who are replaced with padel players.”

In Camden, councillor Hamza Chowdhury campaigned to stop a free children’s sandpit and play area being bulldozed to make way for padel courts. After more than a year of protests, the £2m proposal was rejected last week.

“If the goal was to get more people active, why not invest in a free, all-weather basketball or football court?” says Chowdhury. “Growing sport should never come at the cost of shrinking free public space. We should be adding to our communities, not taking away from them.”

Oli Mould, professor of social, cultural and historical geography at Royal Holloway, University of London, says the plans in Camden, Bethnal Green and Barking reflect a broader pattern of rising gentrification across London.

“Gentrification is about the restriction of land,” he says.

“What’s happening is people taking land away and putting a physical barrier around it – so it can be given to people who will pay. Any time that happens, that is gentrification.”

Though Barking Skatepark officially closed on Sunday, Dunlop and her fellow campaigners are still fighting to halt construction. With backing from the local MP, Nesil Caliskan, and Skateboard GB, the sport’s national governing body, as well as an online petition that has gained more than 4,500 signatures, she hopes they can stop the development, as Chowdhury did in Camden.

“Not listening to people who occupy a space, and then going in and changing it, is gentrification,” Dunlop says.

“I can’t comment on padel as a sport, whether I like it or not. I just don’t believe that it should displace the people who are already there. Having community spaces is so important – and they’re being taken away.”

A spokesperson for Tower Hamlets Council said the padel court at Bethnal Green Gardens is part of a trial using one out of five multi-use areas available. “The trial supports our work to increase access to a wider range of sports and improve the health and wellbeing of our residents,” they said.

GLL and Camden Council have been approached for comment.

All bodies of water in England polluted with toxic chemicals, official data shows

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 10:03:50 GMT

Environment Agency assessments find just 14.3% of country’s surface waters in good ecological status

Every single English water body is polluted with toxic chemicals, new government data shows, while just 14.3% of surface waters achieved good ecological status.

Each of the country’s rivers, lakes and estuaries was assessed by the Environment Agency as part of a six-yearly evaluation of England’s water quality. The EA checked for a range of toxic chemicals, from Pfas – or “forever chemicals” – to microplastics. Waters were also checked against a range of standards covering wildlife, water quality and physical habitat.

If concentrations of the chemicals exceed the set standards, the water body fails to meet good chemical status. In the latest assessment, every surface water body in England failed on this measure.

Under water framework directive regulations, the official target date for all water bodies to reach good chemical and ecological status is December 2027, although some chemicals have deadlines in the 2030s.

The Environment Agency said this failure was driven almost entirely by the presence of mercury, Pfos – a type of Pfas with links to cancer - and PBDEs, which were formerly used as flame retardants. These chemicals are persistent, meaning they do not break down and can accumulate in the environment.

England’s water bodies are not predicted to reach good chemical status until 2063, when the EA says the persistent chemical pollutants should have degraded sufficiently for waters to again be considered unpolluted.

Ami McCarthy, Greenpeace UK’s head of politics, said the scale of the crisis was “sobering”. The government needed to take “urgent action to turn off the chemicals that are destroying our land at the source”, they said.

The UK government has been accused of failing to take action on toxic chemicals after its plan to tackle Pfas chemicals failed to match the tougher stance being taken in Europe. It has also been accused of failing to tackle mercury pollution, with Britain being one of the few countries yet to ban mercury in dental fillings. The metal is a potent neurotoxin that can harm the nervous, digestive and immune systems, as well as the lungs, kidneys, skin and eyes, even at low levels of exposure.

Craig Bennett, chief executive of The Wildlife Trusts said if it was a “foreign power maliciously poisoning every single water body in England with cancer causing chemicals, politicians right across the political spectrum would be utterly horrified and demand the government of the day do absolutely everything in their power to fight back, stop it immediately, and seek some sort of retribution”.

Instead he said “politicians across the political spectrum have come together with a conspiracy of silence and inaction”.

Richard Benwell, the chief executive of Wildlife and Countryside Link, said: “With thousands more forever chemicals on the market from cosmetics to clothing, government must act now to stop another wave of contamination by matching EU safeguards and making the polluting companies pay for clean up.”

Water campaigner Feargal Sharkey said the EA has “failed every waterbody in the country” and “overseen the collapse of an issue they were supposed to be policing”.

He called on the environment secretary to rewrite the guidance and enforce the law as it stands.

The Environment Agency said it was undertaking a range of activities to improve understanding of chemicals in the environment and identify potential sources affecting rivers, groundwater and drinking water catchments.

“Water companies must be made to take responsibility for their part, but pollution from agriculture is now one of the biggest drivers of environmental damage in UK rivers. It’s time for the government to work with farmers, providing proper support to rein in runaway use of fertilisers and pesticides, and boost nature-friendly practices,” McCarthy said.

Assessment against a range of standards covering wildlife, water quality and physical habitat also showed that just 14.3% of England’s surface waters achieved good ecological status, a decline from 16.3% in 2019. However, the EA said the two datasets were not directly comparable because it had updated its analytical methods.

The environment secretary, Angela Eagle, said the results “underline the need for wholesale change across the water sector”.

The chief executive of the campaign group River Action said despite successive government’s promises, England’s rivers remained among the “filthiest in Europe, poisoned by sewage from polluting, profit-driven water companies and by industrial-scale agriculture, including chicken manure runoff from intensive poultry units that rear tens of millions of birds for fast-food chains and supermarkets”.

Prof Alex Ford, professor of biology at University of Portsmouth, said he is “not surprised” by the analysis and said if regulators added more chemicals to the list that should be monitored, he is “confident we would be failing on a larger list of contaminants.”

‘They were told bikes were for men’: how Latin America’s city of cycling is breaking gender barriers

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 10:00:46 GMT

With less than a third of cycling journeys taken by women, Colombia’s capital, Bogotá, is installing bike lanes, teaching cycling and making sure ‘stereotypes are left behind’

Eliana González has a busy morning ahead of her, dropping off her son at school and picking up groceries. Her trusted vehicle to get around in Bogotá is a colourful cargo bike, adapted to carry her two children and occasionally her dog.

“For me, my cargo bike is a way to carry my children safely and comfortably without polluting the environment,” she says.

Widely regarded as a global cycling success story, the Colombian city of 10 million people records nearly 900,000 bicycle trips each day – more than any other city in Latin America.

Now, city officials are working towards another milestone: achieving gender parity in cycling by 2039. Women accounted for only 28% of Bogotá’s daily bicycle trips in 2023, according to the city’s latest mobility survey. “Our goal is to move from a [nearly] 30–70 split to 50–50 parity,” says Claudia Díaz, Bogotá’s secretary of mobility.

Closing the gender gap makes for a more inclusive city, but also brings environmental benefits. Transportation is Bogotá’s largest source of greenhouse emissions, and officials say that boosting the number of female cyclists could support the capital’s goal of becoming carbon neutral by 2050.

“The challenge we face is how to increase the number of cycling trips,” says Díaz. “The more we increase the number of cycling trips, the more environmental benefits we see for our city.”

Experts say gender equality is essential for cities to fully realise the benefits of investing in sustainable transportation, which can lead to lower greenhouse gas emissions, cleaner air and reduced traffic congestion.

“Those impacts aren’t really going to happen if only half the population is ever going to use that [transport] system,” says Dana Yanocha, a senior manager at the Institute for Transportation and Development Policy, a nonprofit organisation promoting sustainable transport.

Increasing women’s participation in cycling remains a challenge, especially across the global south, Yanocha says. In many of the cities where her organisation works, women make up only a small share of cyclists, often accounting for less than 10% of daily bicycle trips.

In 2021, Bogotá adopted a new cycling public policy, the first of its kind in Colombia, that incorporated a gender perspective. As part of the initiative, researchers with C40 Cities Finance Facility, a programme that helps cities develop climate infrastructure projects, looked at why women cycle less than men in Bogotá.

They identified several barriers. About 60% of women surveyed said they avoided cycling because they feared theft or assault, 40% expressed concerns about being hit by a vehicle and nearly one-third said they had never learned to ride a bicycle.

One way officials have since been addressing safety concerns is by building more cycle lanes, which research shows helps female cyclists feel safer. Bogotá’s network of protected bike lanes – the largest in Latin America – now spans 425 miles (683.9km), according to the city council.

The city is also repairing deteriorated lanes, installing lighting, improving connectivity and increasing police patrols along busy cycling corridors. “By improving infrastructure, we can help women feel that riding a bike is a viable option for them,” says Diaz.

For many women, however, the biggest barrier is simply never having learned to ride. Sergio Prieto helps to oversee Bogotá’s Bike School, a city programme that teaches about 40,000 residents to cycle each year. He says that about 80% of participants are women.

“Many older women come here because they were never allowed to ride a bicycle as girls,” Prieto says. “They were told bikes were for men, that women shouldn’t be riding them. Here, those barriers and stereotypes are left behind.”

In 2018, González founded Mamacitas en Bici an initiative that encourages mothers to cycle. Her work addresses an often overlooked reality: the leading reason why women move across Bogotá is for caregiving trips, such as taking children to school, according to one study.

But caregivers face discrimination for choosing to cycle, González says. When she first started riding with her baby, strangers shouted at her, calling her irresponsible, she says. But rather than quit, she created a community, helping mothers customise their bikes to safely carry children, organising group rides for families and teaching women and children to cycle.

“I realised how important it is to have safe spaces where we can move through the world as women, in a body that is treated differently by society and subjected to violence,” she says.

González says she encourages women to take up cycling because of its social benefits, including greater independence and improved health. But for her, riding a bicycle is also a way to help shape the kind of city she wants for herself and her children.

“We still have so many green spaces in our city, and I want to do my part to help protect them,” she says. “If I get around by bicycle, I’m contributing to that environmental effort.”

Tech companies know everything about me – so why do they try to sell me so much rubbish?

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 10:00:45 GMT

No, Amazon, I do not want to buy another version of the thing I just bought, or any other random object I don’t recognise or understand

We live, as I’m sure someone’s chief growth officer has recently boasted on an earnings call, in a golden age for data capture. Jeff Bezos knows what I buy, read and watch; Mark Zuckerberg will be aware that I recently sold a car transport box for a medium-sized dog. I’ve been ruthlessly conditioned into clicking Accept All Cookies every time I want to check how much cumin my favourite chilli needs, and I simply accept that my washing machine is probably spying on me.

All of which raises the obvious question: with all of these terabytes of personal information available, why can’t advertisers try to sell me something I might actually like? Every time I swipe open my Kindle, for instance, I dismiss an advert for a bestselling trilogy called something like Ruthless Faerie Werewolves or Evil Mafia Hunk, even though I have never once – in my life – read a book where the main character could be described as a “morally grey shadow daddy”. I stopped watching Stranger Things after one season, and yet Netflix, which should know this better than anyone, has suggested the stage-play version to me so many times that I can recite its ad from memory. Amazon seems to have given up on predicting my needs and advertises the same one-off purchases that I’ve just bought, while Reddit and X want me to buy software products that I genuinely don’t understand.

Part of me is heartened by this: maybe I’m too dazzlingly individual to be defined by the things I click on. Another part is saddened: what would be better, after all, than being bombarded with recommendations for the sort of books I can never find enough of (micro-histories of things like cod, say, or AK-47s, or 19th-century navigation).

But a tiny part of me is desperately worried that the algorithm really does know me better than I know myself, and that I’m denying myself by refusing to heed its call. I’ll let you know, just as soon as I’m done with Mean Pixie Mob Daddy.

Joel Snape is a freelance writer

I knew Rod Liddle and hated what he became. He would have wanted me to say so

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 09:00:43 GMT

A man who prized blunt speaking has been selectively eulogised. There’s a balance between decency and honesty: I’m sad he caused such harm

As tributes poured in for Rod Liddle, the Sunday Times and Sun columnist who has died at the age of 66, they were markedly coy and sanitised. Paradoxically, those were the exact deficiencies obituaries praised Liddle for avoiding – they said he shot from the hip and ruffled feathers, remorselessly attacked the liberal establishment and was ebullient. Michael Gove called him “special and brave”. But brave in the face of what? Attacked the liberal establishment how?

This delicacy was particularly noticeable in a segment on Radio 4’s Today programme, of which Liddle was editor in the 90s, between Justin Webb and Amol Rajan. “If there was a golden thread that connected the person you saw back then with the person of a few weeks ago,” Webb said, “it was a distrust of authority.” But Liddle’s targets as a columnist were not the authorities. Often they were Muslims and immigrants, transgender people and chronic illness sufferers, African-Caribbean men from Harlesden. He did not attack the establishment, he attacked the marginalised, constantly.

There is sometimes a dilemma in how we process death. Decently, we seek not to speak ill of the dead, and certainly one hopes to never increase the grief of those who loved them. But does that mean we are also duty-bound not to discuss more uncomfortable issues? Here I feel the dilemma.

I was friends with Rod Liddle in the 90s. He was a different Rod then. The principal target of his satire was himself. He would lampoon guys having affairs, guys who were a shambles, guys who had run out of road. If there was any ethno-caricaturing, it read as a footnote to a worldview in which nobody was more ridiculous than he, Rod Liddle. This carried on into his collection of short stories, Too Beautiful for You (2003), in which the most memorable escapade was a man getting into a train crash, after seeing his mistress, rushing across a field carrying his severed arm so that he could get to a hospital without blowing his alibi, and realising as he bleeds out that he must actually really love his wife.

In 1983, he was a member of the Socialist Workers party and by 1990, a researcher for the Labour party, but what made him seem left-left, rather than centre left, didn’t have a membership card. It was the self-parody coupled with an overall dishevelment that conveyed a deep-seated humanity and pluralism: “I’m a mess, you’re a mess, let’s get out of this mess together.” I know that is maddeningly unspecific, but I also know that anyone on the left will get what I mean.

So his transformation into an attack dog for the race-baiting right was painful to watch, if not exactly unprecedented. On Tuesday, sociologist Will Davies characterised this post-68 type, “drawn to norm-breaching, moving via adolescent rebellion, punk, revolutionary socialism and eventually ending up at racism, because by the 21st century that was the most efficient transgression still on offer”. The rightwing media will pay absolutely top dollar for a big-name left-to-right defector.

Peter York, in his book A Dead Cat on Your Table, examines the nexus of rightwing thinktanks, the mainstream right and “alt-right” media to argue that what we call “culture wars” aren’t ideological, they’re about hegemonic capture in the service of capital. Depressingly, it does work: GB News, which hedge-funder Paul Marshall hosed money at, to widespread ridicule, now secures higher average audiences than Sky News or BBC News. Arguably, the greater victory is that all we ever talk about is what GB News wants to talk about.

One thing the obituaries did mention was Liddle’s feud with Yasmin Alibhai-Brown – “they loathed each other,” Justin Webb said, then, later he asked: “Deep down, did he really? There was no loathing in Rod that I could ever divine.” But “feud” is doing some heavy lifting there: Liddle attacked Alibhai-Brown constantly in his columns, for opinions which many of us hold but seemed unaccountably more obnoxious to him coming from her. This culminated in a clash on Channel 4 in 2014, after which the then Conservative MP Michael Fabricant, tweeted that he might have ended up punching Alibhai-Brown in the throat.

Liddle the Today editor, listening to much of the discussion, would have said, “what the fuck are you playing at, trying to describe this outrageous character without naming any of his outrages?” Not least as they are so easy to Google – the time he said he couldn’t have been a teacher because he would have ended up shagging the children, “right in there, on day one”; the endless attacks on Muslims, arguing that it was the faith itself, not unhinged individuals, that drove terrorism, that the 2019 election should be held on a day when “Muslims are forbidden to do anything on pain of hell” to suppress their vote. The editor Liddle of the 90s would have also said: “You can’t have two blokes on the radio, explaining why whipping up racist misogyny is fine so long as, underneath, you have a heart of gold.” Not because of diversity and whatnot, but because it’s just not cricket.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

One of the last times I saw Liddle was a couple of months ago when we were both on Sky News. He looked really different, because he had COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease). I asked him how he was and he said “depressed”, and I asked why, but I was just being tactful, because it was obvious why. My mum died with COPD last year, and by the time your face goes grey, life is pretty horrible, like drowning in air. “I’m no longer priapic,” he replied.

I felt ineffably sad; that privately, his persona was still the same, standing there with his arm hanging off, insisting that the first thing he would do, once he got it sewed back on, was get a hard-on; sad at the pantomime of it, cartoon prejudices with real-life consequences, trotted out on command, funded by people with mountains of money who wish society ill; sad about the empathy and solidarity that had once built a collective firewall against hate-for-fun, which had been slowly extinguished.

In fact, I wanted to start crying but I’d just had my makeup done, so we went on air and argued about Andy Burnham in Makerfield, and he said he would only win it if he “sorted out” immigration. I won’t miss Rod Liddle, but I miss the person he was when the world was different, and I miss that different world.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

Should I try the ‘18 summers’ parenting trend? Only if I want to ruin the school holidays

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 07:00:42 GMT

Long days with nothing to do is the whole point of summer. Turning it into a ‘making memories’ exercise is creepy and controlling

There are a great many things to dislike about modern parenting trends – take your pick from helicopter to snowplow to Fafo – but the least appealing, perhaps, is the temptation present in all of them to treat raising a child like an extended school project.

The latest addition is something called 18 summers, in which clingy parents count down the school holidays they have left with their children before they leave home, pre-grieving the end as they go. There is no quicker way to ruin something than by filtering it through an internet trend, but this one is particularly insidious: an invitation to inject weird notes of anxiety into what might otherwise be an unstudied thing.

Let’s put to one side for a moment the fact that, in these economic times, kids don’t stop going on holiday with their parents until they’re roughly 35. The idea behind the “viral concept” of 18 summers – tagline “you only get 18 summers with your kid” – is to remind us that life is short and we should cherish each moment, a banality that, if it is ever true, is particularly untrue during the summer holidays, which are very, very long indeed. I would rather sign up to a movement called 18 minutes, in which we recognise the time-warping effect of the slow-crawl towards September, or even 18 seconds, in which we study the fascinating variables in time perception as it relates to unstructured periods with children, which might also be marketed as 18 millennia.

Eighteen summers on the other hand is designed, like most social media trends, to make us feel as if we’re misusing our time by showing us how other, better motivated people are using theirs. This is achieved via a set of social media posts carrying the 18 summers hashtag and which, no matter where in the world the images are generated, looks like a set of adverts for Center Parcs Longleat.

There has always been something creepy about the formalisation of quotidian parts of life, and I would put the phrase “making memories” into that category. It’s the animating ethos behind 18 summers, which comes with a retail shelf full of diaries, binders and other products to ensure we document every precious moment with our children – without enjoying any of them. I’m currently in New York, ground zero of acute parenting trends, where “experiencing joy” may be tackled with the same, furrow-browed intensity as “learning Mandarin” and where parents can become so feverishly intent on “making memories” for their children that they badger them into a state of complete mania. (In this world, going for a bike ride becomes so fraught with meaning it becomes Going For A Bike Ride and you’d better hope it hits that platonic ideal).

The bigger drag behind this concept is the need to turn every last human impulse into an item on a to-do list. Do you enjoy summer while also finding it enraging and boring? Well, try holding it up against an idealised version that relies for its power on a sense of loss, fear and competition with others. The word “magical” hangs heavily over this scene, too, and, who among us needs reminding that anyone who uses the word magical more than once or twice a year is a joyless weirdo. Other phrases encountered when you browse the endless Instagram reels around 18 summers: “ultimate family formula” (sounds fun!), “three steps to deepen your relationship with your child”, and “holding sand”, which refers to how fast the time goes (although in the case of this particular scene, not fast enough).

All of this is, of course, just another form of parental overreach, a way of normalising and celebrating controlling personalities. The flipside to 18 summers is the romanticisation of our own childhoods, in which, to listen to us go on, we spent six weeks out on bikes like the kids in ET rather than, say, inside watching telly. Still, no one interfered with us much. I took my kids to a climbing wall this week – making memories! – and it was like a comedy sketch, watching parents stand at the foot of the wall directing their perfectly able kids to the top. (“Honey, put your left foot on that one diagonally – no, not that one, the one next to it; up and to the right, yep, yep. YES! Good job! You’re so good at this!” As one dad standing next to me muttered bleakly, “back-seat climbing”).

I love the summers. Even when things get frazzled towards the end, I love the sense of having nothing to do, which makes a walk to the shops with my kids something to draw out for as long as we can, rather than race through to get to the next thing. The whole point of summer is that you’re not held to account, or a schedule, or in this case, a hashtag. For a short time, we can inhabit that state hovering right on the edge of boredom that – if we don’t ruin things by overthinking – seems to go on for ever.

Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist

The takedown of Jason Arday has overjoyed the right, and must be a wake-up call for the left

The Guardian Thu, 06 Aug 2026 05:00:39 GMT

The Cambridge academic has rightly now resigned. But that won’t end the targeting of senior black figures or the lazy way institutions promote faux equality

‘To be honest with you, I thought you’d just believe me.” That was the breathtaking response of Prof Jason Arday when the Guardian interrogated the details he provided of an alleged racist campaign of intimidation against him, which involved a severed pig’s head, a masked man wielding a knife and bullets in the post. Arday had been unable to provide evidence, and when the Guardian contacted the relevant parties, including a south London butcher and the police, his claims were either refuted or could not be verified.

Arday, whose appointment as professor of sociology of education at Cambridge became a widely lauded moment in the aftermath of Black Lives Matter, has found himself in the eye of the storm. Allegations of extensive plagiarism in his doctoral thesis, completed at Liverpool John Moores University, recently made their way from the Substack of self-described “race realist” academic Nathan Cofnas into the national press. The defence of Arday had rested on the fact that an investigation had already been conducted, and cleared him of plagiarism. And yet the case has taken on a life of its own.

In recent weeks, more of Arday’s story has come under scrutiny: from claims of having installed water points in South America and west Africa with the charity WaterAid (WaterAid said it does not send volunteers abroad), to having run 30 marathons in 35 days, the last dozen or so after suffering a hairline fracture in his leg. After mounting pressure, Cambridge announced that it had launched a formal investigation into his academic qualifications and honorary appointments. Following this announcement, Arday resigned from his positions at the university. Though he has chosen to step aside to preserve his “wellbeing”, this has become a national story that will not go away.

Allegations of plagiarism in a doctoral thesis do not usually make for riveting, front-page news. Indeed, in 2023, when the Cambridge history professor William O’Reilly faced allegations of plagiarising student essays, the press coverage consisted of barely half a dozen articles (a tribunal ruled the plagiarism was “the product of negligent acts but was not deliberate”). Few people could care less about what academics get up to.

But Arday could not expect to be similarly insulated by academia’s remoteness. This story has endured, stubbornly, because it is so perfectly calibrated for some of the most combustible charges of Britain’s culture wars: namely, that academic standards have been surrendered to a woke orthodoxy, and that minorities are unfairly advanced in the name of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) initiatives.

The instinct of progressives had been to defend Arday; indeed, many went on to sign an open letter in support of him, seeing him as simply another black man under a sustained press attack. This was not least because the charges against him originated with Cofnas, who had been dismissed from his post at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, in 2024 after making pseudo-scientific claims that under a true meritocracy black people would “disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment”. And for many in the rightwing press, this is their victory lap, their vindication. The spectacle of it is just too grim to behold. The headlines of “DEI darling” and “diversity poster boy” barely conceal their excitement. Gotcha!

I do not care to examine the quality of Arday’s scholarship, research or life story beyond what has already been written elsewhere. What concerns me is how little space remains for a genuinely progressive critique of institutional diversity practices – one capable of scrutinising how for many organisations and corporations symbolic representation has been a substitute for deeper reform, leaving it vulnerable to just this kind of backlash. It has also meant that the right has enjoyed a near monopoly on criticism of DEI, leaving it to frame it entirely on its own terms.

Let’s take a look back at the coverage of Arday’s appointment at Cambridge in 2023. The headline was that Arday, then 37, was to become the “youngest black professor” ever appointed at Cambridge and that his feat was particularly remarkable considering that he supposedly only learned to speak at 11, and to read and write at 18, having been diagnosed with global development delay and autism spectrum disorder as a child. The media circus around this appointment rivalled Hollywood press junkets, with newspaper, television and radio slots covering him on both sides of the Atlantic, including an NBC News item on his “inspiring story”.

I am not privy to the hiring process for a professorial chair at Cambridge. I do not know exactly why and how Arday got the job or who else was in the running. But what happens when an academic’s story is sold through him being the “youngest black ever” (sitting alongside familiar monikers such as “the first black” or “black excellence”) and asterisked by a tale of hardship? You are not encouraged or invited to engage with the substance of their scholarship; instead, you are invited to clap. Instead of his appointment conjuring the question “what new opportunities for research will this lead to?”, it was “doesn’t this make you feel good?”

What this means is that Arday was treated not as a scholar but as a mascot, one who was particularly expedient for an institution that had been regularly embarrassed by its historic record on race: too few black students (in my cohort at Cambridge matriculating in 2015 there were only 15 black males out of 3,449 students); single-figure black academics (which is still the case); allegations of institutional racism. Independent of the merits or pitfalls of his own scholarship, what success looked like for Arday in this role was limited; what accountability could look like if misconduct occurred was constrained by him being a vehicle for Cambridge to signal its institutional progress.

These are not arguments that progressives should shy away from. Instead, they should own them. There is a real risk of this case being used to undermine black academics and others in positions of seniority. For all the talk of preferential treatment for black people in academia, it remains true that there are documented, systemic barriers for black students, including in their access to funding to advance their studies.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The mass investigation into Arday’s PhD may be presented as the pursuit of public and intellectual integrity, and yet the origin of this is grievance politics from those who feel diversity has blocked their own advancement. It comes with that malign charge of being a “DEI hire” or being in your position to “fill a quota”, the accusation that so often stalks black people elevated to senior positions. And so with Arday as an avatar for the black colleague who was promoted over you, the black child who was made head boy over your son, that process turbocharges.

In Arday, those on the right feel that they have found what they are looking for; that is why every drop is being wrung out of this story. His resignation will not end that. The next step will be to make this single case bear the weight of the ideological arguments they pile on it.

How do you resist that? By embracing and learning from the mistakes that were made here, not avoiding them out of discomfort. That means advocating for diversity without tokenism, the celebration of excellent black scholarship without the need for exceptionalism or academic celebrity. If we let only our opponents tell the story, then it becomes a parable about the hazards of striving for progress and equality, rather than about the institutions that reduced equality to a mere PR exercise.

Jason Okundaye is an assistant Opinion editor at the Guardian
