Trump Administration to Deregulate Head Start

The New York Times August 06, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

While administration officials say the changes will save money by lifting onerous requirements, advocates fear the anti-poverty program will be gutted.

By Coral Davenport

Reporting from Washington

The Trump administration announced on Thursday that it would move forward with a plan to eliminate hundreds of federal regulations governing Head Start, in what advocates fear is a push to gut a 61-year-old antipoverty program aimed at helping the nation’s most impoverished young children.

The proposed plan, detailed in earlier reporting by The New York Times, would remove most of Head Start’s 133 pages of federal requirements for math and literacy curricula, class sizes, medical screenings, home visits. Even a requirement that children brush their teeth after meals would end.

Administration officials say the changes will save money by lifting onerous requirements, serve more children by increasing class sizes, and give states and municipalities more control in how the program is run. Critics say the changes will gut the core components of a singular institution that has served 30 million young children with high classroom standards and more health and antipoverty services than most states provide.

Head Start was launched 61 years ago as part of President Lyndon B. Johnson’s War on Poverty, and a key figure in its early design and creation was Sargent Shriver, an uncle of Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the health secretary leading the push to deregulate the program. It provides early education and poverty support services for children up to age 6.

In a statement, Mr. Kennedy said the changes would honor his uncle’s legacy.

“My uncle, Sarge Shriver, founded the program on a simple conviction: strong families, wholesome nutrition, and healthy childhood development can change the course of a child’s life,” he said. “Today we are returning Head Start to those roots, We are removing unnecessary bureaucracy, strengthening nutrition and physical health, trusting parents and local communities, and opening Head Start to hundreds of thousands more children.”

Health and Human Services Department officials claimed that the changes — particularly the lifting of rules on small class sizes — would allow Head Start to serve up to 236,000 more children than the 700,000 it does today. They also said that stripping away requirements such as classroom curricula, or rules that require Head Start staff to ensure that students have dental exams, would save about $2.2 billon. And they noted that the proposed changes would also include new requirements for children’s physical activity and nutrition.

Advocates for the program said the changes would wipe out the distinctive features and benefits of Head Start.

“Head Start works because it does far more than provide preschool,” said Joel Ryan, director of the Washington State Association of Head Start. “It ensures children receive health care, developmental screenings, nutritious meals, disability services, highly qualified teachers, and strong partnerships with families. Those aren’t bureaucratic requirements — they are the reason Head Start has changed millions of lives. This proposal would weaken those protections for hundreds of thousands of children and undermine what has made Head Start one of America’s most successful early childhood programs.”

The Health and Human Services Department is expected to post the proposed changes on the Federal Register in the coming days. They will then be open to public comment for 60 days, and could still be changed and amended before being finalized in the coming months. The changes are expected to be implemented in Head Start classrooms sometime in 2027.

Coral Davenport covers energy and environment policy, with a focus on climate change, for The Times.

Houthi Strikes on Yemeni Military Threaten to Reignite Civil War

The New York Times August 06, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The Iran-backed militia said they had targeted the armed forces in two resource-rich provinces, as escalating violence in Yemen imperils a fragile truce.

By Ismaeel Naar

Reporting from Dubai, United Arab Emirates.

The Yemeni military said Thursday that the Houthis, an Iran-backed militia, had attacked the armed forces of the internationally-recognized government, an escalation that threatens to reignite Yemen’s long-simmering civil war.

The Houthis targeted “several camps and units of the Armed Forces,” the military said in a statement posted on social media, “resulting in human and material losses.” The military did not say how many people were killed in the attacks but local media outlets reported dozens had been killed.

Hours later, a Houthi military spokesman, Yahya Saree, said the group had launched “a large number of drones and ballistic missiles” at Yemeni military camps in Marib and Hadramout, two oil-rich provinces controlled by the government.

Mr. Saree said the group had launched the attack after they “monitored a large Saudi military mobilization” who were “aiming to escalate” against them.

Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition in Yemen since 2015 to oust the Houthis and restore the internationally-recognized government, after the militia seized control of the capital Sanaa.

The civil war in Yemen killed hundreds of thousands of people not only from direct violence, but also hunger and disease stemming from the conflict. A fragile cease-fire was agreed between the government and the Houthis in 2022, and Saudi Arabia pulled back from its extensive bombing campaign in Yemen.

The latest round of fighting has prompted fears that the truce is nearing collapse, after months of escalating tensions and intermittent ground skirmishes between government and Houthi forces.

The Houthis have also clashed with Saudi Arabia in recent weeks and declared a blockade of Saudi oil shipping last month in the Red Sea, firing on passing commercial vessels. Mr. Saree warned the Saudi government on Thursday that it “will bear the consequences of any escalation.”

While in the past the Houthis have acted in support of their main ally, Iran, they also have their own reasons for stepping up attacks on Saudi Arabia now, according to researchers who study the group.

Over the past decade, the Houthis have cemented their control of the country’s north, effectively dividing Yemen into two states. Analysts say the group now appears to be looking to consolidate their control over Yemen and its oil resources, believing they have little left to lose after years of political stalemate since the cease-fire.

The province of Marib, where the armed forces were attacked on Thursday, is one of the last strongholds of the Yemeni government in the north.

Located east of the capital Sanaa, it is home to the country’s largest concentration of displaced persons who fled the fighting over the years. Last week, Yemeni authorities declared a state of emergency in Marib to counter a deadly measles outbreak.

Hadramaut, which also came under attack from the Houthis, is home to much of Yemen’s modest oil reserves that has been a key source of funding for the beleaguered government.

Saeed Al-Batati contributed reported from al-Mukalla, Yemen.

Ismaeel Naar is an international reporter for The Times, covering the Gulf states. He is based in Dubai, United Arab Emirates.

Bernie Sanders Is Not Doing the Democrats Any Favors

The New York Times August 06, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Matthew Yglesias

Mr. Yglesias, a contributing Opinion writer, writes extensively about politics, economics and more at the newsletter Slow Boring.

The primary win in the Michigan Democratic Senate race by Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive former public health official, marks the latest, and perhaps most surprising, instance of the insurgent left’s electoral success at beating establishment incumbents or candidates. It is another episode in the political story of the summer — the sense that something like a left-wing Tea Party is afoot.

These candidates are running for a very progressive policy program. In primaries, they have also run against something: the Democratic establishment. They have stressed the perceived political failings of the establishment — above all, its inability to defeat Donald Trump. The prominent figure at the center of this critique is Bernie Sanders, the Vermont independent.

Primaries are the place to have party fights about issues and hash out those disagreements. But victories like Dr. El-Sayed’s call for greater scrutiny of the political judgments of Mr. Sanders and his movement, forcing us to reckon with exactly what their project is all about. Their focus on factional organizing, while narrowly effective, has sometimes left them at odds with the Democratic Party. And some candidates — particularly those in the Democratic Socialists of America — are articulating a vision that could make it more difficult for Democrats to expand their appeal across America.

The Sanders presidential primary campaigns of 2016 and 2020 set the foundation for the ascendance of the progressive left. Mr. Sanders responded to his losses in those primaries by working tirelessly to promote the political careers of people who supported him. When Sanders-backed candidates have won offices — figures like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Zohran Mamdani — they have gone on to pay it forward.

The insurgent left has shown an impressive display of organizing. But they are building this organization in part out of misleading narratives about the Democratic Party.

Take the 2024 election. For all the effort to hang that defeat on the flawed judgments of the establishment, in the critical weeks after Joe Biden’s debate fiasco, it was often moderate Democrats who led the charge to replace him. By contrast, Mr. Sanders endorsed Mr. Biden, standing by him long after the debate and urging Democrats to stop trying to get him out of the race.

Had Democrats listened to his advice, Mr. Biden would almost certainly have lost in a landslide. Successful Democratic Senate candidates in Michigan, Arizona, Wisconsin and Nevada would likely have floundered, and House seats in Virginia, New Mexico and Minnesota would have been at risk. Mr. Trump would have been able to inflict far more damage with huge congressional majorities at his back.

In the wake of Ms. Harris’s loss, Mr. Sanders proclaimed that “it should come as no great surprise that a Democratic Party which has abandoned working class people would find that the working class has abandoned them.” Yet earlier that summer he explained that he was standing by Mr. Biden precisely because he so strongly endorsed the Biden economic agenda.

The influence of Sanders-aligned advisers in the Biden administration was enormous. And it continues. Lina Khan, the former Federal Trade Commission chair, and a top aide Sam Levine — are leading economic policy in Mr. Mamdani’s administration.

The progressive left has been savvy about obscuring their influence on Bidenomics by shifting the center of the intraparty debate to Israel, where they have the upper hand among Democratic Party primary voters. But the Middle East is a low priority for most Americans (as foreign policy issues typically are).

The party is already suffering from dismal favorability ratings. And broadly speaking, a leftward tilt of the Democratic Party is not what voters want. A June New York Times/Siena poll of voters in the Senate battleground states found that 53 percent of likely voters think Democrats are too far to the left. That — the party brand, and not a difficult map — is the most basic, high-level reason that Republicans are favored to retain control of the Senate, and the Sanders faction has no answer to the problem.

It’s true that, in Michigan, Democratic Party primary voters nominated Dr. El-Sayed and were happy to blow off warnings not only from national party leaders but also their own governor. Still, history suggests a leftist politician like Dr. El-Sayed will be expected to run somewhat weaker than a conventional Democrat — meaning he would likely lose a swing state like Michigan in a neutral political environment. Current polling indicates that the national mood favors Democrats by six or seven points. You would expect an effective politician like Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan — who won narrowly in 2024 — to coast to an eight-point victory this year. So Dr. El-Sayed has room to run four to five points weaker than her and still win — which a scrupulous person would characterize as a disappointment, but Mr. Sanders and his followers would hail as a triumph.

Many rank-and-file Democrats respect the progressive left’s zeal for punching back hard at the Trump administration, which is easier to do from the safety of Vermont or New York City than from the electoral front lines. What they have not been as good at is winning in places that aren’t deep blue. In House races, for example, members of the centrist Blue Dog and New Democrat caucuses perform better than the average Democrat, while members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus perform worse. Elevating Sanders supporters can also lead to vetting failures, as we saw with Graham Platner in Maine and with Nate Blouin, a House candidate in Utah with an unfortunate track record of posts mocking sexual assault and Mormons.

The very top electoral performers among Democrats — lawmakers who have a record of results in districts most liberals would lose, like Vicente Gonzalez of Texas, Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington State, Tom Suozzi of New York and Don Davis of North Carolina — are independent thinkers who are critical of Democratic Party leaders and the establishment. The difference is that rather than positioning themselves even further left than a party that most Americans think is too left-wing, they pick issues and rhetoric that are heterodox and often more restrained.

The insurgents benefit — or suffer, depending on your point of view — from a sort of political conflict of interest. If their wild rhetoric or fanciful position-taking hurts Democrats’ national image, that doesn’t hurt their members in safe seats. Instead, moderate Democrats in competitive seats end up losing. This in turn intensifies grass-roots anger at party leaders’ failure to win, and benefits the insurgents.

Given Mr. Trump’s unpopularity and Democrats’ generic ballot lead, Dr. El-Sayed could carry Michigan in November. A useful way to de-escalate factional tensions would be for people like Mr. Sanders to acknowledge that the bar for proving their case that leftists can teach Democrats how to win is higher than narrowly winning in a favorable cycle. Can he beat Ms. Slotkin’s performance by the eight points suggested by the national swing? Can he outperform Roy Cooper and Mary Peltola by amounts that account for Michigan’s bluer partisan lean than North Carolina or Alaska? It’s fair to have a debate about the best direction of the party, but that debate should be conduced on honest terms.

Matthew Yglesias (@mattyglesias), a contributing Opinion writer, is the author of “One Billion Americans: The Case for Thinking Bigger” and writes at the newsletter Slow Boring.

Fled to America at 11. Stole at 18. Deported to Vietnam at 44.

The New York Times August 06, 2026

In 1993, Mong Tran came to the United States as an 11-year-old refugee from Vietnam.

In 2004, the United States wanted to deport her after she committed a crime. But Vietnam would not accept her, and she stayed, building a life with her husband and children.

The Trump administration recently deported her. Now she, like hundreds of other Southeast Asian refugees, is living in a country she barely knows.

Supported by

The Trump administration is sending back record numbers of Vietnamese, Laotians and Hmong. Many came to the United States as young war refugees and later committed crimes.

By Amy Qin and Albert Sun

Thousands of Southeast Asians, many of them long spared from deportation since the end of the Vietnam War, are being sent back as part of a Trump administration push.

As of early March, Immigration and Customs Enforcement had deported more than 1,200 people to Vietnam and 400 to Laos, far more than in the past three presidential terms combined, according to a New York Times analysis of official records released by the Deportation Data Project.

Among them is Mong Tran.

Born in Vietnam, she arrived in the United States in 1993 as an 11-year-old after living in a refugee camp in the Philippines. Her family settled in Fairfax, Va.

But at 18, she upended her life, stealing thousands of dollars from her workplace, a doctor’s office. She ended up serving four months in jail and losing her permanent residency status.

Normally, she would have been quickly sent back to her home country. But Vietnam and Laos had long refused to take refugees back. And the United States did not aggressively press the issue, even for those who had committed serious felonies — partly in recognition of America’s involvement in the Vietnam War and other regional conflicts that had displaced these refugees in the first place.

But the Trump administration, in both its first and second terms, has pressured Vietnam, Laos and other countries into accepting more deportees.

Ms. Tran, 44, was sent back last November. She left behind her husband, four children and a nail salon business. Her record was otherwise clean, said her lawyer, Vicky Dobrin.

Now in a country she barely knows, Ms. Tran, who also goes by the name Melissa, is living with distant relatives outside Ho Chi Minh City.

Her husband and children remain in Hagerstown, Md.

“Although this is the country where I was born,” she said in an interview, “I don’t feel like it’s home.”

The Trump administration’s aggressive deportation push has revived a painful question about America’s historical obligation to these Southeast Asian refugees. Should those who fled here decades ago as children and committed crimes — including nonviolent offenses — be subject to permanent exile?

There are an estimated 15,000 Southeast Asian refugees in the United States with final removal orders.

Like Ms. Tran, many of these deportees fought or had parents who fought alongside U. S. troops, endured years in Communist re-education camps or fled the chaotic aftermath of the fall of Saigon. They came legally as refugees when they were children and have called America home for decades.

But compared to the broader deportee population, these Southeast Asian deportees were much more likely to have a past criminal conviction, the data shows. And the 400 or so Vietnamese deportees who entered before 1995 all had past criminal convictions. Their crimes range in severity, from check fraud to homicide, which are grounds for revoking green cards.

Some lawmakers and immigrant groups point out that most served their sentences and were then left in limbo for years, even decades, because of diplomatic reasons beyond their control. And, they note, some people facing imminent deportation were born in refugee camps elsewhere and have never been to their home countries. Others have faint memories, and English is the only language they speak fluently.

To deport them decades later, advocates argue, is effectively a second punishment.

“We have laws against double jeopardy,” said ThaoMee Xiong, executive director for the Coalition of Asian American Leaders, a nonprofit based in Minnesota.

The Trump administration has argued that expelling criminals is necessary to maintain the rule of law and protect the safety of Americans.

“Every single illegal alien removed on these flights had full due process,” said the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees immigration enforcement, in a statement. The department credited President Trump’s “strong leadership” for convincing the Southeast Asian countries to take back the deportees.

Some supporters of immigration enforcement also say that the United States has already repaid these refugees by resettling them and offering pathways to citizenship.

“These individuals have already been accorded significant grace by the United States,” said Matthew O’Brien, deputy executive director at the Federation for American Immigration Reform, which lobbies for curbing immigration. “Does that mean that the United States is also obligated to turn a blind eye to criminal behavior?”

Between 1975 and the late 1990s, more than 1.3 million refugees from Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia were resettled across the United States, in what was the largest humanitarian resettlement initiative in modern U. S. history.

Once in the United States, adults, with little schooling or savings, often scraped out a living in low-paying jobs. Many resettled with their children in high-crime neighborhoods.

Mark Phommachanh was 5 when he and his mother landed in the United States from Laos around 1980. They eventually settled in Fresno, Calif., which later experienced high crime rates related to crack cocaine.

“I became part of a gang, to protect myself and to kind of find my own family,” he said.

Mr. Phommachanh said that like many refugees at the time, his mother, who worked full time at a doughnut shop, did not realize the advantages of acquiring citizenship. Most thought that permanent residency was all they needed.

In 2003, Mr. Phommachanh was in the process of applying for citizenship when he was arrested on charges of trafficking marijuana. In 2006, after serving more than three years in prison, he was ordered deported. Laos would not take him, and he was allowed to remain on supervised release.

The number of deportations of Southeast Asian refugees remained low over the years, until Mr. Trump’s first term, when deportations increased significantly.

But the Trump administration still faced obstacles.

The Laotian and Vietnamese governments continued to resist pressure to take back large numbers of people with old removal orders like Mr. Phommachanh.

Vietnam in particular had long refused to accept people who first entered the United States before 1995, seeing them as more likely to be loyal to the former South Vietnamese government. On the U. S. side, there was also widespread criticism, including from the U. S. ambassador to Vietnam, who resigned from the State Department in protest.

But in 2020, at the end of the Trump administration, U. S. officials quietly reached a new agreement with Vietnam to allow the deportation of people who first entered the United States before 1995. The agreement laid the groundwork for Mr. Trump’s second-term deportation campaign.

Since last year, the administration has deported more than 400 people in this pre-1995 group to Vietnam. Under the first Trump administration, only 26 people in this group were sent back over four years.

Laos, too, has been accepting deportees in much greater numbers during the second Trump administration.

Mr. Phommachanh was working as a manager at an R. V. company in Virginia last fall when he learned that immigration authorities wanted to see him, even though he had just had his annual check-in.

“I was out shopping for steaks to grill for me and my wife, and I just dropped everything,” Mr. Phommachanh, 51, recalled in an interview.

In November, he was deported to Laos. He considers himself one of the lucky ones. So far, he has been able to live off savings. And his wife, who had never traveled abroad until she recently came to visit, plans to join him. He documents his new life in Vientiane, the capital city, on YouTube.

Other deportees have had a much harder time, said Chanida Phaengdara Potter, director of ROOTS Laos, which helps people resettle in Laos. Separated from their families, some have struggled to find jobs or medical care. Depression is common.

“There’s a lot of uncertainty and isolation,” Ms. Potter said. “America was supposed to be their safe haven.”

Some refugees facing imminent deportation have found ways to stay by applying for state-level pardons or reopening their old criminal cases. But for most, the options are limited.

Ms. Tran is trying to adjust to her new life in Vietnam.

She is studying Vietnamese while working toward her English teaching certification. She plans to learn how to ride a motorbike for local transportation. She talks to her family every day and helps her younger children, ages 11 and 8, with their homework via FaceTime.

But she is up at night. She worries about her husband, Danny, who now has to run the nail salon on his own while solo parenting. She worries about her daughter Rachel, who recently paused her undergraduate studies because of stress from the deportation. And there is Jacob, her son with autism.

“For the last 20 years, I tried to be a better person and teach my children that there are always consequences,” Ms. Tran said. “But being apart from them now, that’s the hardest part for me to accept.”

As part of my beat covering Asian Americans, I’ve been looking into the recent surge in deportations to Southeast Asia. I learned in my reporting that decades ago, the United States saw its resettlement of more than 1 million Southeast Asian refugees as a moral obligation for its role in the Vietnam War. Now, the Trump administration’s push to deport many of these Southeast Asian refugees who committed crimes is resurfacing that chapter of history.

Kitty Bennett contributed research.

Amy Qin is a national correspondent for The Times, writing primarily about Asian American communities.

Albert Sun is a data reporter and graphics editor at The Times who covers immigration.

How Fauci Got to This Point and the Legal Peril He Faces

The New York Times August 06, 2026

Fauci Contempt Vote

Advertisement

Supported by

The case is unique, legal scholars say, because of the tension between the Fifth Amendment and the reach of a presidential pardon. The potential consequences could be grave.

By Jan Hoffman

Health reporter

A Senate committee voted Thursday to hold Dr. Anthony S. Fauci, the scientist who led the country’s Covid response, in contempt of Congress for declining to answer questions during a hearing last week.

Dr. Fauci invoked his constitutional right under the Fifth Amendment to remain silent, refusing to respond to a single question during the three-hour session of the Senate Homeland Security Committee. Republicans on the panel, led by the chairman, Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky, say that he is ineligible for Fifth Amendment protection. The reason, they say, is that President Joseph R. Biden Jr. granted him an unconditional pardon for public service actions during a period that includes the pandemic.

Many people, including Trump administration officials, and even the president himself, have invoked the Fifth Amendment. But the case is unique, legal scholars say, because of the tension between the reach of a presidential pardon and that of the Fifth Amendment.

The potential consequences could be grave for Dr. Fauci. Here are some things to know.

Almost immediately after President Trump was elected to a second term in 2024, Republicans vowed to pursue several prominent figures, among them Dr. Fauci, the government’s top infectious disease expert, for his management of the pandemic. On his last day in office, Mr. Biden issued Dr. Fauci, and others, an unconditional “pre-emptive pardon” that protects him from federal prosecution for his actions from 2014 through Jan. 19, 2025.

There were many pandemic-related issues that senators sought to explore. They accused Dr. Fauci of funding research that led to the creation of the coronavirus and of lying to Congress about it under oath, allegations that Dr. Fauci has long denied. They sought to hold him responsible for school lockdowns, masking and vaccine mandates, and other Covid-era restrictions imposed by states, communities and employers.

This is the question at the heart of the legal debate.

Republican senators on the committee contend that because Dr. Fauci had a presidential pardon, he was already protected: By refusing to answer their questions, he had effectively violated their subpoena of him. “You don’t have any rights under the Fifth Amendment because you’ve been pardoned, as you very well know,” Senator Josh Hawley, Republican of Missouri, told Dr. Fauci at the hearing.

Legal scholars say the issue is not that clear.

Jonathan Turley, a constitutional law expert at George Washington University Law School, said that the impact of pardons on a witness’s ability to invoke the Fifth was “murky,” noting that there is little case law on the issue.

“There are good-faith arguments that his pardon would afford him effective immunity,” rendering Dr. Fauci ineligible for the Fifth Amendment protection, Mr. Turley said in an interview. He noted that there were also claims that Dr. Fauci’s opening statement could be construed as waiving his Fifth Amendment privilege, negating the cloak of immunity granted by the pardon itself.

Other scholars maintain that Dr. Fauci’s invocation of the Fifth was proper because he was legally vulnerable. His pardon period ended roughly 18 months before the Senate hearing, from which fresh, contemporaneous charges could have emerged. Mr. Paul has said for years that Dr. Fauci belongs in prison.

Pleading the Fifth Amendment is an acceptable strategy, “given the pretext of the investigation, which is that they are looking for a way to put him in jail, and given the president’s own track record of vindictive prosecutions,” said Kimberly Wehle, a professor at the University of Baltimore School of Law who is an expert on the pardon power.

In his opening statement to the committee, Dr. Fauci essentially said he believed that the purpose of the hearing was to capture evidence against a preselected defendant.

If the committee wanted frank testimony and a full exploration of unresolved pandemic questions, senators could have offered him limited or full immunity covering the testimony, a number of law experts said.

Not doing so “debunks their claim that he’s completely protected by presidential pardon,” said Representative Jamie Raskin, Democrat of Maryland, who is a constitutional law professor. “It’s only because they imagine that he can still be prosecuted that they wouldn’t offer him immunity.”

Yes. The presidential pardon applies only to federal prosecutions, not those brought by states. The Fifth Amendment applies to both.

Shortly after Dr. Fauci refused to testify last week, officials in Alabama, Louisiana and Florida vowed to commence state investigations against him.

Mr. Paul said he will send the resolution directly to federal prosecutors, bypassing a full Senate vote. They could convene a grand jury and seek an indictment. If they succeeded, Dr. Fauci would be charged with the misdemeanor of criminal contempt, for which a conviction could result in fines and a prison sentence of up to a year.

A Federal District Court judge in the District of Columbia would decide whether the case should go forward, a ruling likely to address whether Dr. Fauci was entitled to plead the Fifth.

Many scholars predict the case will end there, if not sooner.

Professor Turley, who maintains that the impact of Dr. Fauci’s actions and the many entries in his diary raise questions about his thinking that should have resulted in a robust hearing, believes that courts are more likely to side with Dr. Fauci’s right to invoke the Fifth. But, he said, “having the right to do something does not make it the right thing to do.”

Professor Wehle also thinks Dr. Fauci will prevail, in part because the Fifth Amendment was intended to shield witnesses against overbearing government prosecution.

If a court did say that Dr. Fauci could not claim the Fifth, she said, the precedent would be truly upending.

“That would say you take the Fifth at your own risk of going to jail,” she said. “And that turns the Fifth Amendment upside down.”

Sheryl Gay Stolberg contributed reporting.

Jan Hoffman is a health reporter for The Times covering drug addiction and health law.

Drought Threatens a Vital Economic Artery in the Heart of Europe

The New York Times August 06, 2026

The Rhine conveys vessels and cargo that power European industry. Record low water levels are disrupting supply chains, adding costs and presenting fresh risks to growth.

The wreck of a fishing boat that sunk in 1996 is one of several long-submerged relics exposed by low water levels. Credit...

Supported by

By Christopher F. Schuetze and Patricia Cohen

Photographs and Video by Patrick Junker

Christopher F. Schuetze reported from the harbor in Duisburg, Germany. Patricia Cohen reported from London.

Ferocious heat waves, wildfires and freakish storms have pulverized Europe this summer. Now a series of droughts, magnified by climate change, have crippled some of the continent’s key waterways, bringing further economic pressure on a region struggling with stagnating growth and fierce global competition.

One center of the crisis is the “wide and winding Rhine” river, as Lord Byron put it, which stretches nearly 800 miles through six countries as it journeys from the Swiss Alps to the North Sea.

This vital economic artery conveys thousands of vessels and millions of tons of cargo a year that stoke trade and industry throughout the continent.

“It’s one of the most important heart chambers of the German economy,” said Carsten Brzeski, global head of macro research at ING, as well as a devoted rower.

This week, water levels hit their lowest point since 1880, when official measurements were first recorded, disrupting supply chains, raising shipping costs and possibly forcing companies to scale back on production.

The New York Times

The wave of extreme weather is also affecting the Danube, the second longest river in Europe, where record low water levels are exposing the previously hidden hulks of warships sunk during World War II.

That water crisis is forcing a scramble to keep electricity flowing in Hungary and Romania, which use water from the Danube to cool nuclear power reactors. Governments in both countries have appealed to households and businesses to reduce their power use.

The ripple effects of low water levels on the economy can be seen in Duisburg, Germany, where goods were being moved from bigger ships onto smaller ships, rail cars or trucks. Other boats have unloaded as much as two-thirds of their cargo so they can safely navigate the river, which at some points has a depth of little more than four feet of water.

“Now you see who is a good captain and who is a bad captain,” said Wilma van Ingen, part of a Dutch husband-and-wife team that brought the 564-foot push freighter, W. De Beijer Sr, up from Rotterdam carrying iron ore.

Her ship, which can normally carry 5,000 tons, has been reduced to carrying just 1,200 tons.

Fewer loads mean heavier traffic.

“We are working at our limit,” said Markus Bangen, the chief executive of Duisburg harbor, which processes some 100 million tons of a cargo a year and handles more than 20,000 ships a year.

The Rhine shaped the geography of Germany’s industrial might as companies built their factories and trading routes along its shores. Titans of German manufacturing — BASF, Mercedes-Benz, Bayer and ThyssenKrupp — are along the route.

Nearly 300 million tons of cargo are carried by its waters each year. The Rhine connects the North Sea port of Rotterdam to three of Germany’s largest industrial clusters, linking oil refineries, steel and chemical factories, coal-fired power plants and more along the way.

It would require as many as 100 trucks or an entire freight train to transport the cargo from a single river barge, Mr. Brzeski of ING said. But even substitutions are complicated. “The railways are a disaster as well,” he added. And at the moment, construction work means one of the routes that runs along the river is not available.

A punishing drought in 2018 shuttered factories and ended up shaving 0.3 percent off Germany’s overall output at the time, according to analysts.

The experience, though, prompted industry and officials to be more nimble, said Jens Schwanen, the director of the Federal Association of German Inland Navigation, an industry group.

“We cannot make water magically appear,” he said.

Instead, companies have adapted. They have gotten better planning for times when water levels run low. They have built more storage space in deep water ports, so goods can continue to be delivered even when waterways run dry. This has been a strategy of Siemens Energy, whose 300-ton turbines are so bulky they cannot be transported by rail or road.

There has also been a move to build ships that travel higher in the water, using different materials and wider designs.

Big propellers, though more efficient, stop working in shallow water. So some new designs feature multiple smaller propellers or special encasements that protect propellers from riverbeds.

“It’s good to see that the measures are working,” said Mr. Bangen, the Duisburg harbor chief. “We’re in a much better position than we were eight years ago.”

But the upgrades are slow. Of the nearly 8,000 cargo ships plying the Rhine, only about a dozen have been designed to handle low water levels.

And slower traffic, lighter loads and alternate routes cost more. Consumers in Germany whose petrol is shipped on the river are paying as much as 11 cents more per liter, according to the German cartel office.

An analysis by the Kiel Institute for the World Economy, a German research center, concluded: “Low water levels lead to severe disruptions in inland water transportation and cause a significant and economically meaningful decrease of economic activity.”

After a month of low water, “industrial production in Germany declines by about 1 percent,” Kiel found.

That’s quite a lot in a country that “for a prolonged period of time has been stagnating rather than growing in any significant way,” said Stefan Kooths, a research director at Kiel.

Shipping crises outside of Europe’s borders have also battered the region’s economies. The war in Iran and disruption of trade and energy deliveries through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab Strait have pushed up oil prices and fed inflation.

Concerns about rising prices caused by the conflict prompted the European Central Bank to raise interest rates in June.

At the same time, Europe is essentially fighting two trade wars: one with China, over a flood of cheap goods, and a second with the United States over a range of tariffs.

The forces of geopolitics and geography are both taking their toll, with more to come. Less snowfall in the alps during the winter months caused lower river levels this summer. The drought now means there is less rain flowing into the river. The heat has made things worse, causing surface water to evaporate and lowering water levels at a very early point in the season.

And more baking weather without rain is expected in the coming weeks.

Christopher F. Schuetze is a reporter for The Times based in Berlin, covering politics, society and culture in Germany, Austria and Switzerland.

Patricia Cohen writes about global economics for The Times and is based in London.

Moderate Democrats Prepare for ‘War’ Against an Ascendant Left

The New York Times August 06, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

One moderate group says the progressive wins are “deeply troubling” and is planning a $15 million effort against democratic socialism.

By Shane Goldmacher

Shane Goldmacher is a national political correspondent who has been covering the Democratic Party’s efforts to win back power in 2026.

The embattled establishment of the Democratic Party searched furiously for a political reset after Dr. Abdul El-Sayed’s progressive victory in Michigan handed the party’s long-dominant moderate wing its most painful defeat of the year.

Some strategists urgently pressed to adopt a sharper edge to tap into the fury among Democratic voters that was felling its centrist candidates. Others wanted to attack democratic socialism, undercutting a budding movement now set to have far more than a toehold in the next Congress. Yet another young democratic socialist ousted an incumbent congressman in Detroit on Tuesday.

“We are preparing for the next war that is coming,” said Jonathan Cowan, the president of Third Way, a leading centrist Democratic group, revealing to The New York Times a new $15 million effort between now and 2028 to discredit democratic socialism.

Dr. El-Sayed’s win was not the blowout that some pre-election polls had predicted. But his narrow nomination in one of the country’s signature swing states still represented a critical moment for the party’s middle, which had previously sought to cast the far left’s successes as contained within the country’s most urban and liberal corridors.

Their fear: Dr. El-Sayed was paving a path for a progressive to seize the party’s presidential nomination in 2028 — and then go on to lose the general election.

“It is deeply troubling to see radical, far-left candidates winning in places that are potentially presidential swing states,” Mr. Cowan added.

Most party leaders — from Gov. Gretchen Whitmer of Michigan to Senator Chuck Schumer of New York to former Vice President Kamala Harris — quickly embraced Dr. El-Sayed’s Senate candidacy, given the stakes of the Michigan seat at the play. But some moderates see the emerging left as a danger.

The fact that Democrats recently put Michigan in the early lineup of presidential nominating states — a race just 18 months away — only heightened the significance of Dr. El-Sayed’s victory.

For now, the next big test is only a week away. In Wisconsin, Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist and state assemblywoman representing the progressive hotbed of Madison, has emerged as the party’s front-runner for governor in another key battleground race.

Mr. Cowan said the $15 million his group would spend through 2028 was not directed at individual candidates. Instead, the group plans to target the Democratic Socialists of America movement, which he believes poses a “mortal danger” for Democrats.

He said the effort would include opposition research into D. S. A., polling, social media programs and educating Democratic activists and leaders. It would target both proud democratic socialists and those such as Dr. El-Sayed, whom he derided as performing the “D. S. A. dodge” — flirting with democratic socialists enough to get their organizing manpower and support while remaining distant enough to avoid the explicit label.

How this discrediting campaign will affect the current midterm cycle — potentially undercutting Democratic nominees in swing-state races and undermining the party’s chances of retaking Congress — remains unclear.

Centrist Democrats say their purpose is to make progressives understand the risks of some of the more radical planks of the official D. S. A. platform: defunding the Department of War, taking “steps toward fully abolishing the police and prison system,” enacting “reparations” and establishing a 32-hour workweek.

“The upside of being associated with more extreme movements is you get attention and real and perceived energy and outsider status,” said Liam Kerr, the co-founder of another centrist group called Welcome PAC.

Mr. Kerr said that the far left was currently receiving all of those benefits without “the baggage” of particular positions — a dynamic he hoped would shift with added attention.

On Wednesday, one progressive Democrat who won his party’s House nomination distanced himself from the D. S. A. Will Lawrence, a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement who defeated two more moderate Democratic rivals in Michigan on Tuesday, said he allowed his D. S. A. membership to lapse in the last month. Mr. Lawrence, 35, now faces a Republican incumbent, Representative Tom Barrett, in one of the country’s premier battleground districts.

Whatever comes next, Dr. El-Sayed’s triumph was a watershed moment for the progressive movement, a statewide success in Middle America that could not easily be dismissed. This was not Zohran Mamdani’s win over Andrew Cuomo in New York City, or a congressional primary win in Manhattan, Brooklyn, Philadelphia or Denver.

After all, the party establishment had the one-on-one race it had wanted against Dr. El-Sayed. The state’s Democratic governor delivered a late endorsement of Representative Haley Stevens, the moderate alternative. And Ms. Stevens enjoyed a gargantuan advertising advantage that swelled into the tens of millions of dollars.

More than $32 million of that money came from a super PAC linked to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, which signaled that it would continue opposing Dr. El-Sayed through the fall.

Dr. El-Sayed has made running against AIPAC a centerpiece of his candidacy. On MS NOW on Wednesday, he said the links between Israel and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu were “inextricable.”

“Netanyahu is a big reason why they’ve gotten so aggressive and, frankly, so bloodthirsty under his reign,” Dr. El-Sayed said.

Progressives have not won every race this year. On Tuesday, Cori Bush, a left-wing former congresswoman, lost badly in her bid to win back her old seat.

But they have won convincingly in enough places — including Graham Platner’s Senate nomination in Maine before his withdrawal — to put the party’s establishment on its heels.

“The Democratic Party is now Blockbuster,” Van Jones, the Democratic commentator and former Obama administration official, said on CNN on Tuesday. “These kids are Netflix.”

Colin Mortimer, the director of the centrist Center for New Liberalism, said that moderates needed to stop tempering their tone to appeal to voters sick of the status quo.

“It seems to me a lot of energy is on the left, but the big energy we are seeing from the base of the Democratic Party is just a rejection of the establishment and a rejection of incumbents,” Mr. Mortimer said.

He pointed to some upcoming races as key tests where it was younger center-left candidates doing the challenging of older incumbents, including the bid of Representative Seth Moulton, a moderate, to unseat Senator Ed Markey in Massachusetts, as well as Luke Bronin’s challenge to Representative John Larson of Connecticut.

Maurice Mitchell, the national director of the progressive Working Families Party, sharply disagreed.

“They’re missing the plot,” Mr. Mitchell, who spent the last week campaigning in Michigan, said in an interview. “There is a populist insurgency taking place in this country.”

Moderates, he said, were misreading the room if they did not believe voters were animated by specific ideas as much as tenor. “I can tell you what they’re missing,” he said. “They’re missing a point of view.”

Or as Hasan Piker, the lightning rod live-streamer who campaigned in Michigan with Dr. El-Sayed, said in a text message on Wednesday, “70 million dollars worth of smears couldn’t make up for a lack vision demonstrated by the establishment dems.”

With a signature fitted V-neck black T-shirt, Dr. El-Sayed built his successful campaign with a call-and-response set of catchphrases that captured the scope of his ambitions: “Money out of … politics. Money in your … pocket. Medicare for … all.”

Some Democratic strategists hoped he would focus, in particular, on the second of the three in the coming months as polls show that voters are ready to punish President Trump and his party for failing to bring down cost.

Republicans appeared most eager to frame the race around crime, linking Dr. El-Sayed to past movements and comments about defunding the police or prisons. Chris Gustafson, a spokesman for the top Senate Republican super PAC, previewed that line of attack, calling Dr. El-Sayed “a dangerous threat to the safety and freedoms of every American.”

The contours and coalitions of the Stevens-El-Sayed primary are likely to provide a road map for progressives who decide to run for president. Dr. El-Sayed campaigned with Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez — and featured them both prominently in his closing ad.

The Senate primary was not the first time that Michigan opted for a left-wing candidate in a marquee contest. In 2016, the state delivered an upset win for Mr. Sanders in his presidential primary against Hillary Clinton, who went on to lose Michigan that November to Mr. Trump.

The Michigan Senate race of 2026 was already a must-win for Democrats if they hope to wrest control of the Senate from Republicans this fall. At the same time, for Mr. Schumer, Dr. El-Sayed would add to the ranks of Democrats opposed to him as a leader.

It is also a must-win for progressives aspiring to prove they can succeed not just in primaries but also in crucial and competitive general elections.

For now, the party’s moderate wing was hoping to learn lessons after a painful defeat.

“Necessity is the mother of invention,” Mr. Kerr said. “It’s a tough but necessary time.”

Shane Goldmacher is a Times national political correspondent.

Alcohol. Manliness. Flushable Wipes. Since When Are These ‘Scams’?

The New York Times August 06, 2026

Supported by

on language

It’s a young word with obscure origins. But the fact that it’s so common shows just how ubiquitous fraud seems today.

By Nitsuh Abebe

The word “scam” keeps getting more expansive.

I used to see it as suggesting some element of fraud: A specific bad actor is materially misrepresenting a transaction in order to take advantage. But that may be a bit old-fashioned. Take the phrase “alcohol is a scam,” which is widespread enough online to qualify as a meme. “Once you realize that alcohol is a scam, everything changes,” writes the podcast host Nicole Behnam; liquor is advertised with images of happiness, prestige and sophistication, “but the misuse of alcohol actually diminishes and ultimately destroys those qualities if you drink enough.” It’s “the biggest scam ever,” writes a life coach named Gretchen Kamp: “We are told” that drinking makes us glamorous and connected, but those lies once turned her into “the alcohol industry’s perfect sucker.”

You might resist this usage. Alcohol isn’t phony! It reliably affects consumers in the way they expect. It has its negative impacts on the body and on society; advertisers, naturally, emphasize the aspects that people enjoy. We have access to plenty of information about both. Someone might fairly conclude that drinking is a terrible choice, or an insidious cultural habit we should resist — but is that a “scam?”

This slippage isn’t limited to alcohol. On Reddit, somebody posts a pet peeve: customer reviews that call unsatisfying products scams. For this person, “scam” implies real deception, false advertising — not just “something that cost more than you think it’s worth.” (I tend to notice this too: These shoes are a scam. The soles wore out in barely a year of daily wear.) Elsewhere on the site, someone asks which product is “basically a huge scam but people keep buying it anyway.” Answers include bottled water, flushable wipes and insurance.

The American public has been taken with scams and scammers for years now, a fascination that swelled during the first Trump presidency — the era of Anna Delvey and the Fyre Festival, “Joanne the Scammer” and N. F. T. s, when people began to see a steadily larger share of American life as some kind of racket. Attention, though, still focused on specific characters and events, concrete grifts Hulu could make documentaries about. Now it embraces whole broad concepts. The comedian and writer Alex Falcone, for instance, makes a series of short internet videos called “Is It a Scam? Yep,” in which he explains the deception and advantage-taking embedded in all sorts of things, including the Hollywood Walk of Fame (stars are actually just purchased), computer progress bars (not reflective of actual progress, just there to placate you), Bass Pro Shops (exploit subsidies and tax incentives to build stores), manliness (lets powerful people convince you to suffer) and white chocolate (no cocoa solids, “for people whose tongues are broken”).

This version of “scam” isn’t just carelessness or hyperbole; there’s an argument embedded in it. “I am using it more liberally than I think other people do,” Falcone told me. “On purpose, because I think it’s funny. But to me, it’s any time you’re getting money from somebody using dishonesty.” He likes to apply the concept in places viewers may not have considered it, “finding a thing that you didn’t realize was tricking you.”

Falcone has noticed others doing something similar: using “scam” for any system, however legitimate, that ends with somebody profiting at your expense. Taking “this thing that I know of as a scam, like someone on the street corner with a fake Gucci bag, and connecting that to the alcohol industry,” he says, “is a very edifying metaphor.” He suspects we’re near the peak of that metaphor’s usefulness and will eventually run it into the ground. But for now, calling a disappointing purchase a scam doesn’t especially bother him. If we’re expected to see through the puffery in corporate ads, he says, we can use the same media literacy on consumers’ responses: “This person is saying that the value is incorrect. Not that this company should be in jail — just, like, don’t buy this shoe at this price.”

Part of Falcone’s interest in scamming comes from a remarkable place. His grandfather, he says, was a pitchman with traveling carnivals before settling in Atlantic City, where he’d work the piers selling decks of cards rigged for magic tricks. This happens to be the source of the word “scam” itself: All we know for sure, etymologically, is that as of the early 1960s, it was carnival slang for fleecing the public. Beyond that, speculation runs wild. Is it related to “scamp” or “scamper” or “sham?” Does it come from British dialects that used it for “the impurities in rocks and minerals?” From Irish American criminal slang? From the French “escamoter” — to evade, or to conjure away? No theory seems to come with any real evidence. Beyond 20th-century carnies, all is mystery.

So if you’re inclined to set a high bar of deception before calling things scams, you don’t have much history to appeal to; it’s a young word with obscure origins. Others will use it liberally, metaphorically, for just about any phenomenon that feels extractive. They don’t care why a company is claiming tax breaks or switching sole materials — only that you’re being coaxed toward another transaction that leaves you with less and them with more.

In the meantime, Falcone is working on a book version of his “Is It a Scam? Yep” videos. The writing is done; he’s now working with his publisher to finesse a text that their lawyers describe as “having a lot of plaintiffs.” The semantics turn out to be important. “The liberal use of the word ‘scam,’ or the artistic use of it, doesn’t tickle the legal department the same way it tickles me,” Falcone says. “They see it as, like, a very specific accusation of fraud.”

Nitsuh Abebe is a story editor for the magazine.

Uvalde School Shooting

The incident, one of thousands of times that school officers in Texas have used physical force in recent years, underscores long-held concerns about policing in schools.

Judson High School in Converse, Texas. Credit... Meridith Kohut for The New York Times

Supported by

By Clare Amari

Photographs by Meridith Kohut

This article was reported in collaboration with The San Antonio Express-News as part of The Times’s Local Investigations Fellowship.

Officer Marc Laue was seething.

Minutes earlier, while patrolling the hallways of Judson High School in Converse, Texas, he had confronted a 15-year-old accused of pushing an assistant principal. The teenager, Jeremiah Johnson, cursed at the officer and walked away.

Officer Laue grabbed repeatedly at Jeremiah’s arms and backpack, body camera footage of the encounter shows. When the boy pushed away, the officer wrapped his arms around him and took him to the floor.

Now Jeremiah was handcuffed in the school’s cramped police office. As another officer tried to lower Jeremiah into a chair, Officer Laue rammed his fists into the boy’s belly.

“Sit the fuck down!” Officer Laue shouted.

Since 2022, when a gunman killed 21 people at Robb Elementary in Uvalde, Texas has spent billions of dollars installing police officers at public schools. Under state law, officers are supposed to stay out of “routine student discipline.” But over the past few years, they have used physical force in thousands of cases, including to stop seemingly minor misbehavior.

The incident at Judson High offers an extraordinary glimpse into a confrontation gone wrong. What makes it so unusual is that the student and the officer, as well as a teacher, discussed it with a reporter. The 33-minute episode, from November 2023, was also captured on body camera footage, which was reviewed by The New York Times and The San Antonio Express-News.

The case underscores a concern that has been raised by parents and advocates since schools began stationing law enforcement on their campuses: that officers might clash with vulnerable students, derailing their lives.

Ian Adams, a professor of criminology at the University of South Carolina who reviewed the footage for The Times and The Express-News, called it “horrific.” The way Officer Laue shoved his fists into Jeremiah, Mr. Adams said, went beyond the bounds of “normal policing.”

As Jeremiah folded into the chair, he gasped. “I can’t even breathe,” he said.

Officer Laue yelled at him to shut up, using an expletive. Then, he smacked Jeremiah on the side of the head.

That morning, Elizabeth De Alba, an assistant principal, contacted Officer Laue over her walkie-talkie. The two met up in a crowded hallway, his body camera footage shows.

“He pushed me,” she told the officer, pointing out Jeremiah, who was walking ahead of them in a black sweatshirt, his hood up.

Jeremiah grew up in a working-class neighborhood on the eastern edge of San Antonio. His parents used drugs, records show, so his great-aunt and -uncle, Debra and Calvin Johnson, adopted him when he was a toddler. They raised him alongside nine other children.

The Johnsons described Jeremiah as a quiet, serious child who sang in the choir at his family’s Pentecostal church. He enjoyed school, but struggled with his class work. In eighth grade, school officials determined he had a learning disability, records show.

Jeremiah liked typical teenage things: video games and action movies; teasing his sisters and doting on his baby niece. But by the time he enrolled at Judson High, he had been in several fights and was introduced to a gang by his older, biological brother.

He first crossed paths with Officer Laue in February 2023, when he was a freshman. The officer restrained him to keep him from fighting with another student, police records show. The next week, Officer Laue received a tip about two photos on social media that showed Jeremiah in a bedroom holding a gun, according to the records. Jeremiah had it for protection from a rival gang, he told a reporter in a recent interview.

Nine months later, Ms. De Alba accused Jeremiah, then a sophomore, of pushing her in the hallway. So Officer Laue navigated his way through a crowd of students to confront him, the footage shows.

The teenager met the officer with profane language and racial slurs.

Officer Laue told Jeremiah he was under arrest, and moved to cuff him. But the boy wrenched free, knocking the officer’s body worn camera to the ground.

Ms. De Alba, a former reserve police officer, picked it up. She filmed the struggle, holding the camera upside down.

Officer Laue, 6-foot-2 with a sturdy frame, kicked Jeremiah’s legs out from under him. The teenager, nearly as tall but thin, fell backward.

The officer straddled him; when a second officer arrived, they put Jeremiah in handcuffs and then hoisted him up.

They led the boy toward the school police office. “Let’s go,” Officer Laue said.

A few minutes later, Officer Laue stood over Jeremiah, berating him. He taunted him for crying. He told him he would go to jail and stay there.

“That’s your future,” Officer Laue said.

The episode inside the office was captured entirely on the second officer’s body camera. That officer, Richard Radziski, repeatedly urged his colleague to calm down. Five times, he raised his hand and signaled Officer Laue to stop. But the disparagement continued.

At one point, Officer Laue accused Jeremiah of assaulting a school administrator. Jeremiah insisted he had not, and urged him to check the school surveillance cameras.

“You think I believe you over her?” Officer Laue asked.

Jeremiah shook his head. “Of course you don’t,” he answered.

Officer Laue, then 41, had been working for the school district police department for two years. It was his first job in law enforcement, and like all new officers, he went through the police academy. He received the 20 hours of state-mandated training specific to school policing. (Texas’ training is half the minimum recommended by the National Association of School Resource Officers.)

Before policing, Officer Laue served in the U. S. Army. He enlisted in 2004, records show, and during his nine years of service he deployed twice to Iraq and once to Afghanistan. For a time after his discharge, he operated technical equipment in the West Texas oil fields.

In an interview earlier this year, Officer Laue told The Times and The Express-News that he had thought his military experience would give him an advantage in law enforcement. But initially, he found Judson High unnerving. The crowded hallways made him “a little agoraphobic,” he said.

Still, he enjoyed mentoring students. Some, he said, had even asked him to come to their graduations.

When asked about the incident with Jeremiah, Officer Laue said that he had “put pressure on his midsection” only to get him into the chair.

He acknowledged that he had been “riled up” in the office, but could not say why.

“I don’t get that mad very often,” he added.

Inside the school that day, word was spreading that Jeremiah had been tackled and handcuffed. His physical education teacher, Kirk Logan, raced to the school police office as soon as he heard.

On his mind was the history of violence between police officers and Black people like Jeremiah and himself, he said in an interview.

“I’m not going to let it get there,” he recalled thinking.

Mr. Logan had a friendly relationship with Jeremiah — they talked often about music, sports and making good choices. He had recently served on a school committee that drew up a set of disability accommodations for the teen, records show. Such Individualized Education Program documents, known as I. E. P. s, are used for many students in public schools.

Part of Jeremiah’s plan advised school employees to avoid “power struggles” and to let him cool down if he got upset. It is unclear if that document, which was finalized days before the incident, was provided to Officer Laue.

When Mr. Logan arrived in the school police office, Jeremiah rose from his chair, footage shows. He begged the teacher to call his mother.

“Sit down or I’ll put you down!” Officer Laue shouted.

Mr. Logan positioned himself between Jeremiah and the officer.

He cupped the back of Jeremiah’s head. “Hey, Jeremiah,” he said, touching his forehead to the boy’s. “I got you.”

Several minutes later, Ms. De Alba arrived and shared her account of what had happened: She said that she had caught Jeremiah skipping class and suspended him, and then he pushed her.

Jeremiah interrupted, saying he had not skipped class. “When did I push you?” he asked.

Officials for the Judson school district did not provide any surveillance footage of the interaction between Ms. De Alba and Jeremiah to The Times and The Express-News, saying its release would compromise campus security.

Ms. De Alba and Officer Radziski declined to comment for this article. Both still work for the school district, payroll records show.

Jeremiah was charged as a juvenile with assault and resisting arrest. The assault charge was later reduced to making a threat, court records show. He was put on probation, which was extended after he was caught smoking marijuana and repeatedly broke his evening curfew. At one point, he had to wear an ankle monitor, he said, which he hid under his pant leg around his classmates.

He stopped going to school last fall. Now 18, Jeremiah says he no longer hangs out with the boys in the gang. He spends his free time playing games on his phone and listening to songs by Lil Poppa and NBA YoungBoy, who rap about betrayal and feeling misunderstood.

He recently got a job washing dishes — a step toward getting his life together. He wants an apartment and to be able to support himself. More education may be in his future, but he does not plan to return to Judson High.

Since the episode with Officer Laue, he said, he has a visceral reaction to seeing police officers on the street. “I just go into shock,” he said.

His takeaway from what happened? Officers “show no mercy.”

Officer Laue said that he had been reprimanded for yelling at Jeremiah and ordered to take an anger management course. A district spokeswoman declined requests for an interview and did not respond to written questions about the encounter.

In an email, the spokeswoman said that the district “takes all matters involving student safety and student concerns seriously” and is “committed to continuously reviewing its practices.”

The only record in Officer Laue’s personnel file that the school district released was his resignation letter. He left a year and a half after the incident.

He told The Times and The Express-News that he did not like policing and that he is now an emergency medical technician. “It’s more of a feel-good profession,” he said. “I don’t have to be mean to people.”

The officer added that he had “nothing against” Jeremiah and hoped he was doing well.

After the arrest, he recalled, he watched surveillance footage of the interaction between the teenager and Ms. De Alba. Based on what he could see in that video, it appeared Jeremiah “might have brushed past her,” Officer Laue said.

“I wouldn’t have called that an assault,” he said.

Had he seen the footage before confronting Jeremiah, he said, he would have turned him over to a school administrator and declined to press criminal charges.

Looking back, he added, the whole situation could have unfolded a lot differently. “I wish we didn’t have an ugly day,” he said.

Asher Lehrer-Small contributed reporting. Kitty Bennett and Kirsten Noyes contributed research. Produced by Rumsey Taylor.

Clare Amari is a reporter covering law enforcement in Texas schools as part of The Times’s Local Investigations Fellowship.

Paxton and Talarico Offer Diverging Paths on Affordability

The New York Times August 06, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The candidates are seeking to win over voters with competing proposals on tax, housing and health care that are aimed at lowering household costs.

By Lauren McGaughy

Reporting from Allen and Arlington, Texas

Ken Paxton pitched his plan to make Texas more affordable in a Mexican restaurant crammed with people, working mostly off the cuff from a small, crumpled page of notes.

A day later, on Wednesday night, James Talarico read his plan from a teleprompter at an e-sports arena, under a large American flag and in front of a large crowd.

Both men want the same Senate seat. And both said during events in North Texas this week that the American dream had become too expensive.

With Mr. Talarico leading in some polls and Democrats chasing their first statewide win in Texas in more than 30 years, both campaigns have made affordability the centerpiece of the race. Mr. Paxton, a Republican and attorney general of Texas, would cut taxes. Mr. Talarico, a Democratic state representative, would raise wages and increase taxes on the wealthy.

Mr. Paxton’s plan centered on new tax deductions for second homes, medical bills and gym memberships.

Mr. Talarico’s plan proposed increasing wages, repealing billionaire tax cuts and canceling debt.

“We have an affordability crisis because we have a corruption crisis,” Mr. Talarico said onstage at the Esports Stadium Arlington, the former Arlington Expo Center, flanked by the words “NEW AMERICAN DREAM.” Blue lights shone into the crowd, which his campaign said topped 1,000 people.

He fixed his ire on billionaires and appealed to Republicans and Democrats alike to support his fight against a system he said was built to benefit the ultrawealthy. Mr. Talarico said he wanted to close tax loopholes and provide down payment assistance for first-time home buyers. He wanted an “all-of-the-above energy strategy” that included renewables and oil and gas. He also backed the A. I. dividend, the idea of providing direct payments for people who had lost income or opportunities because of artificial intelligence.

“Whether you’re a little more conservative or a little more progressive — we’re all getting screwed,” Mr. Talarico said.

At his kickoff event on Tuesday, Mr. Paxton told the few hundred supporters gathered in the special events space of Matt’s Rancho Martinez in Allen that he wanted a $25,000 tax deduction for health care costs. He also proposed a $5,000 tax deduction for “healthy living” spending on gym memberships or GLP-1 medications like Ozempic or Zepbound. He said he wanted to make it easier for people to buy first and second homes, with a $50,000 tax deduction for each.

The crowd whooped and hollered, fanning themselves in the hot, packed room.

“We have socialist Democrats like James Talarico who want to become a Texas senator,” Mr. Paxton said, “when he belongs in California.”

Mr. Talarico is not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America. He is not endorsed by the D. S. A., Priscilla Yeverino, the group’s communications director, confirmed. There are no D. S. A. candidates on the ballot in Texas.

That has not stopped Mr. Paxton, or his proxies, from leaning into that messaging. With Mr. Talarico ahead in some polls, and with a much larger war chest, Mr. Paxton hopes to sow doubt among moderates that his opponent is the candidate for them.

Mr. Talarico addressed the tactic in his speech.

“They’re going to claim we’re socialists, or communists, or whatever sounds scariest in a headline,” he said. “And we’ll say, ‘Is that the best you can do?’”

Economists from both parties said Mr. Talarico’s plan was solidly Democratic with a populist bent, and said Mr. Paxton’s tax deductions would not benefit many low-income Americans. They said the one thing that Mr. Paxton and Mr. Talarico agreed on — expanding the child tax credit — could cost trillions of dollars over the next decade.

Jessica Riedl, a budget and tax fellow with the Brookings Institution, said the two candidates’ plans were filled with “poll-tested” proposals she would have expected during campaign season.

“Both candidates are promising a free lunch,” said Ms. Riedl, who has advised Republican presidential candidates, “either with lower taxes or with more spending that can be funded by the top one percent.”

Jared Bernstein, the former chair of President Joe Biden’s Council of Economic Advisers, said Mr. Talarico’s plan had a mix of good “and less good” ideas. He applauded the Democrat for proposing ways to create more housing stock and to crack down on “tax cheats.”

But he, too, was not sold on how everyday Americans would benefit from repealing tax breaks for the top 1 percent.

Both Mr. Bernstein and Ms. Riedl criticized the Paxton plan as expensive and unhelpful to the neediest Americans. The Paxton campaign did not answer questions about how the plan would be financed.

“My take on his plan is that he helped a lot of people like himself,” Mr. Bernstein said, “and from what I can tell, he’s not the one who needs it.”

Lauren McGaughy is the Texas politics correspondent for The New York Times, writing about the ways that policymakers in the second largest state are changing lives for their citizens and influencing American politics.
